title: The Solar System
paras: The Sun is an ordinary star, a ball of hot gas about 1.4 million kilometers across, held together by its own gravity and powered by the fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core. It contains more than 99 percent of the mass of the Solar System. Everything else—planets, moons, asteroids, comets—is debris left from the cloud that formed it about 4.6 billion years ago.

The planets fall into two groups. The inner four are small and rocky: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. The outer four are large and gaseous or icy: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Pluto, once counted as a planet, is now classified as a dwarf planet, one of many icy bodies beyond Neptune.

Mercury is the smallest and closest to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere, a heavily cratered surface, and extreme temperature swings. Venus is similar to Earth in size but utterly different in condition. A thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide produces a runaway greenhouse effect. Surface temperatures exceed 460 degrees Celsius, and the pressure is about ninety times that at Earth’s surface. Probes that landed there survived only briefly.

Earth is the one planet known to have liquid water on its surface and life. Its Moon is unusually large relative to the planet. The leading account of the Moon’s origin is a giant impact early in the Solar System’s history, which threw debris into orbit that then gathered into the Moon. The Moon’s distance is about 384,000 kilometers, a figure first estimated reasonably by Greek astronomers and refined ever since.

Mars is smaller than Earth, cold, and thin-aired. Orbiters and rovers have mapped ancient river valleys, lakebeds, and minerals that form in water. Liquid water is not stable on the surface today. Ice exists at the poles and underground. Whether Mars ever had life remains open. No confirmed evidence has been found.

Jupiter is the largest planet, more massive than all the others combined. It is mostly hydrogen and helium, with a small rocky core. Its Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has persisted for centuries. Jupiter has dozens of moons. The four largest—Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto—were seen by Galileo in 1610. Io is volcanically active. Europa has a subsurface ocean under ice.

Saturn is known for its rings, which are made of ice and rock particles, mostly close to the planet. It too is a gas giant with many moons. Titan, the largest, has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane. Enceladus vents water from a subsurface ocean.

Uranus and Neptune are ice giants, smaller than Jupiter and Saturn, rich in water, ammonia, and methane ices as well as hydrogen and helium. Uranus rotates on its side. Neptune has the strongest winds in the Solar System. Both have ring systems and moons. Triton, Neptune’s largest moon, orbits backward and is geologically active.

Asteroids are rocky bodies, mostly between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy bodies from farther out. When a comet approaches the Sun, ice vaporizes and forms a tail. Meteorites that reach Earth are samples of these smaller bodies. Some are primitive material from the early Solar System. Their ages, measured by radioactive dating, confirm that the system formed about 4.56 billion years ago.

The planets were visited by robotic probes beginning in the 1960s. Every planet has now been studied at close range. Samples have been returned from the Moon, from asteroids, and from a comet. The picture that emerged is more varied than the one available in the 1980s, and still incomplete in its details. The formation process—a disk of gas and dust around a young star, grains sticking together, cores growing, gas giants capturing envelopes before the gas dispersed—is the working account. It fits the evidence from our system and from the disks now seen around other young stars.

title: The Structure of the Earth
paras: The Earth is not a uniform ball. It has layers, and the layers were inferred before they were directly sampled.

The outermost layer is the crust, thin and rigid. Under the oceans it is typically 5 to 10 kilometers thick. Under the continents it is thicker, often 30 to 50 kilometers. Below the crust is the mantle, a thick layer of hot rock that extends to about 2,900 kilometers depth. The mantle is solid but, over long times, flows slowly. At the center is the core, divided into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, both made mostly of iron with some nickel and lighter elements. The inner core is solid because the pressure is high enough to keep iron solid despite the temperature.

The evidence for these layers came first from earthquake waves. P-waves and S-waves travel at different speeds and behave differently at boundaries. S-waves do not travel through liquid. Their absence in certain paths showed that the outer core is liquid. The speeds and reflections mapped the boundaries. Later, the composition was constrained by the density required to match the Earth’s total mass and by the chemistry of meteorites, which sample the material from which the planet formed.

The crust is not fixed. It is broken into plates that move. The idea of continental drift was proposed in detail by Alfred Wegener in 1912. He noted the fit of the continents, the match of fossils and rock formations across oceans, and evidence of past climates. The mechanism was missing, and the idea was resisted. In the 1960s, seafloor spreading and plate tectonics supplied the mechanism. New crust forms at mid-ocean ridges. Old crust sinks at trenches. Continents are carried with the plates. The Atlantic is widening. The Pacific is shrinking in places. Earthquakes and volcanoes concentrate at the boundaries.

The Earth’s magnetic field is generated by motion in the liquid outer core. The field reverses at irregular intervals. Those reversals are recorded in the seafloor as it forms, providing a tape of the spreading. The field also shields the surface from much of the solar wind. Without it, the atmosphere would be more vulnerable to stripping.

The age of the Earth is about 4.54 billion years, measured from the oldest meteorites and from the oldest terrestrial minerals. The oldest known crustal rocks are younger, because the surface has been recycled. Zircon crystals from Australia are more than 4.3 billion years old and show that continental crust and liquid water existed early.

Heat inside the Earth comes from leftover heat of formation and from radioactive decay. That heat drives the mantle’s slow convection, which drives the plates, and it supplies the energy for volcanoes and for the magnetic field. The surface we live on is the cool, thin skin of a planet that is still geologically active.

title: Organic Molecules and Proteins
paras: Life is built from organic molecules—molecules based on carbon. Carbon atoms form stable bonds with each other and with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and other elements. They can make chains, rings, and branches of almost any length. No other element does this as readily under the conditions of a planet’s surface.

The simplest organic molecules are hydrocarbons, chains of carbon and hydrogen. Adding oxygen, nitrogen, or other atoms produces alcohols, acids, amines, and the rest of the vocabulary of organic chemistry. The same rules of bonding that govern a laboratory reaction govern the chemistry inside a cell. There is no separate vital chemistry. There is ordinary chemistry in a special setting.

Proteins are the workhorse molecules of life. They are chains of amino acids. Twenty amino acids are standard in the proteins of Earth life. The chain folds into a specific shape. The shape determines what the protein does. Some proteins are structural. Many are enzymes, catalysts that speed particular reactions by factors of millions or more. Without enzymes, the reactions of metabolism would be too slow to sustain life at ordinary temperatures.

The sequence of amino acids is specified by the gene. Change the gene, and in many cases you change the protein. The folding is determined by the sequence and by the cellular environment. Predicting the fold from the sequence was a long-standing problem. It is now largely solved for many proteins by computational methods trained on known structures. The experimental methods—X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy—still supply the reference structures.

Enzymes are specific. An enzyme that breaks down one sugar usually does not break down a different sugar. That specificity is why metabolism can be regulated. Pathways can be turned on or off by controlling the enzymes. Many drugs work by inhibiting a particular enzyme. The active site, the pocket where the reaction occurs, is the target.

Metabolism is the network of enzyme-catalyzed reactions that extract energy and build the molecules a cell needs. The central pathways—breaking down sugars, capturing energy in ATP, building amino acids and nucleotides—are shared across a wide range of life. The sharing is evidence of common ancestry. The variations are evidence of adaptation. A cell is a chemical system that maintains itself by running these pathways continuously, taking in fuel and exporting waste. Stop the flow, and the structure collapses.

title: The Cell
paras: The cell is the basic unit of life. Every organism is either a single cell or a collection of cells. The idea was established in the nineteenth century. It remains the foundation of biology.

Cells are of two broad kinds. Prokaryotic cells—bacteria and archaea—have no nucleus. Their DNA is in the cytoplasm. Eukaryotic cells—the cells of animals, plants, fungi, and protists—have a nucleus that holds the DNA, and they have other internal compartments. Mitochondria, which produce most of the cell’s usable energy, and chloroplasts, which carry out photosynthesis in plants and algae, were once free-living bacteria. They were taken in and became permanent. The evidence is their own DNA and the structure of their membranes.

A cell is bounded by a membrane made of lipids, with proteins embedded in it. The membrane controls what enters and leaves. Inside, the cytoplasm is crowded with molecules. It is not a bag of dilute solution. It is a dense, organized environment. In eukaryotic cells, an internal skeleton of protein filaments gives shape and moves cargo.

Cells reproduce by dividing. In prokaryotes the process is relatively simple. In eukaryotes, mitosis parcels the chromosomes so that each daughter cell receives a full set. Meiosis, used in sexual reproduction, halves the chromosome number so that fertilization restores it. Errors in these processes cause many genetic diseases and contribute to cancer.

The cell cycle is regulated. Checkpoints ensure that DNA is copied accurately and that the cell is ready to divide. Failures of regulation are a hallmark of cancer. Many cancer drugs target the machinery of division or the signals that drive it.

Cells communicate. They release signals, and they carry receptors that detect signals from other cells or from the environment. Development—the building of a body from a fertilized egg—is a conversation among cells, guided by genes that are turned on and off in sequence. The same genes appear in different animals, used in different combinations. A gene involved in building an eye in a fly has a relative involved in building an eye in a mouse. The parts were reused. The arrangements diverged.

Every cell alive today is the product of an unbroken sequence of divisions stretching back to the origin of life. The sequence is the deepest continuity in biology. Understanding the cell is understanding the unit in which that continuity is maintained.

title: The Human Body
paras: The body is a system of organs that maintain conditions compatible with the life of its cells. Temperature, acidity, salt balance, and the supply of oxygen and fuel are held within narrow ranges. The holding is called homeostasis. It is active. It costs energy. When it fails, illness follows.

Food supplies the energy and the building materials. Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins are broken down by digestion into sugars, fatty acids, and amino acids, which are absorbed and distributed. Vitamins and minerals are required in smaller amounts. Some, like vitamin C and the B vitamins, are cofactors for enzymes. Deficiency diseases—scurvy, rickets, beriberi—were traced to missing vitamins in the early twentieth century. The tracing was one of the clearest demonstrations that specific molecules have specific roles in the body.

Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin in red blood cells. The same protein that makes blood red binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. Carbon dioxide is carried back, mostly dissolved. The heart pumps the blood. The lungs exchange the gases. The system is simple in outline and finely regulated in practice. Exercise, altitude, and disease all change the demands. The body adjusts the rate of breathing and the output of the heart to match.

Hormones are chemical signals carried in the blood. Insulin, produced by the pancreas, regulates blood sugar. Thyroid hormone regulates metabolic rate. Sex hormones regulate reproduction and secondary characteristics. Growth hormone and others regulate growth and repair. The endocrine system and the nervous system are the two main communication networks. They overlap. Many signals are used by both.

The immune system distinguishes self from non-self and attacks the latter. It has an innate arm that responds quickly and broadly, and an adaptive arm that learns specific pathogens and remembers them. Vaccination is the deliberate use of that memory. Antibodies, produced by B cells, bind to specific targets. T cells kill infected cells or help coordinate the response. Autoimmune diseases occur when the distinction fails and the system attacks the body’s own tissues. Allergies occur when it overreacts to a harmless substance.

Aging, infection, injury, and genetic error are the main ways the system fails. Medicine is the attempt to restore or replace the failed function. Surgery, drugs, hormones, and, increasingly, cells and genes are the tools. The body is not a machine in the simple sense. It is a living system that repairs itself until it cannot. Understanding the repair, and its limits, is the practical face of physiology.

title: Motion and Newton’s Laws
paras: Aristotle held that every kind of matter has a natural place. Earthy things seek the center. Fire seeks the heights. An object out of its place moves toward it. Heavier objects, being more eager, fall faster. Forced motion requires a continuous push. Rest is the natural state.

The view lasted nearly two thousand years because it matched ordinary observation. Feathers fall slower than stones. A thrown stone eventually stops. The heavens move in circles while earthly things fall straight.

Galileo tested the claim about falling. He used inclined planes to slow the motion enough to measure with the tools he had. Balls of different weight rolled down the same plane in the same time. The distance covered increased with the square of the time. The acceleration was constant. In a vacuum, a feather and a metal ball fall together. Air resistance, not weight, explains the everyday difference.

Newton put the results into three laws. An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion continues in a straight line at constant speed, unless a force acts on it. Force equals mass times acceleration. For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Mass is the measure of inertia, the resistance to change in motion. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass. The two are proportional on Earth, but they are not the same thing. On the Moon the mass is unchanged and the weight is less.

Momentum is mass times velocity. In an isolated system it is conserved. When two objects collide, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after. Angular momentum is conserved in rotation. A spinning skater who pulls in her arms spins faster. The product of moment of inertia and angular speed stays constant.

Work is force times distance in the direction of the force. Energy is the capacity to do work. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Potential energy is the energy of position. In the absence of friction and other losses, mechanical energy is conserved. A pendulum converts kinetic to potential and back. Friction converts mechanical energy into heat. The first law of thermodynamics says that energy is never created or destroyed, only converted.

These laws are the foundation of classical mechanics. They describe the motion of planets, the flight of a baseball, and the structure of a bridge. They fail only at very high speeds, very strong gravity, or very small scales. In those regimes, relativity and quantum mechanics take over. For everything in between, Newton’s laws remain the working tools.

title: Gravitation
paras: Newton’s law of universal gravitation states that every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The same law that makes an apple fall keeps the Moon in orbit.

The Moon falls toward the Earth continuously. Its sideways velocity is high enough that it keeps missing. The orbit is the path of continuous free fall. The same description applies to every planet around the Sun and every satellite around its planet.

The gravitational constant was measured in the laboratory by Cavendish in 1798. With it, the mass of the Earth can be calculated from the acceleration of gravity at the surface. The Earth is not a perfect sphere. It bulges at the equator because it rotates. The equatorial radius is about 21 kilometers larger than the polar radius. The difference is small but measurable.

Escape velocity is the speed needed to leave a body’s gravitational field without further propulsion. From Earth’s surface it is about 11.2 kilometers per second. From the Moon it is lower. From a black hole it exceeds the speed of light, which is why nothing can leave.

Orbits can be circles, ellipses, parabolas, or hyperbolas, depending on the energy. Closed orbits are ellipses with the central body at one focus. This was Kepler’s first law, deduced from Tycho Brahe’s observations before Newton explained why. The period of an orbit depends on the size of the orbit and the mass of the central body. That relation is used today to weigh stars, planets, and black holes.

Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces, yet it dominates at large scales because it is always attractive and has infinite range. The other forces cancel or are short-ranged. General relativity refined the picture. Gravity is the curvature of spacetime. The predictions differ from Newton’s at high precision or near strong masses. For the Solar System and for most engineering, Newton’s inverse-square law is still accurate enough.

title: Heat and Thermodynamics
paras: Heat is the transfer of energy that raises the temperature of a body or changes its state. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules. The two are related but distinct. A large cold object can contain more thermal energy than a small hot one.

The kinetic theory of gases treats a gas as a collection of molecules in random motion. Pressure is the force from molecules striking the walls. Temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy. Boyle’s law (pressure times volume is constant at fixed temperature) and Charles’s law (volume is proportional to absolute temperature at fixed pressure) follow from the model. Absolute zero, about −273 degrees Celsius, is the temperature at which molecular motion would reach its minimum. It cannot be reached, but it can be approached.

Specific heat is the energy needed to raise the temperature of a given mass by one degree. Latent heat is the energy needed to change state without changing temperature—melting ice or boiling water. Water has a high specific heat and high latent heats. That is why it moderates climate and why sweating cools the body.

The first law of thermodynamics is the conservation of energy. Heat and work are both forms of energy transfer. The second law says that heat does not spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter one. Equivalently, the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. Entropy is a measure of disorder, or more precisely of the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic state. A gas expands into a vacuum because there are more ways for the molecules to be spread out than confined. The reverse is not impossible in principle, but it is so improbable that it is never observed.

Heat engines convert heat into work. They require a temperature difference. The efficiency is limited by the temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs. No engine can convert all the heat into work. That limit is not a matter of engineering. It is a consequence of the second law.

The same laws govern the cooling of a cup of coffee, the operation of a refrigerator, and the evolution of the universe. In an expanding universe, the total entropy increases. Local decreases are possible when energy is supplied from elsewhere. Life is such a local decrease. It maintains order by exporting disorder to its surroundings.

title: Light
paras: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium. It reflects from a smooth surface so that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. It refracts when it passes from one medium to another. The change in direction is described by Snell’s law. Lenses use refraction to focus light. Convex lenses converge rays. Concave lenses diverge them. The eye, the camera, the microscope, and the telescope are all applications of these rules.

White light is a mixture of wavelengths. A prism separates them into a spectrum. Each element produces a characteristic set of spectral lines when heated or when light passes through its vapor. Those lines are the fingerprints used to identify elements in the laboratory and in stars. The Doppler shift of the lines measures motion toward or away from the observer.

Light is an electromagnetic wave. It does not need a medium. The speed in vacuum is a constant, about 299,792 kilometers per second. Experiments designed to detect motion through a supposed ether, most famously the Michelson-Morley experiment, found no such effect. Special relativity took the constant speed of light as a postulate. Time and length are relative. Mass and energy are equivalent. The relation is \( E = mc^2 \).

Light also behaves as particles, called photons. The energy of a photon is proportional to its frequency. The photoelectric effect, in which light ejects electrons from a metal, is explained by that particle nature. The wave and particle descriptions are complementary. Neither is complete alone. Quantum mechanics is the framework that contains both.

Polarization, interference, and diffraction are wave effects. They are used in sunglasses, in holography, and in the measurement of molecular structure. The same light that carries information from distant galaxies also carries the signals in optical fibers. The physics is the same. The applications differ.

title: Electricity and Magnetism
paras: Electric charge comes in two kinds, called positive and negative. Like charges repel. Opposite charges attract. The force follows an inverse-square law, Coulomb’s law. Charge is conserved. It is quantized. The elementary unit is the charge of the electron or the proton.

A current is a flow of charge. In a metal wire the carriers are electrons. Resistance converts electrical energy into heat. Ohm’s law relates voltage, current, and resistance. Power is the product of voltage and current. Batteries convert chemical energy into electrical energy. Generators convert mechanical energy into electrical energy by moving conductors in magnetic fields.

Magnetism and electricity are two aspects of the same interaction. A moving charge produces a magnetic field. A changing magnetic field produces an electric field. Oersted showed that a current deflects a compass needle. Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field induces a current. Maxwell unified the two in a set of equations. Those equations predict that a changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field, and vice versa, and that the disturbance propagates as a wave at the speed of light. Light is that wave.

The Earth is a magnet. Its field is generated by motions in the liquid outer core. The field reverses at irregular intervals. It shields the surface from much of the solar wind. Compasses align with it. Birds and other animals use it for navigation.

Transformers change voltage by electromagnetic induction. Motors convert electrical energy into mechanical energy. The entire electrical grid rests on these principles. Alternating current is used for transmission because transformers can step the voltage up for long distances and down for use. Direct current is used in electronics and in some long-distance lines. The underlying physics is the same.

Semiconductors control the flow of charge with small signals. Transistors, diodes, and integrated circuits are built from them. The electronics of a computer and the power system of a city are different scales of the same electromagnetic interaction.

title: The Atom and the Nucleus
paras: Matter is made of atoms. The idea is ancient. The modern form began with chemistry. Elements combine in fixed proportions. Dalton’s atomic theory explained the proportions. The periodic table, organized by Mendeleev, arranged the elements by atomic weight and revealed families of similar properties. The arrangement is now known to follow atomic number, the number of protons in the nucleus.

Atoms are mostly empty space. The nucleus, containing protons and neutrons, is tiny and dense. The electrons occupy the outer regions. Rutherford’s scattering experiments showed the nuclear structure. Bohr’s model placed electrons in discrete energy levels. Quantum mechanics replaced the orbits with orbitals, regions of probability. The spectra of atoms are the transitions between those levels.

Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei. Alpha particles are helium nuclei. Beta particles are electrons or positrons. Gamma rays are high-energy photons. The half-life is the time for half of a sample to decay. It is characteristic of the isotope and independent of temperature or chemical form. Radioactive dating uses those clocks. Carbon-14 dates organic material up to about 50,000 years. Uranium-lead dates rocks billions of years old.

Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons. Some are stable. Some are radioactive. Artificial isotopes are produced in reactors and accelerators. They are used as tracers in medicine and in research.

Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus into lighter ones, releasing energy. It powers reactors and was used in the first nuclear weapons. Nuclear fusion joins light nuclei into heavier ones. It powers the Sun and the stars. Controlled fusion for power remains an engineering challenge. The physics is understood. The sustained, net-energy reaction on Earth is not yet routine.

The binding energy of the nucleus comes from the strong force. The mass of a nucleus is less than the mass of its separate protons and neutrons. The difference appears as energy, by \( E = mc^2 \). That is the source of nuclear energy. It is also the source of the energy released in the Sun. The same relation that appears in relativity governs the power of a star and the energy of a reactor.

title: The Circulation of the Blood and the Rise of Physiology
paras: For centuries the heart was thought to heat the blood and the blood was thought to move back and forth in the vessels. The lungs were thought to cool it. The idea came from the Greeks and was refined by Galen in the second century. It lasted more than a thousand years.

In 1628 William Harvey published a different account. He measured the volume of blood the heart pumps. The quantity was far too large for the blood to be made and consumed continuously. It had to circulate. He traced the path from the right side of the heart to the lungs, back to the left side, out to the body, and back again. The valves in the veins allow flow only toward the heart. The capillaries that complete the circuit were seen later, with the microscope.

Harvey’s method was quantitative. He counted and measured. The conclusion followed from the numbers. Physiology, the study of function, began to replace anatomy alone. The same approach was later applied to respiration, digestion, and the nervous system.

The blood carries oxygen, bound to hemoglobin, and nutrients. It carries waste. It carries hormones. The heart is a pump. The vessels are a closed system. The pressure is maintained by the heart and regulated by the vessels. High blood pressure damages the vessels and the organs they supply. Low pressure fails to deliver oxygen. The system is simple in outline and tightly regulated in practice.
The same quantitative habit that established circulation established the rest of modern physiology. Measure the input. Measure the output. Find the path. The method is still the one used today.

title: Spontaneous Generation and the Germ Theory
paras: For most of history it seemed obvious that life could arise from non-life. Maggots appeared in meat. Mice appeared in grain. The process was called spontaneous generation. It was accepted by Aristotle and by most writers after him.

Experiments gradually closed the claim. In the seventeenth century Francesco Redi showed that maggots did not appear in meat if flies were kept away. In the eighteenth century Lazzaro Spallanzani showed that broth, boiled and sealed, did not spoil. Critics said the sealing excluded a vital principle in the air. In the nineteenth century Louis Pasteur settled the question with flasks that had curved necks. Air could enter. Dust and microbes could not. The broth stayed clear. When the neck was broken, it spoiled. Life comes from life.

The same work opened the germ theory of disease. Specific diseases are caused by specific microorganisms. Robert Koch set the criteria: the organism must be found in the diseased host, grown in pure culture, produce the disease when introduced into a healthy host, and be recovered again. Those postulates identified the agents of anthrax, tuberculosis, cholera, and many others.

Vaccination uses the immune system’s memory. Edward Jenner showed that cowpox protected against smallpox. Pasteur developed weakened strains that protected against other diseases. Antibiotics, beginning with penicillin, kill or stop bacteria without killing the host. Viruses are not affected by antibiotics. They are stopped by the immune system, by vaccines, or by antiviral drugs.

The disproof of spontaneous generation did not close the question of how life began. It closed the claim that life arises readily and continuously under ordinary conditions. The origin of life is a separate problem, pushed back to the early Earth, where conditions were different and time was long.

title: Classification and the Tree of Life
paras: Aristotle listed hundreds of animals and grouped them. He noticed that the dolphin, though it looks like a fish and lives in the sea, breathes air and bears live young. He placed it with the mammals. The observation was correct. The principle was that structure and function matter more than habitat.

Carl Linnaeus, in the eighteenth century, gave the system its modern form. Every species receives a two-part name, genus and species. Species are grouped into genera, genera into families, families into orders, orders into classes, classes into phyla, phyla into kingdoms. The ranks are a filing system. They are useful for communication. They are not the deepest fact.

The deepest fact is descent. Darwin argued that the groups exist because of common ancestry. The tree of life is the diagram of that ancestry. Modern classification aims to make the groups reflect the branches of the tree. A group that includes an ancestor and all its descendants is monophyletic. Groups that do not are revised or abandoned.

The evidence is now molecular as well as anatomical. DNA sequences can be compared. The more similar the sequences, the more recent the common ancestor, in general. The comparisons have rearranged some branches. Birds are nested inside the dinosaurs. Fungi are closer to animals than to plants. The three domains—Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya—replace the older two-kingdom or five-kingdom schemes.

The number of described species is on the order of two million. The total number of species alive today is estimated in the millions more. Most are insects, microbes, and other small organisms. Extinction removes branches. Speciation adds them. The tree is not static. Classification is an attempt to describe it at a moment in time.

title: Genetics Before DNA
paras: Darwin’s theory of natural selection required that offspring resemble their parents and that variation exist. It did not explain how the resemblance or the variation was transmitted. The mechanism was missing.

Gregor Mendel, working with pea plants in the 1860s, supplied the beginning of the mechanism. Traits are controlled by factors that come in pairs. One factor can dominate the other. The factors separate when gametes are formed and recombine at fertilization. The ratios in the offspring follow from the combinations. Mendel’s work was ignored for decades and rediscovered around 1900.

The factors are genes. They are carried on chromosomes. Chromosomes are visible under the microscope. They duplicate and separate in mitosis so that each daughter cell receives a full set. In meiosis they pair and separate so that each gamete receives half the set. Fertilization restores the full number. The behavior of the chromosomes matches the behavior of Mendel’s factors.

Mutations are changes in genes. They arise spontaneously at low rates. Radiation and certain chemicals raise the rate. Most mutations are neutral or harmful. A few are beneficial in a given environment. Natural selection acts on the variation that mutation supplies. The combination of mutation, selection, and the Mendelian transmission of genes is the modern synthesis. It is the working account of evolution.

The physical nature of the gene was unknown until the middle of the twentieth century. Experiments showed that DNA, not protein, carries the genetic information. The structure of DNA, a double helix with complementary bases, explained how it can be copied. The genetic code maps triplets of bases to amino acids. The code is nearly universal. The universality is evidence of common ancestry.
The history from Mendel’s ratios to the structure of DNA took less than a century. The facts accumulated. The explanations followed. The same pattern continues.

title: Vitamins, Hormones, and the Chemical Control of the Body
paras: In the early twentieth century, diseases such as scurvy, beriberi, and rickets were traced to missing substances in the diet. The substances were named vitamins. They are required in small amounts. Some are cofactors for enzymes. Vitamin C is needed for the synthesis of collagen. The B vitamins are involved in energy metabolism. Vitamin D regulates calcium. Deficiency produces specific diseases. Excess of some vitamins also produces harm. The discovery converted nutrition from general advice about food into a chemistry of specific molecules.

Hormones are chemical signals produced by glands and carried in the blood. Insulin, from the pancreas, lowers blood sugar. Its absence or ineffectiveness produces diabetes. Thyroid hormone regulates metabolic rate. Adrenaline prepares the body for action. Sex hormones regulate reproduction. Growth hormone regulates growth. The endocrine system and the nervous system are the two main networks of control. They interact. Many signals are used by both.

Blood groups are determined by molecules on the surface of red cells. The ABO system and the Rh system are the best known. Transfusion requires matching. Mismatch can destroy the transfused cells. The groups are inherited in a Mendelian pattern. They are also useful as markers in genetics and in anthropology.

The chemical control of the body is precise. Concentrations are regulated by feedback. Too much of a hormone usually suppresses its own production. Too little stimulates it. The same logic appears in enzyme pathways and in gene regulation. The body is a set of chemical systems that maintain themselves by continuous adjustment. When the adjustment fails, disease follows. When the missing molecule can be supplied, as with insulin or a vitamin, the failure can often be corrected.

title: The Double Helix
paras: DNA is a double helix. Two strands of sugar and phosphate wind around each other. The bases point inward and pair. Adenine pairs with thymine. Guanine pairs with cytosine. The pairs are held by hydrogen bonds. The two strands run in opposite directions. The structure was proposed by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953.

The proposal rested on several lines of evidence. Erwin Chargaff had shown that in any sample of DNA the amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine, and the amount of guanine equals the amount of cytosine. The equality suggested pairing. X-ray diffraction images of DNA fibers, produced by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling at King’s College London, and by Maurice Wilkins, showed that the molecule is helical and supplied its dimensions. The best-known image, Photograph 51, is an X-shaped pattern characteristic of a helix. The pitch is about 3.4 nanometers. There are about ten base pairs per turn. The diameter is about 2 nanometers.

Franklin’s data reached Watson and Crick indirectly. Wilkins showed Watson Photograph 51. A report summarizing Franklin’s measurements was also seen. Watson and Crick used the constraints to build a physical model. Earlier attempts had failed because the chemistry was wrong. The successful model placed the sugar-phosphate backbones on the outside and the base pairs on the inside. The pairing of A with T and G with C made every rung the same width. The strands are antiparallel. The structure immediately suggested a copying mechanism. Each strand can serve as a template for a new complementary strand. Watson and Crick noted the implication in their paper.

Three papers appeared together in *Nature* in April 1953. One by Watson and Crick presented the model. One by Wilkins and colleagues presented diffraction data. One by Franklin and Gosling presented their X-ray results. Watson, Crick, and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958 and was not eligible.

The structure explains how genetic information is stored and copied. The sequence of bases is the information. The complementary pairing is the copying rule. Mutations are changes in the sequence. The same double helix is found in bacteria, plants, animals, and humans. The differences are in the sequence, not in the architecture. The architecture is what makes inheritance possible.

title: The Structure and Replication of DNA
paras: The 1953 paper by Watson and Crick proposed a specific structure for the salt of deoxyribose nucleic acid. Two helical chains coil around the same axis. The chains are related by a dyad perpendicular to the fiber axis, so the sequences of atoms run in opposite directions. The bases are on the inside. The phosphates are on the outside. There is a residue every 3.4 angstroms along the axis. The angle between adjacent residues is 36 degrees, so the structure repeats after 10 residues, or 34 angstroms. The distance of a phosphorus atom from the axis is about 10 angstroms.

The chains are held together by hydrogen-bonded pairs of bases. One member of each pair is a purine and the other is a pyrimidine. Adenine pairs with thymine. Guanine pairs with cytosine. The pairing accounts for Chargaff’s ratios. It also makes every rung the same width, so the backbone is regular. The structure is open and contains a good deal of water. At lower water content the bases tilt and the structure becomes more compact. That matches the observation of two forms, A and B, depending on humidity.

A second paper by Watson and Crick, published weeks later, spelled out the genetical implications. The two chains are complementary. The sequence on one determines the sequence on the other. Before duplication the hydrogen bonds break and the chains unwind and separate. Each chain then serves as a template for a new complementary chain. The result is two pairs where there was one. The sequence is duplicated exactly. The genetic information is carried in the sequence of the bases. The paper did not explain how that sequence specifies proteins. That explanation came later.

The X-ray papers published with the model supplied the supporting measurements. Franklin and Gosling described the B form as helical, with a pitch of about 34 angstroms, about ten nucleotides per turn, and a diameter of about 20 angstroms. The phosphate groups lie on the outside. Wilkins and colleagues reported similar dimensions from other samples and noted that the pattern is consistent with a helical structure. The model fit the data. Later crystallographic work confirmed the coordinates in detail.

The technical result is a molecule that can store a sequence and copy it. The sequence is the information. The complementary pairing is the copying rule. Everything that followed in molecular biology rests on that architecture.

title: The Development of Chemistry
paras: Chemistry began as practical craft. Fire, metals, dyes, and medicines were used long before they were understood. The Greeks proposed that matter was made of four elements—earth, water, air, and fire—or of atoms. Neither account was tested by measurement.

Alchemy mixed the practical with the mystical. It sought the transformation of metals and the elixir of life. It developed laboratory techniques—distillation, sublimation, crystallization—that later chemistry kept. It did not develop a quantitative theory.

The transition came with measurement. Robert Boyle defined an element as a substance that could not be broken down further by chemical means. He studied the behavior of gases. The phlogiston theory explained combustion as the release of a substance called phlogiston. The theory was useful until the weights were measured carefully. When a metal burns, it gains weight. If it loses phlogiston, it should lose weight. The contradiction was fatal.

Antoine Lavoisier established the modern account. Combustion is combination with oxygen. Mass is conserved. He introduced a systematic nomenclature. Chemistry became quantitative. The gases were isolated: carbon dioxide, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen. The composition of air and of water was established.

John Dalton’s atomic theory explained the fixed proportions in which elements combine. Each element has atoms of a characteristic weight. Compounds are combinations of atoms in simple ratios. Avogadro’s hypothesis—that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles—resolved the confusion over atomic weights. Berzelius determined accurate atomic weights and introduced the modern symbols.

Organic chemistry was long thought to require a vital force. Friedrich Wöhler’s synthesis of urea from inorganic materials in 1828 undermined the claim. Organic compounds are carbon compounds. They follow the same rules as inorganic compounds. Structural formulas, valence, and the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms followed. Isomers have the same composition and different structures. Optical isomers differ in the arrangement of atoms in space.

The periodic table organized the elements by atomic weight and by property. Mendeleev left gaps and predicted the properties of the missing elements. The predictions were confirmed. The table is now ordered by atomic number. The chemical behavior follows from the arrangement of electrons.

Physical chemistry applied thermodynamics and kinetics to reactions. Catalysis speeds reactions without being consumed. Ionic dissociation explained the behavior of acids, bases, and salts in solution. Synthetic organic chemistry produced dyes, drugs, and polymers. The same principles that explain a laboratory reaction explain the chemistry of a cell and the chemistry of an industry. The history is the progressive replacement of qualitative ideas by quantitative ones.

title: The Nervous System and the Brain
paras: The nervous system coordinates the body. It receives signals from the senses and from the internal organs. It sends signals to muscles and glands. It stores information and generates behavior.

The basic unit is the neuron. A neuron has a cell body, dendrites that receive signals, and an axon that carries signals away. The signal is an electrical impulse, the action potential. It is produced by the flow of ions across the membrane. Sodium and potassium are the main ions. The membrane is polarized at rest. When stimulated past a threshold, it depolarizes and the impulse travels. At the end of the axon the signal is usually passed to the next cell by a chemical neurotransmitter. Acetylcholine and many others are used. The synapse is the junction. Most drugs that affect the brain act at synapses.

The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. The peripheral nerves connect them to the rest of the body. The autonomic system controls involuntary functions—heart rate, digestion, pupil size—and has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions that often oppose each other.

The brain has major divisions. The brainstem controls basic life functions: breathing, heart rate, arousal. The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance. The cerebrum is the largest part in humans. Its cortex is folded. The folds increase surface area. The cortex is divided into lobes. The frontal lobes are involved in planning, decision, and voluntary movement. The parietal lobes process touch and spatial information. The temporal lobes process hearing and aspects of memory. The occipital lobes process vision. The functions are specialized but interconnected. Damage to a region produces characteristic deficits.

The senses convert physical stimuli into nerve signals. The eye focuses light on the retina. Photoreceptors respond to light. The signals travel through the optic nerve to the brain. Color vision depends on three types of cones with different sensitivities. The ear converts sound waves into mechanical vibration and then into nerve signals in the cochlea. Balance is sensed by the vestibular organs in the inner ear. Taste and smell are chemical senses. Touch, temperature, and pain are sensed by receptors in the skin and elsewhere.

Reflexes are rapid, automatic responses. The knee-jerk reflex involves a sensory neuron, a motor neuron, and a synapse in the spinal cord. More complex behaviors involve the brain. Learning changes the strength of connections between neurons. Memory involves changes in synapses and, for long-term memory, changes in gene expression and structure.

Hormones interact with the nervous system. The hypothalamus links the two. It controls the pituitary, which controls other glands. Stress, growth, reproduction, and metabolism are regulated by both nerves and hormones. The brain is not separate from the body. It is the organ that integrates the signals and produces coordinated action. Its capacities—language, abstract thought, planning—are large. They are the product of the same cellular machinery that operates in every other tissue, arranged in a particular architecture.

title: The Principle of Stationary Action
paras: Classical mechanics can be written in more than one way. Newton’s laws describe how forces change momentum from moment to moment. An equivalent description uses the principle of stationary action.

The action of a path is a quantity calculated from the kinetic energy and the potential energy along that path. For a particle moving from one point to another in a given time, the actual path is the one for which the action is stationary—usually a minimum. Nearby paths have nearly the same action. The path nature takes is the one that does not change the action to first order when the path is varied slightly.

This is not a statement that nature calculates. It is a mathematical fact about the equations. The path that satisfies Newton’s second law is the same path that makes the action stationary. The two descriptions are equivalent. One is local: the force at each point determines the acceleration at that point. The other is global: the entire path is the one that satisfies the stationary condition.

The principle extends to fields and to more complicated systems. In Lagrangian mechanics the action is the integral of the Lagrangian. The Euler-Lagrange equations that follow from the stationary condition are the equations of motion. In quantum mechanics the path-integral formulation assigns a phase to every path and sums them. The classical path is the one where the phases reinforce. The stationary-action principle is the classical limit of that sum.

The formulation is useful because it makes symmetries transparent. If the Lagrangian does not depend on a coordinate, the corresponding momentum is conserved. Time translation symmetry gives energy conservation. Spatial translation symmetry gives momentum conservation. Rotational symmetry gives angular-momentum conservation. Noether’s theorem connects continuous symmetries to conservation laws. The connection is clearer in the action formulation than in the force formulation.

The principle does not replace Newton’s laws. It rewrites them. For many problems the rewrite is the more convenient starting point. For the conceptual structure of physics it shows that the same dynamics can be expressed as local forces or as a global condition on paths. Both are correct. Both are used.

title: The Arrow of Time
paras: The laws of mechanics are nearly symmetric under the reversal of time. If a set of particle trajectories is allowed, the reversed trajectories are also allowed. A film of two billiard balls colliding looks almost the same run backward. The exception is friction and other dissipative processes, which convert organized motion into heat.

Thermodynamics supplies the direction. The second law states that the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. Entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic state. A gas that fills a room has far more arrangements than the same gas confined to one corner. The probability of the gas spontaneously returning to the corner is negligible. The direction of time in everyday experience is the direction of increasing entropy.

The universe began in a state of low entropy. The hot, dense early universe was smooth. Gravity later clumped matter into stars and galaxies, increasing the entropy. The low-entropy initial condition is what allows the second law to define a direction. Without it, there would be no preferred direction for the growth of entropy. Why the initial condition was low-entropy is an open question. It is not explained by the second law itself.

Memory and records point in the same direction. A memory is a correlation between a present state and a past state. The formation of that correlation increases the entropy of the surroundings. We remember the past and not the future because the past is the direction of lower entropy. The same asymmetry appears in the fact that causes precede effects in ordinary experience. The microscopic laws do not enforce the asymmetry. The boundary condition does.

The arrow is not absolute in every sense. In small systems fluctuations can temporarily decrease entropy. The decreases are rare and short-lived. On the scales of everyday objects and of the universe as a whole, the second law holds. The direction of time that we experience is the direction in which entropy increases. That is the content of the thermodynamic arrow. Other arrows—the psychological arrow, the causal arrow—align with it under the low-entropy initial condition. The alignment is observed. The ultimate reason for the initial condition is not yet known.

title: Gravity as Spacetime Geometry
paras: Newton’s law of gravity works well for most purposes. It treats gravity as a force between masses. Einstein’s general relativity replaces the force with geometry. Mass and energy curve spacetime. Objects in free fall follow the straightest available paths in that curved geometry. Those paths are called geodesics.

The equivalence principle is the starting point. In a small enough region, the effects of a uniform gravitational field cannot be distinguished from the effects of acceleration. A person standing in a closed elevator that is accelerating upward feels the same as a person standing at rest in a gravitational field. A person in free fall feels weightless, even near a massive body. The International Space Station is in free fall around Earth. Its occupants are weightless because they and the station are following the same geodesic.

What cannot be eliminated by free fall is the difference in the field across a finite distance. That difference is tidal gravity. Two apples dropped side by side fall along slightly converging paths because they are aimed at the center of the Earth. Two apples dropped one above the other separate because the lower one is deeper in the field and accelerates more. The relative acceleration of nearby free-falling objects is the operational signature of spacetime curvature. It is called geodesic deviation. On a flat geometry, parallel paths remain parallel. On a curved geometry, they converge or diverge. The same geometry that produces the tides produces the orbits of planets.

The full field equation of general relativity relates the curvature of spacetime to the distribution of energy and momentum. Pressure also contributes. For ordinary matter the pressure term is negligible. Inside a neutron star it is not. The pressure that supports the star against collapse also adds to its gravity. That feedback limits the maximum mass of a neutron star.

Light follows the geometry as well. During a solar eclipse the apparent positions of stars near the Sun’s limb are shifted by the amount predicted by the theory. The orbit of Mercury advances by an extra 43 arcseconds per century beyond the Newtonian prediction from the other planets. Clocks run slower deeper in a gravitational field. The effect is measured with atomic clocks on the ground and in orbit. GPS satellites require corrections from both special and general relativity. Without them the system would accumulate errors of kilometers per day.

The theory reduces to Newton’s law in the weak-field, low-speed limit. It departs from Newton where fields are strong or speeds are high. The departures have been measured. They match the predictions.

title: Black Holes and Their Thermodynamics
paras: A black hole is a region of spacetime from which no signal can reach distant observers. The boundary is the event horizon. It is not a material surface. It is the set of points beyond which all future-directed paths remain inside. For a non-rotating black hole the radius of the horizon is the Schwarzschild radius, \( R_s = 2GM/c^2 \). For the Sun that radius is about three kilometers. For the Earth it is about nine millimeters. Nothing of ordinary density is compressed that far. Stellar cores that exceed the maximum mass for a neutron star can collapse past that point.

Once an object crosses the horizon, the geometry prevents escape. Tidal forces become extreme near a small black hole. They stretch an object along the radial direction and compress it transversely. For a supermassive black hole the horizon is so large that the tidal forces at the horizon itself are mild. The singularity, where curvature becomes infinite according to classical general relativity, lies in the future of any observer who crosses the horizon.

Black holes have thermodynamic properties. The area of the event horizon never decreases in classical processes. That behavior is analogous to the second law of thermodynamics. Bekenstein proposed that the entropy of a black hole is proportional to the area of its horizon. Hawking showed that a black hole emits thermal radiation at a temperature inversely proportional to its mass. The temperature for a solar-mass black hole is about \( 6 \times 10^{-8} \) K, far below the temperature of the cosmic microwave background. Smaller black holes are hotter and evaporate faster. The entropy is \( S = A/4 \) in Planck units. Information about what fell in is encoded on the horizon, not in the volume. That result is one of the motivations for holographic ideas in quantum gravity.

The classical theory predicts a singularity. Quantum effects are expected to become important near the singularity and possibly near the horizon. No complete theory of quantum gravity yet exists that describes the interior. The exterior geometry, the horizon, the radiation, and the area law are established within the combined framework of general relativity and quantum field theory in curved spacetime. Observations of gravitational waves from merging black holes, of the orbits of stars around the galactic center, and of the shadow of the black hole in M87 match the predictions of the classical theory outside the horizon.

title: Nuclear Binding Energy
paras: The mass of a nucleus is less than the mass of its separated protons and neutrons. The difference is the binding energy. For helium-4 the difference is about 0.75 percent of the mass. That corresponds to about 28 MeV. A chemical bond is a few electron-volts. Nuclear binding is millions of times stronger.

When the binding energy per nucleon is plotted against mass number, the curve rises from hydrogen, peaks near iron and nickel at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon, and then declines slowly toward uranium. Light nuclei release energy by fusing toward the peak. Heavy nuclei release energy by fission toward the peak. Iron sits at the top. A star that has built an iron core has no further nuclear source of energy.

The shape of the curve follows from the competition between the strong force and the electromagnetic force. The strong force is short-range. A nucleon in the interior of a large nucleus is bound to all its neighbors. A nucleon on the surface is bound to fewer. Small nuclei are mostly surface. Adding nucleons helps. The electromagnetic repulsion between protons is long-range. It grows faster with the number of protons. In large nuclei the repulsion begins to win. Extra neutrons add strong-force binding without adding charge. Beyond lead and bismuth no stable combination exists.

Fusion in the Sun requires protons to approach within the range of the strong force. At the temperature of the solar core the typical kinetic energy is far below the Coulomb barrier. Fusion occurs by quantum tunneling. The probability is low. A given proton in the core waits billions of years before it fuses. The Sun’s power density is only a few hundred watts per cubic meter. It shines because it is large and well insulated, not because the reactions are rapid.

Fission of a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235, triggered by a neutron, releases about 200 MeV and two or three additional neutrons. If, on average, one of those neutrons causes another fission, the reaction is sustained. A small fraction of the neutrons are delayed by the decay of fission products. That delay allows a reactor to be controlled. In a bomb the multiplication is rapid and uncontrolled. Natural reactors operated at Oklo in Gabon about two billion years ago, when the uranium-235 abundance was higher and groundwater moderated the neutrons.

Radioactive decay follows an exponential law. After one half-life half the nuclei remain. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years and is used to date organic material up to about 50,000 years. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years and is used to date the solar system. The range of half-lives is explained by tunneling through the nuclear barrier. A small change in the barrier height or width changes the lifetime by many orders of magnitude.

title: Neutrinos
paras: In beta decay the energy of the emitted electron is not fixed. It forms a continuous spectrum. If the nucleus simply emitted an electron, energy and momentum would not be conserved. Wolfgang Pauli proposed in 1930 that a light, neutral particle carries away the missing energy and momentum. Enrico Fermi named it the neutrino and built a theory of beta decay around it. The particle was detected in 1956 by Cowan and Reines using a reactor as the source.

Neutrinos interact only through the weak force and gravity. A typical solar neutrino can pass through a light-year of lead with a substantial probability of no interaction. About 65 billion solar neutrinos pass through each square centimeter of the Earth every second. Over a human lifetime only a few interact with atoms in the body.

There are three flavors: electron, muon, and tau. They have small but nonzero masses. The mass eigenstates are mixtures of the flavor eigenstates. A neutrino produced as one flavor can be detected as another after traveling a distance. This is neutrino oscillation. It was confirmed by experiments with solar neutrinos, atmospheric neutrinos, and reactor neutrinos. The oscillation data determine the mass-squared differences and the mixing angles. The absolute mass scale is not yet known. It is below about 0.1 eV.

Neutrinos are produced in the Sun by the fusion reactions, in supernovae, in the atmosphere by cosmic-ray interactions, in reactors, and in the early universe. They carry information from regions that light cannot leave. The detection of neutrinos from supernova 1987A confirmed that the core collapse releases most of its energy in neutrinos. Neutrino telescopes now observe high-energy neutrinos from distant sources.

The existence of three light neutrino species was established by the width of the Z boson. The Standard Model accommodates the oscillations by giving the neutrinos small masses, either as Dirac particles or as Majorana particles. Which possibility is realized is not yet known. The neutrinos are the lightest known massive particles. They are also the most numerous, after the photons of the cosmic microwave background.

title: Chaos
paras: A system can be deterministic and still be unpredictable in practice. Deterministic means that the future state is fixed by the present state and the laws. Unpredictable means that a small uncertainty in the present state grows so rapidly that the future cannot be calculated usefully beyond a limited time.

The classic example is the logistic map, \( x_{n+1} = r x_n (1 - x_n) \). For some values of the parameter \( r \) the sequence is periodic. For others it is chaotic. Nearby starting points diverge exponentially. The rate of divergence is measured by the Lyapunov exponent. When the exponent is positive, the system is chaotic.

The same behavior appears in continuous systems. Edward Lorenz studied a simplified model of atmospheric convection. The equations are deterministic. The solutions are sensitive to initial conditions. Two trajectories that begin close together separate until they bear no useful relation. The atmosphere is such a system. Weather forecasts lose skill after about two weeks because the initial uncertainties, however small, grow to the size of the weather itself. Climate, which is the statistics of the weather, remains predictable on longer scales.

Chaos is not randomness. The trajectory is unique. It is confined to a strange attractor of lower dimension than the full phase space. The attractor has structure. The structure is fractal. The motion on the attractor is aperiodic. Small changes in parameters can move the system from periodic to chaotic behavior through a sequence of period doublings. The ratios of the parameter intervals approach a universal constant.

Most real systems are neither purely regular nor purely chaotic. The solar system is stable on human timescales and chaotic on timescales of tens of millions of years for the inner planets. Turbulence in fluids is chaotic. The heart and the brain show both regular and chaotic dynamics. The existence of chaos shows that exact laws do not guarantee practical predictability. The distinction is quantitative. It depends on the Lyapunov time and on the precision of the initial data.

title: The Vacuum
paras: Empty space is not empty. Quantum field theory assigns a zero-point energy to every mode of every field. The energy of a harmonic oscillator in its ground state is \( \frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega \). Summing over all modes gives a formally infinite vacuum energy. A cutoff at the Planck scale produces a density many orders of magnitude larger than the observed cosmological constant.

The Casimir effect demonstrates that the vacuum energy has measurable consequences. Two uncharged conducting plates attract each other. The attraction arises because the plates restrict the allowed modes of the electromagnetic field between them. The zero-point energy between the plates is lower than outside. The force has been measured and matches the calculation. The effect is real. The absolute energy of the vacuum is not measured by the Casimir force. Only the difference is.

The observed vacuum energy density, inferred from the acceleration of the expansion, is about \( 10^{-9} \) joules per cubic meter. The naive quantum-field estimate is larger by a factor of order \( 10^{120} \). The discrepancy is the cosmological-constant problem. No accepted solution exists. Supersymmetry would cancel the contributions of bosons and fermions, but supersymmetry, if it exists, is broken at a scale far above the observed vacuum energy. Anthropic selection in a multiverse is one proposed resolution. It is not established.

The vacuum also fluctuates. Virtual particle pairs appear and disappear. They contribute to the Lamb shift, to the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron, and to the running of coupling constants. Those effects are calculated and measured to high precision. The vacuum is therefore both the source of the most precise predictions in physics and the source of the largest discrepancy between theory and observation. The two facts coexist. The resolution is not yet known.

title: Semiconductors
paras: A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator and can be controlled. Silicon is the most common. In a pure crystal the valence band is full and the conduction band is empty. The energy gap between them is about 1.1 electron-volts. At room temperature a few electrons have enough thermal energy to cross the gap. The conductivity is low but not zero.

Doping changes the conductivity by many orders of magnitude. Adding a small fraction of phosphorus or arsenic introduces extra electrons. The material is n-type. Adding boron introduces holes—missing electrons that behave as positive carriers. The material is p-type. A junction between p-type and n-type material forms a diode. Current flows easily in one direction and is blocked in the other. The junction also separates charge and produces a voltage when light falls on it. That is the basis of a solar cell.

A transistor uses a small current or voltage to control a larger current. In a bipolar transistor a small base current controls a larger collector current. In a field-effect transistor a voltage on the gate controls the current between source and drain. Both act as switches and as amplifiers. A modern integrated circuit contains billions of transistors on a single chip. The transistors are formed by doping selected regions of a silicon wafer and depositing insulating and conducting layers. The minimum feature size is now a few nanometers.

The same quantum mechanics that explains the band gap explains the operation of the devices. Electrons in the crystal occupy energy bands. The exclusion principle prevents them from all occupying the lowest states. The gap, the doping, and the junctions are applications of those rules. The technology that processes information is built from the same physics that describes the atom.

title: Quantum Biology
paras: Most biological processes are well described by classical chemistry. A few involve quantum effects that cannot be ignored.

Enzyme catalysis sometimes uses tunneling. In hydrogen-transfer reactions the proton or hydrogen atom can pass through the energy barrier rather than over it. The rate is higher than a classical calculation predicts. Kinetic isotope effects—the change in rate when hydrogen is replaced by deuterium—are larger than expected from mass alone and are consistent with tunneling. The effect is temperature-dependent in ways that match quantum models.

Photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes transfer energy from antenna pigments to the reaction center with high efficiency. Spectroscopic measurements show coherent oscillations in the energy transfer. The coherence persists for hundreds of femtoseconds at physiological temperatures. Whether the coherence improves the efficiency under natural conditions or is a side effect of the structure is still under study. The observation is established. The functional importance is not fully settled.

Avian magnetoreception is another candidate. Some migratory birds orient using the Earth’s magnetic field. One proposed mechanism is a radical-pair reaction in cryptochrome proteins in the eye. The yield of the reaction depends on the orientation of the radical pair relative to the magnetic field because of the interplay of electron spins. The mechanism is plausible and consistent with behavioral experiments. Direct proof that it is the sensor used by the bird is still incomplete.

Quantum effects in biology are real where they have been measured. They do not require that the organism maintain macroscopic coherence. They occur in specific reactions where the energy barriers, the timescales, and the isolation from the environment allow them. The majority of cellular chemistry remains classical. The exceptions show that evolution can use quantum mechanics when it is available.

title: Endosymbiosis and Multicellularity
paras: Eukaryotic cells contain mitochondria. Plant cells also contain chloroplasts. Both organelles have their own DNA, their own ribosomes, and double membranes. The DNA is circular, like bacterial DNA. The sequences show that mitochondria are related to alphaproteobacteria and chloroplasts to cyanobacteria. The organelles were once free-living bacteria that became permanent residents of host cells. The process is endosymbiosis.

The host gained the ability to produce ATP by oxidative phosphorylation or to fix carbon by photosynthesis. The endosymbiont gained a stable environment and a supply of nutrients. Over time most of the endosymbiont’s genes were transferred to the host nucleus. The organelles retained a reduced genome that encodes some of their own proteins. The arrangement is stable. It occurred once for mitochondria, early in eukaryotic history, and once for the primary chloroplast, in the ancestor of the Archaeplastida. Secondary endosymbioses, in which a eukaryotic cell engulfed another eukaryote that already had a chloroplast, occurred several times and produced the chloroplasts of other algal groups.

Multicellularity evolved independently many times. Animals, plants, fungi, and several groups of algae and bacteria all contain multicellular species. The transition requires cells to adhere, to communicate, and to differentiate. In animals the extracellular matrix and cell-adhesion molecules hold cells together. Signaling pathways control division and specialization. Programmed cell death removes cells that are no longer needed. The genetic toolkit for these functions existed in unicellular ancestors and was co-opted. The Cambrian radiation, about 540 million years ago, produced most of the major animal body plans in a geologically short interval. The causes are debated. They include rising oxygen, ecological interactions, and the evolution of developmental gene networks. The fossil record shows the outcome. The precise triggers remain under study.

title: No-Cloning and Quantum Information
paras: An unknown quantum state cannot be copied. Suppose a machine takes a system in an arbitrary state and produces two systems in that same state, while leaving the original unchanged. The linearity of quantum mechanics forbids it. If the machine works for two orthogonal states, it fails for their superposition. The proof is short. It is called the no-cloning theorem.

The theorem has practical consequences. It prevents the use of quantum states as ordinary classical bits that can be duplicated and checked. It is the reason quantum key distribution can detect eavesdropping. Any attempt to measure or copy the quantum signals disturbs them in a way that the legitimate parties can observe. It also limits what a quantum computer can do with an unknown state. The state can be teleported if the original is destroyed, but it cannot be cloned.

Quantum information is carried by qubits. A qubit can be in a superposition of two states. Two qubits can be entangled. The joint state cannot be written as a product of individual states. Measurement of one qubit instantly correlates with the measurement of the other, regardless of distance. The correlation does not allow faster-than-light signaling. The outcomes are random. Only when the results are compared does the correlation appear. Entanglement is a resource for computation and for communication. It is also the feature that makes the measurement problem sharp. The linear evolution produces superpositions. The observed world contains definite outcomes. How the transition occurs is not settled by the formalism.

The no-cloning theorem, entanglement, and the limits on signaling are established. They follow from the linearity and the tensor-product structure of quantum mechanics. They constrain every interpretation and every proposed application.

title: Bell’s Theorem and the Experiments
paras: In 1935 Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen argued that quantum mechanics is incomplete. They considered two particles that have interacted and then separated. A measurement on one instantly determines the result of a corresponding measurement on the other. If the particles have definite properties all along, the correlation is ordinary. If they do not, the theory appears to require a nonlocal influence. Einstein called the second possibility spooky.

John Bell showed in 1964 that the two pictures are not equivalent. Any theory in which the outcomes are determined by local hidden variables must satisfy a certain inequality on the correlations. Quantum mechanics violates the inequality for some choices of measurements. The violation is a quantitative prediction. It can be tested.

Experiments beginning in the 1970s and culminating in the work of Aspect, Dalibard, and Roger in 1982 measured the correlations with polarizers whose settings were changed while the particles were in flight. The results matched the quantum prediction and violated the Bell inequality. Later experiments closed the main loopholes: the detection loophole, the locality loophole, and the freedom-of-choice loophole. The violation is established.

The experiments rule out local hidden-variable theories. They do not by themselves select among the remaining interpretations. The correlations are real. They do not allow signaling. The random outcomes on each side remain random. Only the joint statistics show the violation. Quantum teleportation uses the same resource. An unknown state can be transferred from one system to another by a joint measurement and classical communication. The original state is destroyed. No information travels faster than light. The protocol has been demonstrated with photons and with atoms.

The theorem and the experiments fix one boundary. Any complete account of the correlations must abandon either locality or the assumption that the outcomes are determined by preexisting local variables, or both. The boundary is experimental.

title: The Aharonov–Bohm Effect
paras: A magnetic field can affect an electron that never enters the region where the field is nonzero. In the Aharonov–Bohm effect an electron beam is split, passed on either side of a long solenoid, and recombined. The magnetic field is confined inside the solenoid. Outside, the field is zero. The vector potential is not zero. The relative phase between the two paths depends on the magnetic flux through the solenoid. The interference pattern shifts when the flux is changed. The shift has been measured with the field completely shielded from the electrons.

The effect shows that the vector potential has physical consequences in quantum mechanics even where the field vanishes. In classical mechanics only the fields appear in the force law. In quantum mechanics the phase of the wave function depends on the line integral of the potential. The phase is gauge-dependent, but the phase difference around a closed loop is gauge-invariant and equal to the enclosed flux in appropriate units. The effect is topological. It depends on the flux, not on the local field along the path.

The same principle appears in superconducting rings. A superconducting loop encloses flux in discrete quanta. The quantization follows from the requirement that the macroscopic wave function be single-valued. The Aharonov–Bohm phase is the underlying mechanism. The effect has been observed with electrons, with neutrons, and in solid-state devices. It is a direct demonstration that the electromagnetic potentials are not merely a mathematical convenience.

title: Superconductivity
paras: Below a critical temperature some materials conduct electricity with zero resistance. A current in a superconducting loop persists for years without measurable decay. The material also expels magnetic fields, the Meissner effect. The transition is sharp. It is a phase transition.

The microscopic theory is the BCS theory. Electrons near the Fermi surface form pairs, Cooper pairs, bound by an attractive interaction mediated by lattice vibrations. The pairs are bosons. They condense into a single macroscopic quantum state. The condensate has a well-defined phase. The phase is coherent across the sample. Scattering that would produce resistance in a normal metal cannot occur without breaking pairs, and the energy cost is finite. The resistance is zero.

A junction between two superconductors separated by a thin insulator allows a supercurrent to flow with no voltage, the Josephson effect. The current depends on the phase difference across the junction. An applied voltage produces an alternating current at a frequency proportional to the voltage. The constant of proportionality is \( 2e/h \). The relation is exact and is used to define the volt. Magnetic flux through a superconducting ring is quantized in units of \( h/2e \). The quantization is observed.

High-temperature superconductors, discovered in 1986, become superconducting at temperatures above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen. Their mechanism is not fully understood. The conventional BCS theory does not account for them. They are used in magnets, in sensors, and in some power applications.
