Subtle correlations among successive quanta can, in principle, encode the initial state. The correlations are exponentially small until the final stages of evaporation. Recovering them is impractical. Their existence would restore unitarity.

No consensus exists on the detailed mechanism. Proposals include remnants, information return in the late radiation, and modifications of the horizon itself. The question remains open. It is a precise conflict between the semiclassical calculation and the requirement of unitary quantum evolution. Its resolution is expected to constrain any quantum theory of gravity.

title: The No-Boundary Proposal
paras: Hawking and Hartle proposed that the wave function of the universe is given by a path integral over compact Euclidean geometries. There is no initial boundary. The universe does not begin at a singular edge. It is finite in the past yet without a boundary, in the same way that the surface of a sphere is finite yet has no edge.

The proposal selects a particular solution of the Wheeler–DeWitt equation. In simple minisuperspace models it yields a wave function that is large for geometries close to de Sitter space and small for highly irregular ones. The classical spacetime that emerges is an inflating universe. The arrow of time and the low initial entropy are related to the Euclidean section.

The proposal is a candidate boundary condition. It is not derived from a more fundamental theory. Different choices of contour and different operator orderings produce different wave functions. Observational tests are indirect. They constrain the duration and the spectrum of inflation. They do not uniquely confirm the no-boundary condition. The idea remains a well-defined and influential suggestion for the quantum origin of the classical universe.

title: Singularities and Chronology Protection
paras: The Penrose–Hawking singularity theorems show that, under general conditions, gravitational collapse and cosmological expansion produce incomplete geodesics. Classical general relativity predicts its own breakdown. The theorems assume the null energy condition and the existence of a trapped surface or a cosmological focusing condition. Both are satisfied in realistic collapse and in the hot early universe. The classical theory therefore cannot be the final description.

Hawking also examined the possibility of closed timelike curves. Such curves permit paths that return to the same event. He conjectured that the laws of physics prevent their formation. The conjecture is called chronology protection. Quantum effects near a would-be chronology horizon produce a divergent stress-energy tensor. The back-reaction is expected to destroy the horizon before closed timelike curves appear. The argument is plausible. It is not a theorem. No confirmed example of a chronology-violating spacetime is known. The protection, if it holds, keeps the causal structure of the observed universe intact.

title: String Theory and M-Theory
paras: String theory replaces point particles with one-dimensional objects. The different vibrational modes of a string correspond to different particles. One mode is a massless spin-2 particle. That particle has the couplings of a graviton. The theory therefore contains gravity automatically. Consistency requires additional spatial dimensions. The simplest supersymmetric versions are formulated in ten spacetime dimensions. The extra dimensions are compactified or otherwise hidden at accessible energies.

Five consistent superstring theories exist in ten dimensions. In the mid-1990s it was shown that they are related by dualities. A single eleven-dimensional framework, called M-theory, contains all five as different limits. Membranes and higher-dimensional objects appear in the eleven-dimensional description. The low-energy limit of M-theory is eleven-dimensional supergravity.

The theories are ultraviolet finite. Perturbative quantum gravity is not. That is a structural advantage. They also contain gauge fields and fermions and can accommodate chiral matter. No compactification has yet reproduced the precise particle content and couplings of the Standard Model together with a small positive cosmological constant. The number of possible compactifications is large. The set is often called the landscape. No principle that selects our vacuum from the landscape is established.

Direct experimental tests are absent. The characteristic energy scale is the Planck scale or a high compactification scale. Both lie far above collider energies. Indirect tests—deviations from Newtonian gravity at short distances, cosmic strings, or specific patterns of supersymmetry—have not produced a confirmed signal. The framework remains mathematically consistent and physically unconfirmed. It is a candidate theory of quantum gravity and of unification. It is not yet a demonstrated one.

title: Branes
paras: A brane is an extended object on which open strings can end. A p-brane has p spatial dimensions. A 1-brane is a string. A 2-brane is a membrane. Higher-dimensional branes appear in string theory and in M-theory. The endpoints of open strings are confined to the brane. Closed strings propagate in the full spacetime, the bulk.

In some constructions the Standard Model fields are localized on a brane while gravity propagates in the extra dimensions. The weakness of gravity relative to the other forces can then be a consequence of the volume of the extra dimensions rather than of a high fundamental scale. The idea is called a brane-world. No experimental signature of large extra dimensions or of brane-localized matter has been confirmed.

Branes carry charges under antisymmetric tensor fields. They are stable when the charge is conserved. Parallel branes of the same charge repel. Branes and anti-branes attract and can annihilate. The annihilation can end an inflationary phase in some models. The process is calculable within the theory. It has not been observed.

Branes are therefore part of the extended-object spectrum of string theory and M-theory. They supply a geometric setting for gauge fields and a possible explanation for the hierarchy between gravity and the other forces. Both uses remain theoretical. No direct evidence for branes exists.

title: Everything, Everywhere, All at Once
paras: The many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics asserts that the universal wave function evolves unitarily at all times. There is no collapse. Every outcome that has a non-zero amplitude is realized in some branch of the wave function. The branches do not interact once they have decohered. An observer who records one outcome is correlated with that branch and has no access to the others.

The interpretation was introduced by Everett in 1957. It reproduces the statistical predictions of ordinary quantum mechanics because the measure of branches in which a given relative frequency occurs matches the Born rule in the limit of many trials. The derivation of the Born rule from the unitary evolution alone is still debated. Decision-theoretic and envariance arguments have been offered. None is universally accepted.

The interpretation removes the measurement problem by denying that measurement is a special process. It multiplies the ontology. Every possible outcome occurs somewhere in the wave function. The multiplication is not observed. Decoherence explains why the branches do not interfere, but it does not by itself select one branch as the experienced world. The selection remains an open question within the interpretation.

No experiment distinguishes many-worlds from other interpretations that yield the same probabilities. The choice is metaphysical. The formalism is the same. The claim that all outcomes occur is an additional assertion about what the formalism describes. It is consistent. It is not required. It is not ruled out.

title: Folded Dimensions
paras: Extra spatial dimensions can be compactified. Their size is finite and small enough that they have not been detected. A circle of radius \( R \) is the simplest example. Momentum around the circle is quantized in units of \( 1/R \). From the viewpoint of the large dimensions the quantized momentum appears as a tower of massive particles. The masses begin at \( 1/R \) and rise in steps of the same size. The tower is called a Kaluza–Klein tower.

If \( R \) is near the Planck length the tower begins at the Planck mass and is unobservable. If \( R \) is larger, the lightest modes could appear at accelerator energies. Searches for missing energy or for deviations from Newtonian gravity at short distances have set limits. No signal has been found. The radius of any flat extra dimension accessible to those searches must be smaller than roughly a tenth of a millimeter.

Compactification need not be a simple circle. The internal space can be a Calabi–Yau manifold or another curved geometry. The shape determines the spectrum of particles and the couplings that appear in the large dimensions. Different shapes produce different low-energy theories. The number of known shapes is large. No principle selects the shape that would reproduce the observed Standard Model.

Folded dimensions therefore remain a consistent theoretical possibility. They supply a geometric origin for gauge symmetries in the original Kaluza–Klein construction and for the particle spectrum in string compactifications. They have not been observed. Their size, if they exist, lies below present experimental bounds.

title: Time Prevents Everything from Happening at Once
paras: The geometry of spacetime limits what can influence what. An event can affect another event only if a signal traveling at or below the speed of light can pass from the first to the second. The set of events that can be reached is the future light cone. The set that can reach the given event is the past light cone. Events outside both cones are spacelike separated. No causal influence passes between them.

The restriction is not an extra rule imposed on the laws. It is the causal structure already contained in the metric of special and general relativity. The same structure appears in quantum field theory. Operators at spacelike separation commute. Measurements in those regions do not disturb each other. The prohibition on faster-than-light signaling is therefore both geometric and quantum-mechanical.

Without the restriction every event could influence every other event. The notion of a localized experiment, of a record that is stable until it is read, and of a sequence of causes and effects would not exist. The existence of time as an ordering that prevents everything from occurring in one undifferentiated moment is the existence of this causal structure. The structure is observed. Signals do not outrun light. Records persist. The prevention is not metaphorical. It is the light-cone structure of the spacetime we inhabit.

title: Decoherence
paras: A quantum system that interacts with its environment becomes entangled with the environment. The reduced state of the system, obtained by tracing over the environmental degrees of freedom, loses the off-diagonal terms that encode interference. The process is decoherence. It occurs rapidly for macroscopic objects. A dust grain in air decoheres in a time far shorter than any practical observation. Interference between macroscopically distinct positions becomes unobservable.

Decoherence does not destroy the global superposition. The full state of system plus environment remains pure if it began pure. The local description of the system alone becomes mixed. Interference terms are still present in the global state. They are dispersed into correlations with the environment and cannot be recovered without measuring the environment in a precisely controlled way. For ordinary environments that control is impossible.

The process explains why macroscopic superpositions are not seen. It does not by itself select one outcome. The global state still contains every branch. Decoherence makes the branches effectively independent. It supplies the physical reason that the measurement problem is invisible in practice. It does not solve the problem of why one branch is experienced. That question remains interpretation-dependent.

Decoherence rates have been calculated and measured for systems ranging from single ions to superconducting circuits. The agreement is quantitative. The phenomenon is established. Its implications for the ontology of quantum mechanics are not.

title: Faster than Light
paras: Special relativity requires that no signal or causal influence travel faster than light in vacuum. The requirement follows from the invariance of the speed of light and from the demand that cause precede effect in every inertial frame. A signal that outruns light in one frame arrives before it is sent in another frame. The reversal permits closed causal loops. No consistent physics of such loops is known.

Quantum mechanics does not evade the limit. Entanglement correlates measurement outcomes. It does not transmit controllable information. The no-communication theorem shows that local operations on one subsystem cannot alter the reduced state of the other. Any protocol that appears to signal faster than light either fails when the statistics are computed correctly or relies on a classical channel that itself respects the light-speed limit.

Tachyonic fields—fields whose quanta have imaginary mass—appear in some unstable theories. They signal an instability, not a usable faster-than-light particle. The instability is removed by shifting to the true vacuum. No stable tachyon has been observed.

Group velocities greater than \( c \) occur in regions of anomalous dispersion. The signal velocity, defined by the front of a sharp pulse, remains at or below \( c \). The apparent superluminal group velocity does not carry information outside the light cone. Experiments confirm the distinction.

No confirmed observation has shown a causal influence propagating faster than light. The light-cone structure of spacetime and the no-communication theorem remain intact. Claims to the contrary have not survived scrutiny.

title: Everything Moves at the Speed of Light in Spacetime
paras: In special relativity the four-velocity of any massive particle has constant magnitude \( c \). The particle’s path through spacetime is parameterized by proper time. The components of the four-velocity satisfy

When the particle is at rest in a given frame, the entire four-velocity points in the time direction. When the particle moves, part of the four-velocity is spatial. The spatial speed can never reach \( c \) because the time component would then vanish and the magnitude condition would fail. The trade-off is exact. Motion through space reduces the rate at which the particle advances through coordinate time, which is the observed time dilation.

Massless particles travel on null geodesics. Their four-velocity is undefined in the same sense, but their world-lines satisfy \( ds = 0 \). They move at \( c \) through space and do not advance in proper time. The same geometric fact covers both cases: every causal trajectory is limited by the light cone, and every massive trajectory maintains a four-velocity of fixed magnitude \( c \).

The statement is therefore not that every object races through space at light speed. It is that every object moves through spacetime at light speed. The division between the time part and the space part depends on the frame. The magnitude does not. The geometry enforces the division. Nothing massive can convert its entire motion into spatial motion. The conversion would require the time component to disappear, which the invariant interval forbids.

title: Relativity Visualized
paras: Lewis Carroll Epstein presented special relativity through diagrams in which every object moves at the speed of light through spacetime. A vertical axis is proper time. A horizontal axis is space. A particle at rest traces a vertical line. A moving particle traces a diagonal line. The length of the spacetime path between two events is the same for every traveler. The division between the time part and the space part changes with velocity. The diagrams make time dilation and length contraction geometric facts rather than algebraic surprises.

In the diagram a light ray runs at 45 degrees. Any massive particle’s world-line lies inside that angle. The faster the particle moves through space, the less proper time it accumulates between two coordinate-time slices. The slowing of clocks is the reduced vertical progress. Length contraction appears when one asks for the simultaneous positions of the two ends of a moving rod. Simultaneity is a horizontal slice in the rod’s rest frame and a tilted slice in the laboratory frame. The tilted slice intersects a shorter segment of the rod’s world-tube. The contraction is the difference in the slices.

The same pictures display the twin paradox. The traveling twin follows a bent path. The bent path is shorter in proper time than the straight path of the stay-at-home twin. The difference is visible as a shorter vertical projection. No acceleration is required for the comparison once both twins are reunited; the acceleration merely allows the paths to meet again. The diagram shows the result without coordinates.

Epstein’s construction does not alter the predictions of special relativity. It supplies a geometric reading in which the invariance of the spacetime interval is primary and the familiar effects are projections. The reading is pedagogically effective. It is fully equivalent to the standard algebraic treatment.

title: Conformal Cyclic Cosmology
paras: Penrose has proposed that the universe consists of a sequence of aeons. Each aeon begins with a Big Bang and expands forever. In the remote future, after black holes have evaporated and massive particles have decayed or redshifted beyond relevance, only massless radiation remains. For massless particles the conformal geometry is all that matters; scale becomes meaningless. The infinite future of one aeon can be matched, by a conformal rescaling, to the Big Bang of the next. The low gravitational entropy of the new Big Bang is inherited from the smooth, empty state of the previous aeon.

The proposal requires no inflation and no multiverse. It uses only classical general relativity plus the assumption that rest mass eventually becomes irrelevant. It predicts concentric circles of anomalous temperature in the cosmic microwave background, produced by gravitational waves from black-hole encounters in the previous aeon. Claims of such circles have been published and disputed. The statistical significance remains contested.

The model is a possible extension of general relativity. It is not required by existing data. It offers one account of the low entropy of the Big Bang without invoking a special initial condition inside a single universe. Whether the predicted circles exist at the required amplitude is an observational question still under examination.

title: The First Three Minutes
paras: The early universe was hot and dense. At temperatures above \( 10^{10} \) K neutrons and protons were in equilibrium through weak interactions. As the universe expanded and cooled, the weak interactions froze out. The neutron-to-proton ratio was then fixed at about one to six. Below roughly \( 10^9 \) K deuterium became stable. Almost all the remaining neutrons were incorporated into helium-4. The process left roughly 75 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium by mass, plus trace amounts of deuterium, helium-3, and lithium-7.

The abundances match the observations of the oldest stars and of interstellar gas once the baryon density is set to the value measured by the microwave background. The agreement is one of the principal successes of the hot Big Bang. It fixes the conditions between about one second and three minutes after the initial singularity.

The same expansion that set the nuclear abundances later cooled the photon gas. When the temperature fell to about 3000 K, electrons and nuclei formed neutral atoms. The universe became transparent. The photons released at that moment are the cosmic microwave background. Their present temperature is 2.725 K. The spectrum is thermal. The small anisotropies record the density fluctuations that existed at recombination.

The first three minutes therefore determined the composition of ordinary matter. The subsequent three hundred thousand years determined the radiation we still detect. Both calculations rest on measured particle-physics cross-sections and on general relativity. Both match observation.

title: Barbour on Time
paras: Julian Barbour argues that time is not a fundamental entity. What exists are configurations of the universe—complete specifications of the relative positions and velocities of all particles, or of the geometry of space. Each configuration is a point in a vast configuration space. There is no external time in which these configurations occur. Change is the difference between configurations. The experienced flow of time is the reading of records that correlate one configuration with another.

The proposal is motivated by the structure of general relativity and of quantum gravity. The Einstein equations can be cast in a form that contains no explicit time. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation is likewise timeless. Barbour interprets the absence of a time variable as evidence that time is absent from the fundamental description. Dynamics is replaced by a relation among configurations. A path through configuration space is a history. The path is selected by a principle of least action or by a quantum amplitude. No meta-time is required for the path to exist.

Records supply the arrow. A configuration that contains structures correlated with other configurations is a record of those configurations. The correlation is asymmetric because of the low-entropy boundary condition of the early universe. The asymmetry is not a property of time. It is a property of the distribution of configurations. Observers inside a configuration that contains records experience a direction. The direction is real as a relation. It is not an additional flowing substance.

The account does not deny the utility of time in laboratory physics. Clocks work. The Schrödinger equation with an external parameter is an excellent approximation when a suitable internal clock exists. The claim is that the parameter is emergent. It is constructed from correlations among the timeless configurations. Whether the construction can be carried through in a realistic quantum cosmology is an open technical question. The conceptual proposal is that the question has an affirmative answer and that time is therefore not fundamental.

title: Max Planck
paras: Planck introduced the quantum of action in 1900. To fit the spectrum of black-body radiation he assumed that the energy of an oscillator of frequency \( \nu \) is an integer multiple of \( h\nu \). The constant \( h \) is Planck’s constant. The assumption was empirical. It reproduced the observed spectrum, including the high-frequency fall-off that classical theory could not explain.

The same constant sets the scale of quantum phenomena. The energy of a photon is \( h\nu \). The angular momentum of an electron orbit is quantized in units of \( \hbar = h/2\pi \). The uncertainty principle is written with \( \hbar \). Every confirmed quantum calculation contains \( h \). Its measured value is \( 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \) joule-seconds.

Planck also defined the natural units constructed from \( h \), \( G \), and \( c \). The Planck length is \( \sqrt{\hbar G/c^3} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-35} \) m. The Planck time and Planck mass follow similarly. These units mark the scale at which quantum gravity is expected to become important. No experiment has reached them. They remain the characteristic scales of any theory that unites quantum mechanics and general relativity.

The introduction of \( h \) was the first step of quantum theory. The subsequent development replaced the original oscillators with the operators and amplitudes of modern quantum mechanics. The constant itself is unchanged.

title: Max Born
paras: Born gave the statistical interpretation of the wave function. The quantity \( |\psi|^2 \) is the probability density for finding the particle. The interpretation was proposed in 1926. It turned the Schrödinger equation from a classical wave equation into a probabilistic theory. Every subsequent calculation of cross-sections, decay rates, and spectra uses the rule.

Born also developed the theory of ionic crystals and, with Heisenberg and Jordan, the matrix formulation of quantum mechanics. The matrix formulation and the wave formulation were shown to be equivalent. Both are in use. The probabilistic reading of the wave function remains the link between the formalism and laboratory counts.

The interpretation does not specify what occurs in a single run. It specifies the distribution of outcomes over many runs. That is the content that has been tested. The tests confirm the rule to high precision. Alternative readings exist. They are constrained by the same rule.

title: Max von Laue
paras: Von Laue predicted that X-rays would diffract from the regular lattice of a crystal. The experiment, performed in 1912, confirmed the prediction. The diffraction pattern established both the wave nature of X-rays and the atomic periodicity of crystals. The wavelengths of X-rays were thereby measured. The spacing of atomic planes was determined.

The same technique, extended to electrons and neutrons, maps the structure of solids, proteins, and viruses. The phase problem—the loss of phase information in the intensity pattern—is solved by direct methods, by isomorphous replacement, or by anomalous dispersion. The structures of thousands of biological macromolecules have been obtained. The method remains the principal source of atomic-resolution models of large molecules.
Von Laue’s demonstration converted crystallography from a macroscopic description of faces into a quantitative determination of atomic positions. The conversion is complete.

title: Max Tegmark
paras: Tegmark has argued that the mathematical structure of physical law is not a description of reality but is reality itself. The hypothesis is called the mathematical universe. Every consistent mathematical structure exists. The physical world we inhabit is one such structure. Observers arise inside those structures that are complex enough to contain self-aware subsystems.

The proposal implies a form of multiverse. Structures that differ in their equations or in their solutions are equally real. The anthropic selection of our particular laws is then a selection among existing structures rather than a selection among possibilities. The hypothesis is metaphysical. It is not contradicted by existing data. It makes no unique empirical prediction that distinguishes it from ordinary physics inside our structure.

Tegmark has also classified multiverse proposals into four levels: regions beyond our horizon, universes with different constants, the many-worlds branches of quantum mechanics, and the ensemble of mathematical structures. The classification organizes existing ideas. It does not establish that any level beyond the first is realized. The first level is already implied by standard inflationary cosmology if the inflationary volume is infinite.

The mathematical-universe hypothesis and the multiverse taxonomy are therefore frameworks for organizing questions. They are not established theories. They remain options for interpreting the relation between mathematics and the physical world.

title: Einstein’s Contributions
paras: In 1905 Einstein published four papers that altered physics. The first explained the photoelectric effect by treating light as quanta of energy \( h\nu \). The second gave the theory of Brownian motion and thereby a direct estimate of atomic size. The third presented the special theory of relativity. The fourth showed that mass and energy are related by \( E = mc^2 \).

Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same in every inertial frame. The consequences are the relativity of simultaneity, time dilation, length contraction, and the invariance of the spacetime interval. The theory has been confirmed by particle lifetimes, by the operation of the Global Positioning System, and by every high-energy experiment.

In 1915 Einstein completed the general theory. Gravity is the curvature of spacetime. The Einstein field equation relates that curvature to the distribution of energy and momentum. The theory predicts the deflection of light by the Sun, the precession of Mercury’s perihelion, gravitational redshift, and gravitational waves. All have been observed. The same equation, applied to the cosmos, yields the expanding universe and the existence of black holes.

Einstein also introduced the cosmological constant, later set to zero, then restored by observation as the simplest model of dark energy. He contributed to the foundations of quantum statistics (Bose–Einstein condensation) and, with Podolsky and Rosen, formulated the argument that quantum mechanics appears incomplete. The argument led to Bell’s theorem and to experiments that confirmed the quantum predictions.

The body of work therefore spans the photoelectric effect, the atomic hypothesis, special and general relativity, the mass–energy relation, and the early critique of quantum completeness. Each part has been tested. Each remains in use.

title: The Principle of Least Action
paras: The principle of least action states that the actual path taken by a system between two configurations is the path that makes the action stationary. The action is the integral of the Lagrangian:
\[ S = \int L\, dt, \qquad L = T - V. \]

For a particle the Lagrangian is kinetic energy minus potential energy. The condition \(\delta S = 0\) yields the Euler–Lagrange equations, which are equivalent to Newton’s laws. The same variational statement works for fields. The action for the electromagnetic field or for the metric of general relativity produces Maxwell’s equations or the Einstein equation when it is required to be stationary.

Feynman regarded the principle as the most fundamental formulation of classical mechanics. It makes no reference to forces. It refers only to the comparison of entire paths. In the path-integral formulation of quantum mechanics the same action appears in the phase of each path. The classical path is the one about which the phase varies least; neighboring paths interfere constructively. The principle is therefore the classical limit of the quantum sum over histories.

The principle does not require the action to be a minimum. It requires it to be stationary. In some cases the stationary path is a maximum or a saddle. The terminology “least action” is traditional and slightly inaccurate. The content is the stationarity condition. That condition is sufficient to generate the equations of motion for every fundamental theory now in use.

title: The Maximum Force
paras: General relativity implies a maximum force. The value is \( c^4 / 4G \), about \( 3 \times 10^{43} \) newtons. No larger force can be exerted. The same limit appears as a maximum power \( c^5 / 4G \). Both follow from the requirement that the horizon of a black hole cannot be crossed by a signal and from the definition of the horizon itself.

The limit is local. It applies to the flow of energy or momentum through a surface. Distant objects can recede faster than light because the intervening space expands. The force limit does not constrain that recession. It constrains what can be done at a single place.

The existence of the limit is equivalent to the existence of black-hole horizons. Any attempt to exceed the force produces a horizon. The statement is therefore not an extra postulate. It is a rewriting of the content of the Einstein equation in the language of force and power. Experimental tests are indirect. They consist of the confirmed predictions of general relativity itself. No violation has been observed.

title: Waves and Their Distinguishing Properties
paras: A wave is a travelling disturbance that carries energy and momentum without a net transport of matter. Sound, water waves, light, and gravitational waves all satisfy the definition. Six properties distinguish wave motion from the motion of rigid bodies.

Superposition: linear waves add and can cancel. The result is interference. Diffraction is the consequence of interference that allows waves to spread around obstacles. Refraction is the change of direction at an interface where the propagation speed changes. Dispersion is the dependence of speed on frequency; it separates colours in a rainbow and stretches distant thunder. Damping is the progressive loss of amplitude. Polarization is the restriction of the oscillation direction for transverse waves.

None of these six effects occurs for the centre-of-mass motion of ordinary rigid bodies. Their presence is therefore diagnostic of wave motion. Light exhibits all six. Gravitational waves have shown superposition, damping, and polarization; the remaining three are still unobserved.

Every sinusoidal wave obeys \(\lambda f = c\), where \(\lambda\) is the wavelength, \(f\) the frequency, and \(c\) the phase speed. When \(c\) depends on \(\lambda\), the wave is dispersive. Sound in air is nearly non-dispersive, which is why speech remains intelligible at a distance. Water waves are strongly dispersive.

The energy density of a harmonic wave is proportional to the square of the time and space derivatives of the displacement. The momentum density is proportional to the product of those derivatives. Reflection from a fixed obstacle reverses the component of momentum normal to the surface, producing equal angles of incidence and reflection.

title: Huygens’ Principle and the Dimensionality of Space
paras: In three spatial dimensions a wave front may be reconstructed by treating every point on the front as the source of a secondary spherical wavelet. The envelope of the wavelets gives the position of the front at a later time. The construction, due to Huygens, correctly describes reflection, refraction, and, with Fresnel’s addition of interference, diffraction. It is a direct consequence of the wave equation in an odd number of dimensions greater than or equal to three.

The principle fails in two dimensions. A circular pulse leaves a wake; the interior never returns to rest. A stone dropped into a still pond continues to radiate after the stone has vanished. The mathematical reason is that the delta-function solution of the wave equation that propagates outward and leaves no residual amplitude exists only when the dimension is odd and at least three. In even dimensions every frequency travels at a different speed, so a sharp pulse cannot be maintained.

The practical consequence is that a room becomes dark when the light is switched off, and that speech ends when the speaker stops. Both facts depend on our living in a three-dimensional space. In a two-dimensional world the same signals would continue indefinitely.

title: The Motions of the Earth
paras: The Earth rotates on its axis once every sidereal day (86 164 s). It revolves about the Sun once every sidereal year (365.256 days). The axis is tilted 23.4° to the orbital plane; the tilt varies between 22.1° and 24.5° with a 41 000-year period. The axis itself precesses with a 25 800-year period and nutates with an 18.6-year period of 19 arc-seconds. These three astronomical cycles—obliquity, precession, and eccentricity—modulate the seasonal distribution of sunlight and have produced the succession of ice ages recorded in ice cores and marine sediments.

The Earth’s orbit is an ellipse of eccentricity 0.017. The semi-major axis is one astronomical unit, 149.6 million kilometres. The orbital speed is 29.8 km/s. The Sun itself orbits the galactic centre at 220 km/s, completing one revolution in about 225 million years. The Solar System oscillates above and below the galactic plane with a period of roughly 62 million years.

Relative to the cosmic microwave background the Solar System moves at 370 km/s. All of these motions are unfelt. Uniform velocity produces no local effect; only accelerations are detectable, and most of the accelerations associated with the larger motions lie below the threshold of human sensation. The principle that uniform motion is equivalent to rest was stated by Galileo and remains the foundation of both Newtonian and relativistic mechanics.

title: Solitons
paras: A soliton is a localized wave that propagates without changing shape and that survives collisions with other solitons intact. The classic example is the solitary wave observed by John Scott Russell in a canal in 1834: a single elevation of water that travelled for miles without dispersing. The mathematical model is the Korteweg–de Vries equation
\[ \partial_t A + A\partial_x A + b\partial_x^3 A = 0. \]
Its solutions interpenetrate and emerge unchanged. The same behaviour appears in optical fibres, in plasmas, and in certain magnetic materials.

A soliton is intermediate between a particle and a wave. It is localized like a particle and extended like a wave. It carries energy, momentum, and, in some cases, topological charge. Because the shape is preserved by a balance between nonlinearity and dispersion, the soliton is stable against small perturbations.

Solitons have been used to transmit data over long optical links and to model domain walls, dislocations, and certain elementary excitations in condensed matter. They remain classical solutions of nonlinear wave equations. Their quantum counterparts appear as stable particles or as topological defects in quantum field theory. No fundamental soliton has been observed that is not already accounted for by the Standard Model or by general relativity.

title: Conservation Laws
paras: Energy, momentum, and angular momentum are conserved in every isolated system. The conservation laws follow from symmetries of the underlying action. Time-translation invariance yields energy conservation. Spatial-translation invariance yields momentum conservation. Rotational invariance yields angular-momentum conservation. The connection is Noether’s theorem.

In mechanics the statements are elementary. The total energy of a collection of particles interacting through forces that derive from a potential is constant. The total momentum is constant when no external force acts. The total angular momentum about any fixed point is constant when no external torque acts. The same statements hold, with the appropriate field expressions, for the electromagnetic field and for the gravitational field.

Apparent violations are always the result of an incomplete accounting. Heat is disordered kinetic energy. Radiation carries both energy and momentum. When those contributions are included, the balances close. No experiment has shown a violation of any of the three laws in an isolated system.

The laws define the quantities they conserve. Energy is the quantity that is constant because the laws do not depend on the absolute time. Momentum is the quantity that is constant because the laws do not depend on absolute position. The definitions are operational and have been confirmed from the scale of elementary particles to the scale of galaxy clusters.

title: The Equivalence of Inertial and Gravitational Mass
paras: Galileo argued that all bodies fall with the same acceleration in the absence of air resistance. The argument is that a heavy body and a light body tied together must fall at the same rate as either alone; otherwise the combination would be inconsistent. Newton later distinguished inertial mass (the quantity that appears in \( F = ma \)) from gravitational mass (the quantity that appears in the inverse-square law). Their equality is required by the observation that all bodies fall alike.

The equality has been tested to better than one part in \( 10^{13} \). Torsion-balance experiments, lunar laser ranging, and satellite measurements all confirm it. In general relativity the equality is elevated to a principle: the local effects of gravity are indistinguishable from the effects of acceleration. The principle is the foundation of the geometric description of gravity.

No composition dependence has been found. Bodies of different materials, different nuclear binding energies, and different gravitational self-energies fall at the same rate within experimental limits. The result constrains theories that attempt to modify general relativity or to introduce new long-range forces.

title: Sound and the Human Voice
paras: Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure wave. Its speed is \(\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}\), approximately 340 m/s at room temperature. The speed is nearly independent of frequency, so speech remains intelligible over distance. Dispersion is weak; an echo reproduces the original waveform with only minor distortion.

The human voice is produced by the vibration of the vocal folds. Air from the lungs passes through the glottis. The Bernoulli effect lowers the pressure when the folds approach, drawing them together; the pressure then rises and the folds separate. The cycle repeats at the fundamental frequency of the note. The vocal tract acts as a resonator that filters the harmonic spectrum, producing the formants that distinguish vowels.

The intensity range of the voice exceeds 80 dB. The frequency range of a trained singer can span more than five octaves. The same physical elements—energy source, oscillator, resonator, and radiator—appear in every musical instrument. The voice is distinguished by the continuous control the singer exerts over tension, airflow, and cavity shape.

Otoacoustic emissions confirm that the ear itself generates sound. The hair cells of the cochlea oscillate spontaneously. The emissions can be measured with sensitive microphones and are used to diagnose hearing without invasive procedures.

title: The Principle of Least Action in Everyday Motion
paras: Nature is lazy. The path taken by a system is the one that minimizes the action. For a particle the action is the integral of kinetic energy minus potential energy. The condition that the action be stationary produces Newton’s second law. The same principle governs light. In a medium of varying index the path is the one that takes the least time. That is Fermat’s principle. It is the optical form of the least-action principle.

The principle explains why a thrown stone follows a parabola, why light bends at an interface, and why a soap film forms a minimal surface. In each case the observed motion is the one for which a simple integral is stationary. No force law need be postulated separately. The force law is the consequence of the variational statement.

The principle remains valid in relativity and in quantum mechanics. In the latter the action appears as the phase of each path in the path integral. The classical path is recovered as the path of stationary phase. Everyday motion is therefore the macroscopic limit of a deeper variational structure that governs all known fundamental interactions.

title: Friction and the Irreversibility of Everyday Motion
paras: Friction converts ordered mechanical energy into disordered thermal energy. The conversion is irreversible. A sliding block comes to rest. The reverse process—a block spontaneously beginning to slide by absorbing heat from its surroundings—has never been observed. The second law of thermodynamics quantifies the irreversibility. The entropy of an isolated system does not decrease.

At the microscopic level every collision is reversible. The irreversibility appears only when the number of degrees of freedom is large. The ordered motion of the block is shared among an enormous number of molecular degrees of freedom. The probability of those degrees of freedom reorganizing so as to return the energy to the block is vanishingly small. Friction is therefore the macroscopic signature of the second law.

The same irreversibility appears in viscosity, in electrical resistance, and in the damping of sound. In each case a macroscopic current or oscillation decays while the entropy of the thermal bath increases. No exception is known. The arrow of everyday time is the arrow of increasing entropy.

title: The Flow of Fluids
paras: A fluid is a substance that cannot support a static shear stress. It flows. The motion is described by the Navier–Stokes equation, which expresses the conservation of momentum for a continuous medium. The equation contains a term for pressure gradients, a term for viscous stresses, and a term for external forces such as gravity.

At low speeds and high viscosities the flow is laminar. Layers slide past one another with little mixing. At high speeds or low viscosities the flow becomes turbulent. Turbulence is characterized by eddies on many scales and by an enhanced rate of mixing and dissipation. The transition is governed by the Reynolds number, the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces. Above a critical value the laminar solution is unstable.

Bernoulli’s principle follows from the steady, inviscid limit of the momentum equation. Along a streamline the sum of pressure and kinetic-energy density is constant when gravity is neglected. The principle explains the lift of an airfoil, the curve of a spinning ball, and the operation of a carburetor. It is an energy statement for an idealized fluid. Real fluids always dissipate some energy through viscosity.

The same equations describe the flow of air, of water, of blood, and of the molten rock in the Earth’s mantle. The mathematics is universal. The observed patterns differ only because the Reynolds numbers and the boundary conditions differ.

title: Heat and Temperature
paras: Temperature is the quantity that is equal when two systems are in thermal equilibrium. It is proportional to the average kinetic energy per degree of freedom in an ideal gas. The proportionality constant is Boltzmann’s constant. Heat is energy transferred by virtue of a temperature difference.

The first law of thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy of a system equals the heat added minus the work done by the system. The law is the conservation of energy applied to thermal processes. The second law states that heat does not spontaneously flow from cold to hot and that the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. The two laws together forbid perpetual-motion machines of both the first and the second kind.

The ideal-gas law, \( PV = NkT \), follows from the kinetic theory once the temperature is identified with the average kinetic energy. Real gases deviate from the law at high densities or low temperatures because of intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume. The deviations are described by the van der Waals equation and by more elaborate equations of state.

Phase transitions occur when the free energy of two different arrangements of the same molecules becomes equal. Melting, boiling, and sublimation are first-order transitions marked by latent heat and by a discontinuous change in density. The critical point is the end of the boiling curve, where the distinction between liquid and gas disappears.

title: The Rotation of Rigid Bodies
paras: A rigid body has six degrees of freedom: three of translation and three of rotation. The rotational motion is governed by the angular-momentum equation. The moment of inertia tensor relates angular velocity to angular momentum. For a principal-axis rotation the relation is scalar. For a general rotation the angular-velocity vector and the angular-momentum vector are not parallel.

Euler’s equations describe the free rotation of a rigid body. They predict that rotation about the axis of intermediate moment of inertia is unstable. A book tossed into the air rotates stably about its longest or shortest axis and tumbles about the intermediate axis. The instability is geometric. It follows from the conservation of energy and angular momentum alone.

Precession occurs when a torque acts on a spinning body. The angular-momentum vector moves perpendicular to the torque. The result is the slow conical motion of a spinning top or of the Earth’s axis under the gravitational torque of the Sun and Moon. The same mathematics describes the motion of a gyroscope and the stabilization of a bicycle wheel.

The kinetic energy of rotation is \(\frac12 I\omega^2\). It is independent of the translational kinetic energy. Both are conserved separately when no external torque or force acts. The separation is a consequence of the rigidity constraint.

title: Oscillations
paras: An oscillation is a periodic motion about an equilibrium. For small amplitudes the restoring force is proportional to the displacement. The motion is then simple harmonic. The period is independent of amplitude and is given by \( 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} \) for a mass on a spring and by \( 2\pi\sqrt{l/g} \) for a simple pendulum.

When friction is present the oscillation is damped. The amplitude decays exponentially. When the damping is light the frequency is nearly unchanged. When the damping is critical the system returns to equilibrium as quickly as possible without oscillating. When the damping is heavier the return is slower and monotonic.

A driven oscillator responds most strongly when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency. The response is resonance. The amplitude at resonance is limited by the damping. The phase of the response shifts from in-phase below resonance to out-of-phase above resonance. The same behaviour appears in electrical circuits, in atoms driven by light, and in mechanical structures driven by wind or earthquakes.

Coupled oscillators exchange energy. Two pendulums connected by a weak spring exhibit beats. The energy flows back and forth at a frequency set by the coupling strength. The normal modes of the system are the patterns in which every part oscillates at the same frequency. Any motion can be written as a superposition of normal modes.

title: The Electromagnetic Field
paras: Electric charge is conserved. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. The force is described by Coulomb’s law at low speeds. Moving charges produce magnetic fields. Changing magnetic fields produce electric fields. The two effects are united in Maxwell’s equations.

In vacuum the equations admit wave solutions that travel at the speed \( 1/\sqrt{\varepsilon_0\mu_0} \). That speed is the measured speed of light. Light is therefore an electromagnetic wave. The same equations describe radio waves, microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays, and gamma rays. They differ only in frequency.

The energy density of the field is proportional to \( E^2 + c^2 B^2 \). The momentum density is proportional to the Poynting vector \( \mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B} \). Both quantities are conserved when the field interacts with charges, provided the mechanical energy and momentum of the charges are included. The field therefore carries energy and momentum exactly as a wave must.

The Lorentz force law gives the force on a charge moving in the field. Together with Maxwell’s equations it constitutes the classical theory of electromagnetism. The theory is accurate from the scale of atoms to the scale of galaxies whenever quantum effects and gravitational curvature can be neglected.

title: Atoms and the Periodic Table
paras: Matter is composed of atoms. Each atom consists of a positively charged nucleus surrounded by negatively charged electrons. The number of electrons equals the number of protons in a neutral atom and is the atomic number. The atomic number determines the chemical identity of the element.

The electrons occupy discrete energy levels. The levels are filled according to the Pauli principle: no two electrons can occupy the same quantum state. The resulting shell structure produces the periodic repetition of chemical properties. Elements in the same column of the periodic table have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell and therefore similar chemistry.

The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. The strong interaction binds them. The binding energy per nucleon reaches a maximum near iron. Lighter nuclei can release energy by fusion; heavier nuclei can release energy by fission. Both processes are observed in nature and in technology.

The sizes of atoms are set by the balance between the electrostatic attraction of the nucleus and the kinetic energy required by the uncertainty principle. Typical atomic radii are a few tenths of a nanometre. Typical nuclear radii are a few femtometres. The emptiness of the atom is therefore extreme.

title: The Structure of Solids
paras: In a crystalline solid the atoms occupy the sites of a regular lattice. The lattice may be simple cubic, face-centred cubic, body-centred cubic, hexagonal, or one of the less symmetric Bravais types. The repeating unit is the unit cell. X-ray diffraction measures the spacing and the symmetry of the cell.

Electrons in a solid form energy bands. When a band is partially filled the solid is a metal and conducts electricity. When a band is full and separated by a gap from the next empty band the solid is an insulator or a semiconductor. The size of the gap determines the electrical behaviour. Silicon and germanium are semiconductors because their gaps are a fraction of an electron-volt. Diamond is an insulator because its gap is several electron-volts.

Defects control many properties. Vacancies, interstitials, and dislocations allow plastic deformation. Impurity atoms donate or accept electrons and thereby dope a semiconductor. Grain boundaries in a polycrystalline material scatter electrons and phonons and raise the electrical and thermal resistance.

The same band structure that determines conductivity also determines optical absorption, magnetism, and superconductivity. The macroscopic properties of a solid are therefore the collective consequence of the quantum states of its electrons and of the geometry of its lattice.

title: Stars and Nuclear Burning
paras: A star is a self-gravitating ball of plasma in which nuclear fusion supplies the energy that balances radiative loss. On the main sequence the fusion reaction is the conversion of hydrogen to helium. The proton–proton chain dominates in stars of solar mass and below. The CNO cycle dominates in more massive stars. Both release about 0.7 percent of the rest mass as energy.

The structure of a star is fixed by four equations: hydrostatic equilibrium, mass continuity, energy transport, and energy generation. The solutions form a one-parameter family labelled by mass. Low-mass stars are cool and long-lived. High-mass stars are hot, luminous, and short-lived. The Sun will remain on the main sequence for about ten billion years.

When hydrogen is exhausted in the core the star contracts, heats, and ignites helium. Subsequent stages produce carbon, oxygen, and heavier elements up to iron. Beyond iron fusion absorbs energy. The core collapses. In stars above roughly eight solar masses the collapse produces a supernova and leaves a neutron star or a black hole. The ejected material enriches the interstellar medium with the heavy elements from which later planets and life are made.
The observed Hertzsprung–Russell diagram matches the predicted tracks. Stellar evolution is therefore one of the best-tested applications of nuclear physics and of hydrostatics.

title: Black Holes in Astrophysics
paras: A black hole is a region from which no signal can escape to infinity. The boundary is the event horizon. For a non-rotating hole the horizon radius is \( 2GM/c^2 \). Stellar-mass black holes form in the collapse of massive stars. Supermassive black holes, millions to billions of solar masses, occupy the centres of most large galaxies.

The Event Horizon Telescope has imaged the shadow of the black hole in M87 and of the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way. The diameter of the shadow matches the prediction of general relativity. Gravitational-wave detectors have recorded the mergers of stellar-mass black holes. The waveforms match the numerical solutions of the Einstein equation.

Matter falling toward a black hole forms an accretion disk. Viscosity transports angular momentum outward and allows the gas to spiral inward. The released gravitational energy heats the disk and can power quasars and X-ray binaries. The efficiency of conversion of rest mass to radiation can exceed 10 percent, higher than nuclear fusion.

No information about the interior can reach an external observer. The classical theory ends at the singularity. Quantum effects are expected to modify the singularity, but no complete theory yet exists. The exterior geometry is nevertheless accurately described by the Kerr or Schwarzschild solution.

title: Quantum Mechanics of the Atom
paras: The electrons in an atom are described by the Schrödinger equation. The solutions are stationary states labelled by quantum numbers. The energy levels of hydrogen are \( E_n = -13.6\,\mathrm{eV}/n^2 \). Transitions between levels emit or absorb photons whose frequencies match the observed spectral lines.

The Pauli exclusion principle requires that no two electrons occupy the same state. The principle, together with the Coulomb interaction, produces the shell structure of the periodic table. Chemical bonding arises when atoms share or transfer electrons so as to fill or empty outer shells.

The uncertainty principle limits the simultaneous knowledge of position and momentum. An electron confined to an atomic volume must possess a minimum kinetic energy. That kinetic energy balances the electrostatic attraction and sets the size of the atom. The same balance determines the sizes of molecules and the lattice spacings of solids.

Measurement collapses the wave function onto an eigenstate of the measured observable. The probability of each outcome is the squared modulus of the corresponding amplitude. The rule has been confirmed in every tested system. The interpretation of the collapse remains open. The predictive content does not.

title: The Standard Model of Particle Physics
paras: The Standard Model describes the electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions. It contains twelve fermions—six quarks and six leptons—and the gauge bosons that mediate the forces. The Higgs boson generates the masses of the W and Z bosons and of the fermions through the Yukawa couplings.

The electromagnetic and weak interactions are unified in the electroweak theory. At energies above the electroweak scale the distinction disappears. The strong interaction is described by quantum chromodynamics. Quarks carry colour charge and are confined. Free quarks are never observed. The observed hadrons are colour-neutral combinations of quarks.

Every particle predicted by the model has been found. The measured couplings and masses agree with the predictions to high precision. The model is nevertheless incomplete. It does not include gravity. It does not explain the values of its own parameters. It does not account for the observed dark matter or for the baryon asymmetry of the universe. It remains the most accurate theory of the non-gravitational interactions.

title: The Origin of the Elements
paras: Hydrogen and most of the helium were produced in the first three minutes. The remaining elements were produced in stars. Helium burning yields carbon and oxygen. Carbon burning and oxygen burning yield neon, magnesium, silicon, and sulfur. Silicon burning yields iron-group nuclei. Beyond iron, neutron-capture processes produce the heavier elements.

The slow neutron-capture process operates in asymptotic-giant-branch stars. The rapid process operates in neutron-star mergers and possibly in some supernovae. The observed abundance patterns of the heavy elements match the predictions of these two processes once the neutron fluxes and the seed nuclei are specified.

Supernovae and stellar winds return the newly synthesized nuclei to the interstellar medium. Subsequent generations of stars form from the enriched gas. The Sun is a third-generation star. The Earth and its inhabitants are made of nuclei that were forged in earlier stars and ejected in their deaths.

The abundances measured in the solar system, in other stars, and in the interstellar medium are consistent with this history. Nuclear astrophysics therefore accounts for the chemical composition of ordinary matter.

title: Life and the Second Law
paras: A living organism maintains a low internal entropy by exporting entropy to its surroundings. It takes in free energy—sunlight or chemical fuel—and returns heat and waste. The total entropy of organism plus surroundings increases. The second law is not violated.

The free energy is used to synthesize ordered macromolecules, to maintain concentration gradients, and to perform mechanical work. The efficiency of the conversion is limited by the Carnot factor and by the irreversibility of the chemical reactions. Typical biological efficiencies lie well below the theoretical maximum.

Evolution by natural selection increases the adaptedness of populations. It does not decrease the entropy of the biosphere. The information stored in genomes is paid for by the entropy exported during the metabolic processes that replicate and repair the DNA. The arrow of biological complexity points in the same direction as the thermodynamic arrow.
No known organism operates outside these constraints. Life is a far-from-equilibrium process that is fully consistent with the second law.

title: The Measurement of Time
paras: Time is measured by counting periodic processes. The rotation of the Earth, the orbit of the Moon, and the vibration of a quartz crystal have all served as clocks. The present definition of the second is 9 192 631 770 periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between two hyperfine levels of the caesium-133 atom.

Atomic clocks achieve stabilities better than one part in \( 10^{16} \). Optical clocks that use transitions in the visible or ultraviolet are expected to reach one part in \( 10^{18} \). At that level the gravitational redshift produced by a height difference of one centimetre becomes measurable. Clocks therefore function as gravimeters.

The same atomic transitions define the metre through the fixed value of the speed of light. Length and time are no longer independent. The practical realization of both units rests on the same quantum standard. The historical separation of the two quantities has been replaced by a single metrological foundation.

title: The Speed of Light as a Conversion Factor
paras: The speed of light in vacuum is defined to be exactly 299 792 458 m/s. The metre is the distance light travels in 1/299 792 458 of a second. The definition makes \( c \) a conversion factor between the units of length and time rather than a quantity to be measured.

The invariance of \( c \) is a physical fact. The numerical value is a convention. Once the value is fixed, measurements of length become measurements of time and vice versa. The same convention appears in the natural units used in particle physics, where \( c = 1 \) and energies are quoted in electron-volts.

The definition does not alter any prediction of relativity. It merely chooses the units in which the invariant speed has the value 1. All measurable ratios remain unchanged. The practical advantage is that length standards can be realized by time standards, which are more stable.

title: Gravitational Waves
paras: A gravitational wave is a ripple in the curvature of spacetime that propagates at the speed of light. It is produced by any accelerating mass quadrupole. The strongest sources are the mergers of black holes and neutron stars.

The waves stretch and compress space transversely. A ring of free particles is deformed into an ellipse that oscillates at the wave frequency. The strain is minute. For a stellar-mass merger at cosmological distance the fractional change in length is of order \( 10^{-21} \).

Laser interferometers have detected dozens of such events. The waveforms match the predictions of general relativity. The arrival of gravitational waves from a neutron-star merger coincided with a gamma-ray burst and with an optical transient, confirming that the waves travel at \( c \) to high precision.

The detections open a new observational window. They measure the masses and spins of black holes, the equation of state of neutron-star matter, and the expansion rate of the universe. Future detectors will extend the reach to the entire observable volume and to lower frequencies.

title: The Cosmic Microwave Background
paras: The cosmic microwave background is thermal radiation that fills the universe. Its spectrum is that of a black body at 2.725 K. The radiation was released when the universe cooled to about 3000 K and electrons combined with nuclei to form neutral atoms. The photons have travelled freely ever since. The expansion has redshifted their temperature by a factor of approximately 1100.

The background is isotropic to one part in \( 10^5 \). The small anisotropies are the imprint of density fluctuations that existed at recombination. Those fluctuations grew by gravitational instability into the galaxies and clusters observed today. The angular power spectrum of the anisotropies measures the baryon density, the dark-matter density, the curvature of space, and the spectral index of the primordial fluctuations.

Polarization of the background records the motion of the plasma at last scattering and, potentially, the presence of primordial gravitational waves. Current limits on the latter constrain the energy scale of inflation. The background therefore supplies the most precise cosmological data set available.

title: Inflation
paras: Inflation is a brief period of accelerated expansion in the early universe. It solves the horizon problem: regions that are now far apart were once in causal contact. It solves the flatness problem: any initial curvature is diluted to an unobservable level. It also generates the nearly scale-invariant spectrum of density fluctuations observed in the microwave background.

The mechanism is a scalar field whose potential energy dominates the density. While the field rolls slowly the expansion is exponential. When the field reaches the minimum of its potential the energy is converted into ordinary particles. The subsequent evolution is the standard hot Big Bang.

No direct detection of the inflaton exists. The predictions for the spectrum of fluctuations and for the absence of large curvature match observation. Alternative scenarios that produce the same spectrum have been proposed. Distinguishing them requires measurements of non-Gaussianity or of primordial gravitational waves that are not yet available.
Inflation remains the simplest framework that accounts for the initial conditions of the hot Big Bang. It is not yet a unique or fully tested theory.

title: The Arrow of Time in Cosmology
paras: The thermodynamic arrow points from the low-entropy early universe to the higher-entropy present. The low entropy is not a consequence of the dynamical laws. It is a boundary condition. The microwave background is smooth. That smoothness is a low-entropy state for the gravitational field. Subsequent clumping into stars and black holes increases the entropy.

The psychological arrow—the fact that we remember the past and not the future—aligns with the thermodynamic arrow. Records form only when entropy increases. The cosmological arrow—the expansion itself—does not by itself define a direction. A contracting universe with the same low-entropy boundary condition would still have a thermodynamic arrow pointing away from that boundary.

Why the initial entropy was low remains unexplained. Proposals include special initial conditions, inflationary smoothing, and selection effects within a larger ensemble. None is established. The existence of the arrow is nevertheless an observed fact about the solution we inhabit.

title: The Doppler Effect
paras: The Doppler effect is the change in observed frequency caused by relative motion between source and observer. For sound the shift depends on whether the source or the observer is moving, because sound propagates in a medium. For light in vacuum the shift depends only on the relative velocity.
In the low-speed limit the fractional frequency change is \( v/c \) for both cases. At relativistic speeds the formula becomes
\[ f = f_0\sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}, \]
where \( \beta = v/c \) and the velocity is the component along the line of sight. Recession lowers the frequency; approach raises it.

The effect is measured in the spectra of stars and galaxies, in radar speed guns, and in the precise timing of pulsars. It also appears in the transverse Doppler shift, a purely relativistic time-dilation effect that has been confirmed with fast ions. The same principle underlies the cosmological redshift once the expansion of space is taken into account.
No experiment has shown a dependence of the vacuum speed of light on the speed of the source. The Doppler formula for light is therefore a direct consequence of the invariance of \( c \).

title: Aberration of Light
paras: Aberration is the apparent displacement of a star’s position caused by the motion of the observer. The Earth moves at 30 km/s around the Sun. A telescope must therefore be tilted by an angle \( \theta \approx v/c \) in the direction of motion in order to keep the star centred. The annual change in the required tilt is the aberration ellipse.

Bradley measured the effect in 1728 and thereby determined the speed of light to within a few percent of the modern value. The same measurement demonstrated that the Earth moves. The classical formula is sufficient for the Earth’s orbital speed. At higher speeds the relativistic expression
\[ \tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta'}{\gamma(\cos\theta'+\beta)} \]
must be used. The formula has been confirmed with particle beams and with precise astrometry.

Aberration is distinct from parallax. Parallax is a change in direction caused by a change in the observer’s position. Aberration is a change caused by the observer’s velocity. Both effects are present in stellar observations and must be separated.

title: The Michelson–Morley Experiment
paras: The Michelson–Morley experiment compared the speed of light in two perpendicular directions. An interferometer was floated on mercury and rotated. No shift of the interference fringes was observed at the level of sensitivity corresponding to the Earth’s orbital speed.

The null result is explained by the invariance of \( c \). Every inertial observer measures the same speed. There is no preferred frame in which light travels at a different speed. Subsequent experiments with lasers, cryogenic resonators, and particle beams have confirmed the isotropy to better than one part in \( 10^{17} \).

The experiment did not disprove the existence of a medium. It showed that if a medium exists, it does not define a rest frame that can be detected by measuring the two-way speed of light. The one-way speed is fixed by convention once the two-way speed is known to be isotropic. The result remains one of the foundations of special relativity.

title: Length Contraction and Time Dilation
paras: A rod moving lengthwise relative to an observer is measured to be shorter than its proper length by the factor \( \sqrt{1-v^2/c^2} \). A clock moving relative to an observer is measured to run slow by the same factor. Both effects follow from the invariance of the speed of light and from the definition of simultaneity.

The proper length is the length measured in the frame in which the rod is at rest. The proper time is the time measured by a clock that travels with the object. Coordinate length and coordinate time differ from these invariants once relative motion is present. The differences have been confirmed by the extended lifetimes of fast muons, by the operation of particle accelerators, and by the frequency shifts of clocks flown in aircraft.

The effects are reciprocal. Each observer finds the other’s rods contracted and the other’s clocks slow. There is no contradiction because the observers disagree on which events are simultaneous. The invariant is the spacetime interval. All measured contractions and dilations are projections of that interval onto different axes.

title: The Twin Paradox
paras: Two twins separate. One remains on Earth. The other travels at high speed to a distant point and returns. The travelling twin ages less. The difference is the difference in proper time along the two world-lines. The stay-at-home twin follows a straight path in spacetime. The traveller follows a bent path. The bent path is shorter in proper time.

The acceleration that reverses the traveller’s velocity is not the source of the asymmetry. The asymmetry exists between any two paths that begin and end at the same events. Acceleration is needed only to make the paths meet again. Once the paths are fixed, the proper-time difference is fixed by the geometry.

The effect has been measured with atomic clocks flown around the world and with unstable particles circulating in storage rings. In every case the moving clock records less proper time. The result is a direct consequence of the invariance of the spacetime interval. It does not require general relativity.

title: Mass, Energy and Momentum in Relativity
paras: The energy and momentum of a particle form a four-vector. Its magnitude is the rest energy \( mc^2 \). The relations are
\[ E = \gamma mc^2, \qquad p = \gamma mv, \qquad E^2 = p^2c^2 + m^2c^4. \]

At low speeds the expressions reduce to the Newtonian kinetic energy and momentum plus the constant rest energy. At high speeds the energy grows without bound as \( v \) approaches \( c \). No finite energy can accelerate a massive particle to the speed of light.

The same relations hold for systems of particles and for fields once the appropriate total four-momentum is used. Mass can be converted into other forms of energy and vice versa. The conversion is observed in particle–antiparticle annihilation, in nuclear reactions, and in the mass defect of bound systems. The factor \( c^2 \) is large, so macroscopic mass changes are minute except in nuclear and particle processes.

The invariant mass of a system is not the sum of the rest masses of its parts. Binding energy and relative kinetic energy contribute. The invariant mass is the magnitude of the total four-momentum. It is the quantity that is conserved in every inertial frame.

title: The Equivalence Principle
paras: The local effects of a gravitational field are indistinguishable from the effects of acceleration. An observer in a freely falling elevator finds that objects float. An observer in a uniformly accelerating rocket in free space finds that objects fall. No local experiment can tell the two situations apart.

The principle implies that light bends in a gravitational field and that clocks run at different rates at different heights. Both effects have been measured. The bending of light by the Sun is 1.75 arc-seconds. The fractional frequency shift between two clocks separated by height \( h \) is \( gh/c^2 \).

General relativity elevates the principle to the statement that spacetime is curved. Freely falling world-lines are geodesics. The curvature is related to the distribution of energy and momentum by the Einstein equation. The equivalence principle is the local limit of that equation. It remains the conceptual foundation of the geometric theory of gravity.

title: Gravitational Redshift
paras: A clock deeper in a gravitational potential runs slow relative to a clock higher up. The fractional shift is \( \Delta\Phi/c^2 \), where \( \Phi \) is the Newtonian potential. The effect is independent of the mechanism of the clock. It has been measured with gamma rays over a height of 22 metres, with atomic clocks over centimetres, and with the frequency standards of the Global Positioning System.

The same shift appears in the light emitted by the surface of a white dwarf or by the accretion disk of a black hole. In the Schwarzschild geometry the exact formula is \( \sqrt{1-2GM/rc^2} \). At the horizon the redshift becomes infinite. No signal from the horizon itself can reach a distant observer.

The redshift is a direct consequence of the equivalence principle. It does not require the full apparatus of general relativity, only the local indistinguishability of gravity and acceleration. Its confirmation is therefore a confirmation of that principle.

title: The Schwarzschild Solution
paras: The Schwarzschild metric describes the spacetime outside a spherical, non-rotating mass. In standard coordinates it reads
\[ ds^2 = -\left(1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\right)c^2dt^2 + \left(1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\right)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2. \]

The coefficient of \( dt^2 \) vanishes at \( r = 2GM/c^2 \). That surface is the event horizon. Inside the horizon the roles of \( t \) and \( r \) interchange. Every future-directed path ends at the central singularity.

The solution predicts the correct perihelion precession of Mercury, the correct deflection of light, and the correct Shapiro time delay. It is the unique spherically symmetric vacuum solution of the Einstein equation. Any departure from spherical symmetry or from vacuum requires a different metric. For slowly rotating bodies the Kerr metric supplies the first corrections.

The horizon is a global feature. A local observer falling through it notices nothing special. The curvature invariants remain finite. Only the inability to send a signal to infinity distinguishes the interior.

title: Geodesics and Free Fall
paras: In general relativity a freely falling particle follows a geodesic—the straightest possible path in curved spacetime. The geodesic equation is
\[ \frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\frac{dx^\alpha}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\beta}{d\tau} = 0. \]
The Christoffel symbols \( \Gamma \) are determined by the metric. In the Newtonian limit the equation reduces to the ordinary acceleration \( \mathbf{g} \).

Light follows null geodesics. The condition \( ds = 0 \) replaces the proper-time parameterization. The same equation therefore governs both massive particles and photons. The observed bending of light and the Shapiro delay are the integrated effects of the Christoffel symbols along the path.

No force appears in the geodesic equation. The curvature of spacetime does all the work. The Newtonian force is the low-speed, weak-field approximation to that curvature. The geometric description is exact within classical general relativity.

title: The Einstein Equation
paras: The Einstein equation relates the curvature of spacetime to the distribution of energy and momentum:
\[ G_{\mu\nu} = \frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu\nu}. \]

The Einstein tensor \( G_{\mu\nu} \) is built from the Ricci tensor and the scalar curvature. It is divergenceless. The energy-momentum tensor \( T_{\mu\nu} \) is likewise divergenceless by local conservation of energy and momentum. The equation is therefore consistent.

In vacuum \( T_{\mu\nu} = 0 \) and the equation reduces to \( R_{\mu\nu} = 0 \). The Schwarzschild and Kerr solutions are vacuum solutions. When matter is present the equation determines the metric once an equation of state is supplied.
