paras: Bell’s theorem demonstrates that the statistical predictions of quantum mechanics for entangled particles cannot be reproduced by any local hidden-variable theory.

Two particles are prepared in an entangled state and sent to distant observers. Each observer chooses a measurement setting and records a binary outcome. A local hidden-variable theory assumes that the outcomes are predetermined by variables carried with the particles and that each observer’s result depends only on the local setting and on those shared variables. Under this assumption the correlations obey an inequality. One standard form (CHSH) states that a certain combination of four correlation functions cannot exceed 2 in absolute value.

Quantum mechanics predicts a larger value. For the spin singlet the correlation is minus the cosine of the angle between the analysers. Suitable choices of angle yield \( 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828 \). The quantum prediction therefore lies outside the bound required by local hidden variables.

Experiments with entangled photons, ions and superconducting circuits have measured the quantum value and violated the inequality. The violations persist when the measurement settings are chosen after the particles have left the source, closing the locality loophole, and when detection efficiencies are high enough to close the detection loophole. The observed correlations cannot be explained by any assignment of predetermined local properties.

The theorem does not imply that signals can be sent faster than light. Quantum mechanics itself forbids controllable signalling. It shows only that the correlations are stronger than those permitted by local pre-existing values. The experimental confirmation of that stronger correlation is one of the sharpest results in the foundations of physics.

title: Quantum Computing
paras: A quantum computer stores information in qubits. A qubit is a two-level quantum system that can exist in a superposition of its basis states. An \( n \)-qubit register can therefore occupy a superposition of all \( 2^n \) classical bit strings simultaneously.

Entanglement and interference allow certain algorithms to extract global properties of a function with fewer queries than any classical algorithm. Shor’s algorithm factors large integers in polynomial time by finding the period of a modular exponential function. Grover’s algorithm searches an unstructured database of \( N \) items in roughly \( \sqrt{N} \) steps. Both rely on the coherent evolution of superpositions and on a final measurement that yields the desired result with high probability.

The practical obstacles are decoherence and gate errors. Interaction with the environment destroys the relative phases that encode the computation. Quantum error-correcting codes spread the logical information across many physical qubits so that local errors can be detected and reversed without measuring the logical state. Fault-tolerant thresholds exist: if the physical error rate lies below a few parts in \( 10^3 \) to \( 10^4 \), arbitrarily long computations are possible in principle.

Present devices contain tens to a few hundred qubits and execute circuits of limited depth. They have demonstrated small instances of quantum advantage on specially chosen sampling tasks. They have not yet run Shor’s algorithm on integers large enough to threaten cryptographic systems. The gap between the theoretical algorithms and large-scale, error-corrected machines remains the central engineering problem.

The computational model does not violate the Church–Turing thesis in its modern form. It supplies a different complexity scaling for particular problems. The scaling originates in the same interference of amplitudes that appears in every other quantum experiment.

title: Artificial Intelligence
paras: Artificial intelligence is the construction of systems that perform tasks ordinarily associated with human cognition: recognition, prediction, planning and the generation of language or images. Contemporary systems achieve these tasks by statistical learning from large data sets rather than by explicit symbolic rules.

A deep neural network is a composition of simple functions whose parameters are adjusted to minimise a loss on training examples. When the network is sufficiently large and the data sufficiently rich, the minimisation produces internal representations that support accurate classification, translation and synthesis. The same architecture, trained on text, yields language models that predict the next token with high fidelity. The models exhibit no independent goals. Their outputs are samples from the distribution implicit in the training data, conditioned on the prompt.

The performance gains have been empirical. Scaling laws relate loss to the number of parameters, the volume of data and the quantity of computation. The laws hold across many orders of magnitude. They do not yet supply a theory of why particular architectures generalise. Interpretability remains limited. The internal activations can be probed, but no complete mapping from weights to human-readable concepts exists for the largest models.

Applications already include medical imaging, protein-structure prediction, code generation and real-time translation. The systems remain narrow. They do not autonomously formulate scientific hypotheses, design experiments or revise their own objectives. Claims of imminent artificial general intelligence are conjectures. The present evidence shows only that statistical models of sufficient scale reproduce many patterns present in human-generated data.

The energy and data requirements are substantial. Training a frontier model consumes megawatt-hours and terabytes of text or images. The resulting capabilities are real and measurable. Their limits are equally measurable. Both are consequences of the same optimisation process.

title: The Origin of the Moon
paras: The Moon formed in a giant impact. A Mars-sized body struck the proto-Earth late in the accretion of the terrestrial planets. The collision ejected a disk of silicate vapour and melt into Earth orbit. The disk cooled and condensed. The Moon accreted from that disk within a few thousand years.

The hypothesis accounts for the Moon’s low density, its depletion in iron relative to Earth, and the identical oxygen-isotope ratios of lunar and terrestrial rocks. It also accounts for the angular momentum of the Earth–Moon system. Alternative models—capture, co-accretion, or fission of a rapidly spinning Earth—fail to satisfy the same constraints simultaneously.

High-resolution simulations show that the impactor’s core merged with Earth’s core while the mantle material formed the disk. Subsequent equilibration between the disk and the Earth’s atmosphere and magma ocean produced the observed isotopic match. The same event left Earth with a molten surface and an atmosphere of rock vapour. Both cooled within a few thousand years.

The impact occurred after the Earth had already differentiated. The Moon is therefore younger than the oldest terrestrial minerals. Radiometric ages of lunar samples place the event between 4.5 and 4.4 billion years ago. The hypothesis remains the only scenario consistent with the dynamical, chemical and chronological evidence.

title: The Origin of the Universe
paras: The observable universe expanded from a hot, dense state. The earliest direct evidence is the cosmic microwave background, released 380 000 years after the expansion began. Its spectrum and tiny anisotropies match the predictions of a nearly uniform plasma that cooled as it expanded. Nucleosynthesis a few minutes after the beginning produced the observed abundances of helium-4, deuterium and lithium-7 once the baryon density is fixed by the same background radiation.

Before nucleosynthesis the energies exceeded those accessible to accelerators. The electroweak transition, the confinement of quarks into hadrons, and any preceding inflationary phase lie in that regime. Inflation, if it occurred, would have stretched a microscopic region to macroscopic size, diluted curvature, and generated the nearly scale-invariant fluctuations later seen in the microwave background. No direct relic of inflation has been detected. The hypothesis remains the simplest account of the initial conditions required by the later evolution.

The expansion itself has no centre and no edge within the observable volume. Every comoving observer sees the same recession. Extrapolation of the Friedmann equation backward reaches a singularity in finite time under the assumptions of classical general relativity and of the energy conditions satisfied by ordinary matter. Quantum-gravitational effects are expected to modify the singularity. No controlled calculation yet replaces it with a definite earlier state.

The origin of the low entropy that permits the thermodynamic arrow, the origin of the baryon asymmetry, and the nature of the dark-matter particles are likewise open. The hot, expanding phase that begins with nucleosynthesis and continues to the present is nevertheless quantitatively confirmed by the background radiation, the light-element abundances and the large-scale distribution of galaxies.

title: The Origin of Life
paras: Life on Earth began with the appearance of chemical systems that could replicate and evolve. The earliest undisputed evidence is isotopic and morphological traces in rocks 3.5–3.8 billion years old. The transition from geochemistry to biochemistry therefore occurred within the first billion years of the planet’s history.

No laboratory experiment has yet produced a living cell from inorganic precursors. Prebiotic chemistry has demonstrated the abiotic synthesis of amino acids, nucleotides, lipids and short polymers under a range of conditions. It has also produced self-replicating RNA molecules and membrane-bounded vesicles that grow and divide. The integration of replication, metabolism and compartmentalisation into a single system remains incomplete.

Two broad settings are under investigation. Surface environments supply ultraviolet energy and wet–dry cycles that concentrate and polymerise monomers. Submarine hydrothermal vents supply continuous chemical gradients and mineral surfaces that can catalyse redox reactions. Both settings generate relevant organic compounds. Which, if either, hosted the first replicators is unknown.

The genetic code, the chiral homogeneity of biological molecules, and the universal core of metabolic pathways are consistent with descent from a single ancestral population. They do not identify the chemical steps that produced that population. The gap between the demonstrated reactions of organic chemistry and a self-sustaining, evolving cell is still unbridged. The existence of the gap is the present state of the evidence.

title: The RNA World Hypothesis
paras: The RNA world hypothesis proposes that early life used RNA both to store genetic information and to catalyse the reactions of metabolism. DNA later assumed the storage role and proteins assumed most catalytic roles. The hypothesis is motivated by the dual capacity of RNA and by the central position of RNA in modern translation and in many coenzymes.

Ribozymes demonstrate that RNA can catalyse specific reactions, including the formation of peptide bonds and the replication of short RNA strands. Laboratory evolution has produced ribozymes with improved polymerase activity. No ribozyme yet copies long RNA templates with the fidelity and speed required for an autonomous cell. The gap is quantitative, not qualitative.

Prebiotic synthesis of nucleotides under plausible early-Earth conditions has been demonstrated in several pathways. Polymerisation on mineral surfaces or in wet–dry cycles yields chains of tens of nucleotides. The spontaneous appearance of a self-replicating ribozyme from such mixtures has not been shown. Once such a molecule exists, Darwinian evolution can in principle improve it.

The hypothesis does not claim that RNA was the first informational polymer. It claims that an RNA-based stage is sufficient to bridge geochemistry and the last universal common ancestor, and that the molecular fossils in modern cells are the expected remnants of that stage. Alternative scenarios that begin with proteins, with lipids, or with other nucleic acids remain possible. The RNA world is the most fully articulated and experimentally supported of the current proposals. It is not yet a demonstrated historical pathway.

title: Prebiotic Chemistry
paras: Prebiotic chemistry is the study of the reactions that could have produced the molecular components of life from inorganic and simple organic precursors under early-Earth conditions. The field began with the demonstration that electrical discharges in reducing gas mixtures yield amino acids. Subsequent work has produced sugars, nucleobases, nucleotides, lipids and short polymers by a variety of pathways.

Aqueous spark-discharge and photochemical reactions generate amino acids and some nucleobases. Formose-type chemistry produces sugars from formaldehyde. More recent pathways synthesise activated nucleotides from cyanosulfidic precursors under conditions that include ultraviolet irradiation and wet–dry cycling. Mineral surfaces catalyse polymerisation. Lipid molecules spontaneously form vesicles that can grow and divide.

No single set of conditions has yet generated all required monomers and assembled them into replicating, compartmentalised systems. Concentrations, pH, temperature and the presence of interfering side reactions remain constraints. The chemical inventory of carbonaceous meteorites shows that many of the same compounds form in abiotic settings beyond Earth. The reactions are therefore cosmochemically plausible.

The experimental results establish that the building blocks of nucleic acids, proteins and membranes can arise without biological catalysts. They do not establish the sequence or the environment in which those building blocks first cooperated. That sequence is the unsolved core of the origin-of-life problem.

title: Quantum Gravity
paras: Quantum gravity is the attempt to reconcile general relativity with quantum mechanics. General relativity describes spacetime as a dynamical geometry whose curvature is fixed by the distribution of energy and momentum. Quantum mechanics describes matter and fields by operators on a Hilbert space and by amplitudes that interfere. At ordinary energies the two frameworks are used in succession: quantum fields propagate on a fixed classical background. The approximation fails when curvature radii approach the Planck length, approximately \( 10^{-35} \) m, or when energies approach the Planck energy, approximately \( 10^{19} \) GeV.

No complete theory is known. Several research programmes exist. String theory replaces point particles by extended objects whose vibrational modes include a massless spin-2 state that couples as a graviton. Consistent quantisation requires additional spatial dimensions and supersymmetry. The theory is perturbatively finite at each order and contains general relativity as a low-energy limit. It has not yet produced a unique four-dimensional vacuum that reproduces the observed particle spectrum and cosmological constant.

Loop quantum gravity quantises the geometry itself. Areas and volumes become discrete operators. The classical singularity of a black hole or of the cosmological big bang is replaced by a bounce in some models. The recovery of a smooth spacetime at large scales and the incorporation of the Standard Model remain open.

Other approaches—asymptotic safety, causal dynamical triangulations, and emergent-gravity scenarios—explore different quantisation schemes or different ontological starting points. None has been experimentally confirmed. The only present evidence that a quantum theory of gravity is required is the existence of singularities in the classical theory and the expectation that quantum effects cannot be neglected at the Planck scale.

The problem is therefore well-posed and unsolved. Its solution will determine whether spacetime is fundamental or emergent, whether information is preserved in black-hole evaporation, and whether the initial conditions of the universe can be derived rather than postulated.

title: Loop Quantum Gravity
paras: Loop quantum gravity is a non-perturbative, background-independent quantisation of general relativity. The fundamental variables are holonomies of the Ashtekar connection along paths and fluxes of the densitised triad through surfaces. These variables are promoted to operators on a Hilbert space of spin-network states. A spin network is a graph whose edges carry SU(2) representations and whose nodes carry invariant tensors.

The area of a surface and the volume of a region become discrete operators. Their spectra are bounded below by multiples of the Planck area and the Planck volume. The classical continuum geometry is recovered only as an approximation when the spin network is finely grained and the expectation values of the geometric operators are large compared with the Planck scale.

The dynamics are encoded in a Hamiltonian constraint. Solutions of the constraint define the physical Hilbert space. In cosmological models the same techniques yield a difference equation for the scale factor. The equation replaces the big-bang singularity by a bounce at a critical density of order the Planck density. The bounce connects a contracting phase to an expanding phase. Whether the bounce is generic in the full theory is not yet established.

Matter can be coupled. Fermions and gauge fields are incorporated by extending the spin-network labels. The recovery of the Standard Model spectrum and of a realistic value of the cosmological constant has not been achieved. The theory also lacks a complete demonstration that its low-energy limit is classical general relativity plus quantum field theory on curved spacetime, although several calculations of graviton propagators and of black-hole entropy are consistent with that limit.

Loop quantum gravity therefore supplies a concrete realisation of discrete quantum geometry and a possible resolution of cosmological singularities. It remains incomplete as a unified theory of all interactions and as a fully controlled continuum limit.

title: The Black-Hole Information Paradox
paras: Hawking radiation is thermal. A black hole that forms from a pure quantum state and evaporates completely therefore appears to leave behind a mixed state of radiation. The map from pure to mixed states is non-unitary. Unitarity is a fundamental requirement of quantum mechanics. The conflict is the information paradox.

The paradox becomes acute for an old black hole. Once more than half the initial entropy has been radiated, the remaining black hole has less entropy than the radiation already emitted. If the evaporation continues to be thermal, the total state cannot purify. The Page curve—the entanglement entropy of the radiation—must therefore rise and then fall if unitarity is to be preserved. A purely thermal spectrum produces a curve that rises indefinitely.

Recent calculations that include quantum extremal surfaces reproduce a Page curve that turns over. The island formula assigns part of the black-hole interior to the entanglement wedge of the radiation after the Page time. The result suggests that information is released in subtle correlations and that the final state is pure. The calculations have been performed in simplified models and in low-dimensional gravity. Their extension to realistic, asymptotically flat black holes is incomplete.

Alternative proposals include remnants that store the information, modifications of the radiation at late times, and non-unitary evolution. None is free of difficulties. The island calculations are the first to recover the Page curve from a semi-classical gravitational path integral. They indicate that the paradox may be resolved without abandoning unitarity or introducing new degrees of freedom beyond those already present in quantum gravity. A fully controlled demonstration for an evaporating four-dimensional black hole does not yet exist.

title: Black-Hole Complementarity
paras: Black-hole complementarity is the proposal that the descriptions of physics given by an observer who remains outside a black hole and by an observer who falls in are both valid, yet cannot be compared by any single observer. The external observer sees infalling matter approach the horizon asymptotically, thermalise, and eventually return as Hawking radiation. The infalling observer crosses the horizon without drama and encounters the matter in a perfectly regular spacetime region. No experiment accessible to either observer reveals a contradiction.

The principle was introduced to reconcile unitarity of the exterior evolution with the equivalence principle at the horizon. It asserts that the two accounts are complementary in the same sense that position and momentum are complementary: both are correct, but they cannot be simultaneously sharp for the same observer. Information that has crossed the horizon is, for the external observer, encoded in the radiation; for the infalling observer it remains in the interior. Because the observers cannot communicate after the horizon is crossed, no direct conflict arises.

Complementarity faces difficulties once the black hole is old. An external observer who collects the early radiation and then jumps in can, in principle, meet the same quantum information both outside and inside, violating the no-cloning theorem. The firewall argument sharpens the tension: preservation of exterior unitarity appears to require a high-energy barrier at the horizon that would destroy an infalling observer. Complementarity alone does not resolve the conflict.

Later developments—entanglement wedges, islands, and the Page curve—modify the original picture. They suggest that the interior degrees of freedom are not independent of the exterior radiation after the Page time. The complementarity of the two descriptions survives in a weakened form, but the precise location of the information and the experience of the infalling observer remain model-dependent. Complementarity is therefore a useful organising idea whose detailed implementation is still incomplete.

title: The Big Bang
paras: The Big Bang is the hot, dense, expanding phase from which the observable universe emerged. It is not an explosion in pre-existing space. It is the expansion of space itself. Every comoving observer sees the same recession of distant galaxies and the same cooling of the radiation field.

The earliest directly probed epoch is Big Bang nucleosynthesis, a few minutes after the classical singularity. The temperature was then about \( 10^9 \) K. Neutrons and protons fused into helium-4, with trace amounts of deuterium, helium-3 and lithium-7. The predicted abundances match observation once the baryon density is taken from the microwave background. Earlier still, at about \( 10^{-12} \) s, the electroweak symmetry was restored. Quark confinement occurred near \( 10^{-6} \) s. These transitions are calculated within the Standard Model and leave no contradictory relics.

The cosmic microwave background was released 380 000 years later, when the temperature fell to 3000 K and atoms formed. Its black-body spectrum and its anisotropies of one part in \( 10^5 \) are the relic of that surface of last scattering. The subsequent growth of those anisotropies under gravity produced the galaxies and clusters observed today.

Extrapolation of the classical equations backward reaches a singularity in finite time. Quantum-gravitational corrections are expected to intervene. No completed theory yet replaces the singularity with a definite prior state. The hot expanding phase that begins with nucleosynthesis and continues to the present is, however, confirmed by multiple independent observations.

title: The Multiverse
paras: The multiverse is the hypothesis that the observable universe is one of many domains that may differ in their physical parameters, initial conditions or even effective laws. Several distinct proposals exist.

Eternal inflation generates a multitude of bubble universes. Quantum fluctuations of the inflaton prevent inflation from ending everywhere at once. Each bubble thermalises with potentially different vacuum energy and low-energy constants. The string-theory landscape supplies a large number of metastable vacua, making such variation conceivable. No observation has identified another bubble.

The many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics treats the universal wave function as a complete description. Every outcome of a measurement occurs in some branch. The branches are effectively non-communicating after decoherence. The interpretation adds no new dynamical law. It reinterprets the existing linear evolution. Empirical distinction from other interpretations is lacking.

Other constructions include cyclic models, varying-speed-of-light scenarios, and mathematical ensembles in which every consistent structure is realised. None yields a unique, testable prediction that has been confirmed. Selection effects (anthropic reasoning) can explain why observers find themselves in a region compatible with life, but they do not predict the values of parameters that are already measured.

The multiverse therefore remains a set of theoretical possibilities. Some versions address the cosmological-constant problem or the initial conditions of inflation. All versions currently lack direct empirical support. The observable universe continues to be described, to high precision, by a single Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker geometry with a single set of low-energy constants.

title: The Holographic Principle
paras: The holographic principle states that the information content of a spatial region is bounded by the area of its boundary, not by its volume. The bound is saturated by a black hole: the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy is proportional to the horizon area measured in Planck units. The principle therefore asserts that a black hole is the maximum-entropy object of a given size.

The strongest realisation is the AdS/CFT correspondence. A gravitational theory in anti-de Sitter space is exactly equivalent to a conformal field theory living on the boundary of that space. Bulk geometry, including black-hole horizons, is encoded in the boundary quantum state. Entanglement entropy in the boundary theory equals the area of a bulk extremal surface. The dictionary has been verified in numerous calculations.

In asymptotically flat space or in de Sitter space no equally precise duality is known. The principle is nevertheless used as a guide. It suggests that the degrees of freedom of quantum gravity are nonlocal and that locality itself is an approximate, emergent notion. It also supplies an upper limit on the entropy that can be stored in any region, a limit already respected by all known physical systems.

No direct experimental test exists. The principle remains a theoretical constraint inferred from black-hole thermodynamics and from the structure of gauge/gravity duality. Its ultimate scope—whether it governs every consistent quantum theory of gravity—is still open.

title: The AdS/CFT Correspondence
paras: The AdS/CFT correspondence is an exact duality between a theory of quantum gravity in \((d+1)\)-dimensional anti-de Sitter space and a conformal field theory in \(d\) dimensions that lives on the boundary of that space. The best-studied example equates type-IIB string theory on \(\mathrm{AdS}_5\times S^5\) with \(\mathcal{N}=4\) super-Yang–Mills theory in four dimensions.

Bulk fields are dual to boundary operators. The mass of a bulk field fixes the conformal dimension of the dual operator. Correlation functions computed by Witten diagrams in the bulk equal correlation functions computed by Feynman diagrams in the boundary theory. The dictionary extends to finite temperature: a black hole in AdS is dual to a thermal state in the CFT. The Bekenstein–Hawking entropy equals the thermal entropy of the boundary theory.

Entanglement entropy in the CFT equals the area of a bulk extremal surface (the Ryu–Takayanagi formula). The relation has been used to reconstruct bulk geometry from boundary entanglement and to study the evaporation of black holes via the island formula. Real-time dynamics, transport coefficients and far-from-equilibrium evolution can likewise be mapped between the two sides.

The duality is a conjecture supported by a large number of matching calculations. It has not been proved in full generality. It applies strictly to anti-de Sitter asymptotics. Its conceptual importance lies in the demonstration that a higher-dimensional gravitational theory can be exactly equivalent to a lower-dimensional quantum field theory without gravity, and that spacetime geometry can emerge from quantum entanglement.

title: String Theory
paras: String theory replaces point particles by one-dimensional extended objects. The different vibrational modes of a string appear, at energies low compared with the string scale, as different particle species. One mode is a massless spin-2 state that couples precisely as a graviton. The theory therefore contains general relativity as a low-energy limit.

Consistent quantisation requires additional spatial dimensions and, in the superstring versions, supersymmetry. The extra dimensions are compactified on a small manifold. The geometry and fluxes of the compact space determine the spectrum and couplings of the four-dimensional effective theory. A large number of distinct compactifications exist—the landscape. No principle yet selects the compactification that reproduces the observed Standard Model and cosmological constant.

The theory is perturbatively finite order by order. Non-perturbative definitions are available in certain backgrounds via dualities, including the AdS/CFT correspondence. These dualities relate apparently different string theories and relate string theory to ordinary quantum field theories. They have not yet produced a unique, realistic vacuum.

Direct experimental tests are absent. The string scale is expected to lie near the Planck energy, far beyond accelerator reach. Indirect signatures—supersymmetric partners, extra dimensions, or modified gravitational laws at short distances—have not been observed. String theory remains the most developed framework that unifies gravity with the other interactions in a quantum-mechanically consistent manner. It is not yet a completed theory of nature.

title: Quantum Field Theory
paras: Quantum field theory is the framework that combines quantum mechanics with special relativity. The fundamental objects are fields defined at every point of spacetime. Particles appear as quanta of those fields. The theory is formulated so that the laws take the same form in every inertial frame and so that no signal propagates faster than light.

Interactions are local. The Lagrangian density at each point depends only on the fields and their derivatives at that point. The resulting S-matrix elements are computed by Feynman diagrams. Each diagram corresponds to a possible sequence of emissions and absorptions. The sum of diagrams yields the probability amplitude for a given process. Renormalisation absorbs the infinite contributions of high-energy virtual particles into a finite number of measured parameters. After renormalisation the predictions are finite and accurate.

The Standard Model is a quantum field theory. Its gauge symmetries dictate the interactions of quarks, leptons and the Higgs field. Quantum electrodynamics, the oldest and simplest part, predicts the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron to more than ten significant figures. Quantum chromodynamics accounts for the spectrum and scattering of hadrons once confinement is accepted. The electroweak theory unifies the electromagnetic and weak interactions and predicted the W, Z and Higgs bosons before they were observed.

The framework fails when gravity becomes strong. No consistent quantum field theory of the metric itself is known. At accessible energies, however, quantum field theory is the most precise description of nature that exists. Every confirmed particle-physics experiment is a test of it.

title: Symmetries of the Standard Model
paras: The Standard Model is defined by its gauge symmetry group \[ SU(3)_c\times SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y. \] The factor \( SU(3)_c \) is the colour group of the strong interaction. Quarks transform as triplets; gluons as an octet. The group remains unbroken. Its coupling grows at low energy and confines quarks and gluons into colour-singlet hadrons.

The factor \( SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y \) is the electroweak group. Left-handed fermions transform as doublets under \( SU(2)_L \); right-handed fermions are singlets. The Higgs field is a doublet. Its vacuum expectation value breaks \( SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y \) to the electromagnetic \( U(1)_{\mathrm{em}} \). Three of the four gauge bosons acquire mass and become the \( W^\pm \) and \( Z \). The unbroken generator is the photon. The same vacuum expectation value generates fermion masses through Yukawa couplings.

The gauge symmetries dictate the form of every interaction vertex. They forbid proton decay at the renormalisable level and guarantee the cancellation of anomalies once the observed fermion content is included. Global symmetries are fewer. Baryon number and lepton number are accidental consequences of the gauge structure and the particle content. They are conserved by all renormalisable terms. Neutrino masses, if Majorana, violate lepton number by two units and lie outside the minimal Standard Model.

No continuous global symmetry protects the Higgs mass. Quadratic divergences therefore appear. The observed lightness of the Higgs remains unexplained within the model. Discrete symmetries (charge conjugation, parity, time reversal) are violated by the weak interaction. Their observed pattern is reproduced by the complex phases in the Yukawa matrices. The gauge symmetry group, together with the representation content of the fermions and the Higgs, constitutes the entire defining structure of the Standard Model.

title: Grand Unified Theories
paras: Grand unified theories embed the Standard Model gauge group in a single simple group. The smallest example is \( SU(5) \). Larger groups such as \( SO(10) \) and \( E_6 \) are also studied. At energies far above the electroweak scale the unified symmetry is unbroken. Quarks and leptons occupy common multiplets. The strong, weak and electromagnetic couplings are different low-energy manifestations of a single coupling.

Unification predicts that the three Standard Model couplings meet at a single high scale when evolved with the renormalisation-group equations. In the minimal non-supersymmetric \( SU(5) \) model they miss. In the minimal supersymmetric extension they meet near \( 10^{16} \) GeV. The same scale suppresses the rate of proton decay. Present experimental limits on the proton lifetime already exclude the simplest non-supersymmetric models and constrain the supersymmetric ones.

The theories also relate quark and lepton masses and, in \( SO(10) \), naturally accommodate a right-handed neutrino, supplying a seesaw mechanism for the observed neutrino masses. They do not explain the number of generations or the hierarchy of Yukawa couplings. Supersymmetric versions introduce new particles that have not been observed. Non-supersymmetric versions are already ruled out by coupling unification and proton decay.

No direct evidence for grand unification exists. The ideas remain the most economical framework that links the three non-gravitational forces and that relates the matter content of the Standard Model. Their confirmation or exclusion will require either the discovery of proton decay, the observation of supersymmetric partners, or a decisive mismatch in the high-scale extrapolation of the couplings.

title: The Seesaw Mechanism
paras: The seesaw mechanism accounts for the extreme smallness of neutrino masses. In the Standard Model the left-handed neutrinos are massless. The introduction of a right-handed neutrino that is a singlet under the Standard Model gauge group permits two additional mass terms: a Dirac mass \( m_D \) that couples the left-handed neutrino to the right-handed neutrino, and a Majorana mass \( M \) for the right-handed neutrino alone.

Because no gauge symmetry forbids the Majorana term, \( M \) may lie near the grand-unification or Planck scale. Diagonalisation of the resulting mass matrix yields a light eigenvalue \[ m_\nu \approx \frac{m_D^2}{M} \] and a heavy eigenvalue approximately equal to \( M \). A large \( M \) therefore forces \( m_\nu \) to be tiny. The ordinary neutrino mass is suppressed by the ratio of the electroweak scale to the high scale.

The same construction violates lepton number by two units. It thereby permits neutrinoless double-beta decay. In \( SO(10) \) grand unified theories the right-handed neutrino is required to complete the spinor representation that contains one generation; the seesaw appears automatically. The mechanism remains the most economical explanation of the observed neutrino masses within a grand-unified framework. Direct evidence for the heavy right-handed states is absent.

title: Conservation of Energy from Time-Translation Invariance
paras: Noether’s theorem associates a conservation law with every continuous symmetry. Invariance of the action under time translation implies conservation of energy. If the Lagrangian does not depend explicitly on time, the quantity \[ E = \sum_i \dot q_i\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i} - L \] is constant along the motion. For the standard mechanical Lagrangian this quantity is \( T + V \).

The same reasoning applies to fields. Invariance under time translation yields a conserved energy-momentum tensor. The integral of its time-time component over a spatial volume is the total energy. Apparent non-conservation always signals that the system under consideration is not isolated or that the Lagrangian has an explicit time dependence.
The link between time-translation symmetry and energy conservation is exact within the domain of the variational principle. It supplies the deepest reason that energy is conserved.

title: The Speed of Light and the Structure of Spacetime
paras: The invariance of the speed of light forces the replacement of Galilean spacetime by Minkowski spacetime. The interval \[ ds^2 = c^2dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 - dz^2 \] is the same for every inertial observer. Surfaces of constant interval are hyperboloids. The light cone, \( ds = 0 \), bounds the causal future and past of every event.

Coordinates of different inertial frames are related by Lorentz transformations. These transformations mix space and time and leave the interval unchanged. The classical notions of absolute simultaneity and absolute time are thereby eliminated. All observable relativistic effects—time dilation, length contraction, the relativistic velocity addition law—follow from the geometry of the light cone and from the invariance of \( ds \).

The same geometry persists locally in the presence of gravity. Global curvature modifies the relation between neighbouring light cones but does not alter the local limiting speed. The invariance of \( c \) remains the structural foundation of both special and general relativity.

title: Chemical Kinetics
paras: Chemical kinetics is the study of reaction rates. The rate of an elementary reaction is proportional to the product of the concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient in the rate-determining step. The constant of proportionality is the rate constant \( k \).

The temperature dependence of \( k \) is given by the Arrhenius equation \[ k = A e^{-E_a/RT}, \] where \( E_a \) is the activation energy. Only collisions that supply at least \( E_a \) produce products. Catalysts lower \( E_a \) by providing an alternative path. They do not change the equilibrium constant.

Integrated rate laws give the concentration as a function of time. First-order reactions decay exponentially. Second-order reactions follow a different algebraic form. The half-life is independent of concentration only for first-order processes. Radioactive decay is the classic example.

The same formalism describes enzyme kinetics once the Michaelis–Menten mechanism is adopted. At low substrate concentration the rate is first-order in substrate. At high concentration the enzyme is saturated and the rate is zero-order. The framework therefore covers both ordinary chemical reactions and the catalytic steps of biochemistry.

title: Chemical Equilibrium
paras: Chemical equilibrium is the state in which the forward and reverse rates of a reaction are equal. The equilibrium constant \( K \) is the ratio of the rate constants and is related to the standard free-energy change by \[ \Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K. \] When \( \Delta G^\circ \) is negative, \( K > 1 \) and products are favoured. When \( \Delta G^\circ \) is positive, reactants are favoured.

Le Chatelier’s principle states that a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting in the direction that reduces the disturbance. Addition of a reactant, increase of pressure for a reaction that reduces the number of gas molecules, or removal of a product all drive the reaction forward. Temperature changes shift the equilibrium according to the sign of \( \Delta H \).

The equilibrium constant is independent of the path and of the presence of a catalyst. It depends only on temperature. The approach to equilibrium, by contrast, is accelerated by catalysts. The distinction between thermodynamics and kinetics is therefore sharp. Equilibrium fixes the final composition. Kinetics fixes the time required to reach it.

title: Electrochemistry
paras: Electrochemistry is the coupling of chemical reactions to the flow of electric charge. In a galvanic cell a spontaneous redox reaction generates a potential difference. The cell potential under standard conditions is the difference of the standard reduction potentials of the two half-reactions. The relation to free energy is \[ \Delta G = -nFE, \] where \( n \) is the number of moles of electrons transferred and \( F \) is Faraday’s constant.
The Nernst equation corrects the potential for non-standard concentrations: \[ E = E^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q. \] At equilibrium \( E = 0 \) and the equation reduces to the expression for \( K \).

Electrolytic cells reverse the process. An external voltage drives a non-spontaneous reaction. The same half-reactions occur, but in the opposite direction. Industrial production of aluminium, chlorine and many organic compounds relies on electrolysis. Corrosion is an uncontrolled galvanic process in which a metal is oxidised by atmospheric oxygen. All of these phenomena are governed by the same thermodynamic and kinetic relations.

title: Organic Chemistry and Functional Groups
paras: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon forms stable chains and rings because the C–C bond is strong and because carbon can form four covalent bonds. The resulting molecular diversity is organised by functional groups—local arrangements of atoms that confer characteristic reactivity.

Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes are saturated. Alkenes and alkynes contain multiple bonds and undergo addition. Aromatic rings exhibit special stability due to delocalisation. Substitution of heteroatoms produces alcohols, ethers, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amines and amides. Each class displays a limited set of typical reactions.

The same functional-group logic governs biochemistry. Proteins are polyamides. Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. Lipids are largely hydrocarbon chains with polar head groups. Nucleic acids are phosphate-linked sugars bearing heterocyclic bases. The reactions of metabolism are the reactions of these functional groups, catalysed by enzymes and regulated by the cell.

Stereochemistry adds a further layer. Carbon atoms bearing four different substituents are chiral. Biological systems almost invariably use one enantiomer. The preference is a historical fact of terrestrial evolution, not a chemical necessity. The functional-group classification nevertheless remains the organising principle of both laboratory and biological organic chemistry.

title: Polymers and Macromolecules
paras: A polymer is a large molecule built by the repetition of smaller units. Synthetic polymers are produced by chain-growth or step-growth polymerisation. The degree of polymerisation, the architecture (linear, branched, cross-linked) and the tacticity determine the mechanical properties. Thermoplastics soften on heating. Thermosets do not. Elastomers return to their original shape after large deformations.

Biological macromolecules are polymers of defined sequence. Proteins are linear polypeptides that fold into specific three-dimensional structures. Nucleic acids are linear polynucleotides that store and transmit information. Polysaccharides serve structural and storage roles. In each case the covalent backbone is formed by condensation reactions. Non-covalent interactions—hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, ionic pairs—stabilise the higher-order structure.

The physical chemistry of polymer solutions and melts is described by scaling laws. The radius of a flexible chain grows as a power of its length. Entanglements dominate the viscoelasticity of concentrated solutions and melts. The same concepts apply, with modifications, to the crowded interior of a cell. Polymer science therefore links synthetic materials to the macromolecules of life.

title: Surface Chemistry and Catalysis
paras: Surface chemistry studies reactions that occur at interfaces. Adsorption may be physical (van der Waals) or chemical (covalent or ionic). The Langmuir isotherm describes monolayer adsorption when sites are equivalent and non-interacting. Real surfaces are heterogeneous. Coverage depends on temperature and on the partial pressure or concentration of the adsorbate.

Heterogeneous catalysis occurs when a reactant adsorbs, reacts on the surface, and the product desorbs. Metals, metal oxides and zeolites are common catalysts. The surface lowers the activation energy by stabilising the transition state. Industrial processes—ammonia synthesis, petroleum cracking, catalytic converters—rely on such surfaces. Homogeneous catalysis uses soluble complexes. The distinction is practical rather than fundamental. Both accelerate attainment of equilibrium without shifting its position.

Enzyme catalysis is the biological counterpart. The active site binds the substrate, stabilises the transition state, and releases the product. Rate enhancements of \( 10^{6} \) to \( 10^{17} \) are common. The underlying physical chemistry—adsorption, activation-energy reduction, and product release—is the same as in industrial catalysis. Surfaces and active sites are therefore central to both technology and metabolism.

title: Photosynthesis
paras: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy. In oxygenic photosynthesis water is the electron donor and oxygen is released. The overall reaction is \[ 6\,\mathrm{CO}_2 + 6\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \to \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_6 + 6\,\mathrm{O}_2. \] Light is absorbed by chlorophyll and accessory pigments in the thylakoid membranes. Two photosystems operate in series. Photosystem II splits water. Photosystem I reduces NADP\(^+\). The electron transport chain between them generates a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis.

The ATP and NADPH are consumed in the Calvin cycle. Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase fixes carbon dioxide into organic molecules. The cycle regenerates the acceptor and produces triose phosphates that are converted to sugars, starch or other compounds. The enzyme also reacts with oxygen, initiating photorespiration. The competition is an unavoidable consequence of the active-site chemistry.

Photosynthesis supplies the free energy and the reduced carbon that support almost all ecosystems. Its oxygen byproduct transformed the atmosphere. The same core reactions operate in cyanobacteria, algae and plants. Variations in carbon-concentrating mechanisms and in pigment composition adapt the process to different light and carbon regimes. The quantum efficiency of the light reactions is high. The overall energy efficiency of biomass production is far lower.

title: Cellular Respiration
paras: Cellular respiration extracts energy from organic molecules. Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate in the cytosol, yielding a net of two ATP and two NADH. In aerobic organisms pyruvate enters the mitochondria. The citric-acid cycle oxidises the acetyl group to two molecules of carbon dioxide and produces additional reduced coenzymes. The electron-transport chain transfers electrons from NADH and FADH\(_2\) to oxygen. The free energy is used to pump protons. The return of protons through ATP synthase produces the majority of the ATP.

The overall yield from one glucose is approximately thirty ATP under cellular conditions. The theoretical maximum is higher. Proton leaks and the cost of transporting metabolites reduce the net gain. Anaerobic pathways regenerate NAD\(^+\) by reducing pyruvate to lactate or to ethanol and carbon dioxide. They yield only the two ATP from glycolysis.

The same respiratory chain operates in bacteria and in mitochondria. Mitochondria are the descendants of endosymbiotic bacteria. The chemiosmotic mechanism—proton gradient coupled to ATP synthesis—is universal among aerobic organisms. Respiration and photosynthesis are complementary. One stores energy in organic molecules and oxygen. The other releases it.

title: Gene Expression and Regulation
paras: Gene expression is the conversion of genetic information into functional products. Transcription produces an RNA copy of a DNA segment. In eukaryotes the primary transcript is processed: introns are removed, a cap and a poly-A tail are added. Translation on the ribosome converts the messenger-RNA sequence into a polypeptide. The genetic code is read in non-overlapping triplets.

Regulation occurs at every step. Transcription factors bind specific DNA sequences and recruit or block RNA polymerase. Chromatin structure modulates access. Alternative splicing generates multiple protein isoforms from one gene. Messenger-RNA stability and translational efficiency are controlled by proteins and small RNAs. Post-translational modifications activate, inhibit or target the finished protein.

The regulatory network of a cell is dense. A single transcription factor may control dozens of genes. Feedback loops, both positive and negative, produce switches, oscillators and homeostatic responses. The same basic machinery operates in bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes. The additional layers of chromatin, splicing and compartmentalisation in eukaryotes allow more elaborate control. The outcome is that genetically identical cells can adopt different phenotypes according to their history and their environment.

title: The Immune System
paras: The immune system distinguishes self from non-self and eliminates pathogens. Innate immunity is immediate and non-specific. Barriers, phagocytes, complement and inflammatory cytokines constitute the first response. Pattern-recognition receptors detect conserved microbial molecules and trigger the innate pathways.

Adaptive immunity is slower and specific. Lymphocytes carry receptors generated by somatic recombination. Each clone recognises a different antigen. Clonal selection expands those clones that bind antigen. Helper T cells coordinate the response. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. B cells secrete antibodies. Memory cells persist after the pathogen is cleared and accelerate the response upon re-exposure.

Self-tolerance is established by deletion or inactivation of clones that recognise self antigens. Failure of tolerance produces autoimmune disease. The system is not perfect. Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. The host evolves countermeasures. The result is a continuous coevolutionary arms race. Vaccination exploits immunological memory by presenting antigen without causing disease. The same principles underlie both natural immunity and medical immunisation.

title: Development and Differentiation
paras: Development is the progressive specialisation of cells from a single zygote. Early cleavage produces a blastula. Gastrulation rearranges the cells into three germ layers. Subsequent inductive interactions between layers generate the organs. The process is controlled by gradients of signalling molecules and by sequential activation of transcription-factor networks.

Cell differentiation is usually irreversible under normal conditions. The differentiated state is maintained by feedback loops in the gene-regulatory network and by chromatin modifications that are copied at mitosis. Stem cells retain the capacity to produce multiple cell types. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent. Adult stem cells are multipotent and replenish specific tissues.

Regeneration varies widely. Some animals replace entire limbs or organs. Mammals regenerate liver and blood but not limbs. The difference lies in the persistence of patterning information and in the ability of differentiated cells to re-enter the cell cycle or to be replaced by stem cells. The molecular toolkit—signalling pathways, transcription factors, and adhesive molecules—is ancient. The deployment of the toolkit differs. Development is therefore both conserved and plastic.

title: Ecology and Ecosystems
paras: Ecology studies the distribution and abundance of organisms and the flows of energy and matter that sustain them. A population grows exponentially when resources are unlimited. Density-dependent factors—competition, predation, disease—limit growth. The logistic equation is the simplest description that incorporates a carrying capacity.

Communities are assemblages of interacting populations. Competition, predation, mutualism and parasitism structure the assemblage. Keystone species exert effects disproportionate to their abundance. Removal of a keystone predator can allow prey to overgraze and collapse the community. Energy enters most ecosystems through photosynthesis. It is transferred with low efficiency. Approximately 10 percent passes to each successive trophic level. Nutrients cycle. Energy does not.

Ecosystems are open. They exchange gases, water and organisms with their surroundings. Succession follows disturbance. The trajectory is influenced by the remaining species pool, by soil conditions and by climate. Human activity now dominates many of these exchanges. The basic constraints—energy degradation, nutrient conservation, and density dependence—remain those of any ecological system.

title: Epigenetic Inheritance
paras: Epigenetic inheritance is the transmission of information from one cell or organism to the next without a change in the DNA sequence. The principal molecular carriers are DNA methylation, histone modifications, and certain non-coding RNAs.

DNA methylation in vertebrates occurs mainly at cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides. Methylation patterns are copied by maintenance methyltransferases at replication. They typically repress transcription when present in promoters. Histone modifications—acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation and others—alter chromatin compaction and recruit regulatory proteins. Some modifications are re-established after replication by reader-writer complexes. Small RNAs can direct both DNA methylation and histone modification in a sequence-specific manner.

These marks are mitotically heritable and therefore maintain cell identity through development. Meiotic heritability is rarer. In mammals extensive reprogramming erases most methylation marks in the primordial germ cells and again in the early embryo. A few loci, including imprinted genes, escape erasure and produce parent-of-origin effects. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance beyond one or two generations has been documented in plants, nematodes and, under special conditions, in mammals. Its frequency and stability in humans remain limited.

Epigenetic mechanisms allow genetically identical cells to adopt stable, different phenotypes. They also provide a route by which environmental conditions can influence gene expression in the next generation without altering the nucleotide sequence. The nucleotide sequence itself remains the primary hereditary material. Epigenetic marks modulate its use.

title: Genomic Imprinting
paras: Genomic imprinting is the parent-of-origin-dependent expression of certain genes. An imprinted gene is expressed from only the maternal or only the paternal allele. The silent allele is marked by DNA methylation and histone modifications established in the respective germ line. The marks survive the genome-wide demethylation that occurs in the early embryo and are maintained through somatic cell divisions.

Approximately one hundred mammalian genes are imprinted. Many lie in clusters controlled by imprint control regions. The clusters frequently contain genes that regulate growth. Paternally expressed genes tend to promote growth. Maternally expressed genes tend to restrain it. The pattern matches the parental-conflict hypothesis: in species where offspring of one mother may have different fathers, paternal alleles favour greater maternal investment while maternal alleles favour conservation of resources for future offspring.

Imprinting is reset each generation. In the primordial germ cells the existing marks are erased. New marks are placed according to the sex of the developing individual. Failure to erase or reset an imprint produces disorders such as Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes, which result from opposite parental deletions or uniparental disomy of the same chromosomal region. Imprinting is known in mammals and in flowering plants. It is absent in birds and in most other vertebrates. It constitutes a regulated exception to the usual rule of biallelic expression.

title: Parental-Conflict Theory of Imprinting
paras: Parental-conflict theory accounts for the evolution of genomic imprinting. In species in which a female may produce offspring by different males, the genetic interests of maternal and paternal alleles diverge. Every offspring carries a full complement of the mother’s genes but, on average, only half of any given father’s genes relative to future half-siblings. A paternal allele therefore gains by increasing the resources extracted from the mother. A maternal allele gains by conserving those resources for later offspring.

Imprinting is the molecular consequence. Growth-promoting genes are expressed from the paternal chromosome and silenced on the maternal chromosome. Growth-restraining genes show the opposite pattern. The two sets of imprints reach an evolutionary equilibrium. Disruption of either imprint produces the over-growth or under-growth phenotypes observed in human imprinting disorders and in experimental deletions.

The theory predicts that imprinting will appear only where mothers provision offspring after fertilisation and where multiple paternity is possible. It predicts the absence of imprinting where offspring are nutritionally independent at birth or where lifelong monogamy eliminates the conflict. The phylogenetic distribution of imprinting matches these predictions. The theory therefore supplies both a selective explanation for the existence of imprints and a set of comparative tests that the explanation has passed.

title: Blood
paras: Blood is a specialised connective tissue that circulates through the vascular system. It transports oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones and waste products. It also distributes heat and contributes to immune defence and haemostasis. In an adult human the volume is approximately five litres.

Plasma constitutes about 55 percent of the volume. It is an aqueous solution of proteins (albumin, globulins, fibrinogen), electrolytes, nutrients and metabolic wastes. The remaining 45 percent is cellular. Erythrocytes (red cells) are anucleate in mammals. They contain haemoglobin and carry oxygen. Their biconcave shape maximises surface area and flexibility. Leukocytes (white cells) comprise neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. They mediate innate and adaptive immunity. Platelets are cell fragments that initiate clotting.

Haemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively. The binding curve is sigmoid. Affinity is reduced by elevated carbon dioxide, lowered pH and increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate—the Bohr effect—facilitating unloading in active tissues. Carbon dioxide is carried partly as dissolved gas, partly bound to haemoglobin, and mostly as bicarbonate after conversion by carbonic anhydrase in the red cell.

Haemostasis begins with vasoconstriction and platelet adhesion to exposed collagen. The coagulation cascade converts fibrinogen to fibrin, stabilising the platelet plug. Anticoagulant pathways and fibrinolysis limit the clot to the site of injury. Disorders of any step produce thrombosis or bleeding.

Blood cells are produced in the bone marrow from haematopoietic stem cells. Erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and colony-stimulating factors regulate lineage output. The average lifespan of a human red cell is 120 days. Senescent cells are removed by macrophages in the spleen and liver. Iron from haemoglobin is recycled. The same fluid and cellular system operates, with variations in detail, throughout the vertebrates.

title: Cosmic Inflation
paras: Cosmic inflation is a brief epoch of accelerated expansion in the earliest universe. It is driven by the potential energy of a scalar field—the inflaton—that rolls slowly toward the minimum of its potential. While the field is slow-rolling the scale factor grows exponentially. A tiny, causally connected region is stretched to a size far larger than the present observable universe.

Inflation solves the horizon problem: regions now widely separated were once in causal contact and could equalise their temperatures. It solves the flatness problem: any initial curvature is diluted to an unobservable level. Quantum fluctuations of the inflaton are stretched to cosmological wavelengths and become the nearly scale-invariant, adiabatic, Gaussian density perturbations observed in the microwave background.

The simplest models predict a tensor-to-scalar ratio \( r \) that measures the amplitude of primordial gravitational waves. Current upper limits are \( r < 0.03 \). Detection of a non-zero \( r \) would fix the energy scale of inflation. Non-detection continues to constrain the shape of the potential. Inflation ends when the inflaton reaches the bottom of its potential and oscillates, reheating the universe and initiating the hot Big Bang. The mechanism is theoretically attractive and consistent with all present data. It is not yet uniquely confirmed.

title: Baryogenesis
paras: Baryogenesis is the generation of the observed excess of matter over antimatter. The universe contains roughly \( 10^9 \) photons for every baryon, and essentially no antibaryons. Sakharov identified three necessary conditions: baryon-number violation, C and CP violation, and departure from thermal equilibrium.

The Standard Model contains all three ingredients. Electroweak sphalerons violate baryon number. The CKM matrix supplies CP violation. The electroweak phase transition can be out of equilibrium if it is strongly first-order. Quantitative calculation shows that the Standard Model CP violation and the strength of the transition are both insufficient to produce the observed asymmetry. Additional physics is required.

Leptogenesis generates a lepton asymmetry through the out-of-equilibrium decay of heavy right-handed neutrinos. Sphalerons then convert part of the lepton asymmetry into a baryon asymmetry. The mechanism operates naturally within the seesaw framework. Electroweak baryogenesis and Affleck–Dine baryogenesis are alternative scenarios. None has been experimentally confirmed. All of them link the cosmic matter excess to particle-physics processes that lie beyond the Standard Model.

title: Large-Scale Structure
paras: Large-scale structure is the pattern of galaxies, clusters, filaments and voids observed on scales from a few to several hundred megaparsecs. The pattern grew by gravitational instability from the primordial density fluctuations. Over-dense regions expanded more slowly, collapsed, and formed bound objects. Under-dense regions expanded faster and became voids.

Cold dark matter supplies the dominant gravitational potential. Baryons fall into the dark-matter wells after recombination. The resulting power spectrum of density fluctuations matches the spectrum measured in galaxy surveys and in the microwave background. Baryon acoustic oscillations—the frozen sound horizon of the pre-recombination plasma—appear as a standard ruler in the galaxy correlation function and provide a geometric probe of the expansion history.

N-body simulations that include cold dark matter, baryons and a cosmological constant reproduce the observed filamentary web, the abundance of clusters, and the internal structure of dark-matter halos. The same simulations show that structure formation is hierarchical: small objects form first and merge into larger ones. The process continues today. The large-scale distribution of matter is therefore the evolved imprint of inflationary initial conditions filtered by gravity and by the cosmic expansion.

title: Dark Energy and the Accelerating Universe
paras: Distant Type Ia supernovae are fainter than expected in a decelerating universe. The microwave-background acoustic peaks and the baryon-acoustic-oscillation scale independently require a component that does not cluster and that has negative pressure. That component is dark energy. It constitutes approximately 70 percent of the present energy density.

The simplest model is a cosmological constant with equation-of-state parameter \( w = -1 \). More general models allow \( w \) to vary with time. Current data are consistent with a constant. The energy density of a true cosmological constant is unchanging. It therefore dominated only recently, when the matter density had fallen sufficiently. The transition to acceleration occurred at redshift \( z \approx 0.7 \).

The cosmological-constant problem is the discrepancy between the observed value and the far larger value expected from quantum-field zero-point energies. No accepted solution exists. Quintessence models replace the constant with a slowly rolling scalar field. Modified-gravity models alter the Einstein equation on large scales. All of these proposals remain viable because the only observational constraints are the expansion history and the growth rate of structure, both of which are still compatible with a pure cosmological constant.

title: The Fossil Record of Life
paras: The fossil record is the sequence of preserved remains and traces of organisms in sedimentary rocks. It begins with chemical and morphological traces of microbial life 3.5–3.8 billion years ago. Multicellular organisms appear in abundance only in the Ediacaran, about 575 million years ago. The Cambrian explosion, beginning 540 million years ago, marks the rapid appearance of most major animal phyla that possess hard parts.

Subsequent radiations and extinctions are documented in increasing detail. The colonisation of land by plants, arthropods and vertebrates occurs in the Palaeozoic. The end-Permian extinction eliminates more than 90 percent of marine species. The Mesozoic is dominated by dinosaurs and gymnosperms. The end-Cretaceous extinction removes the non-avian dinosaurs and many other groups. The Cenozoic radiation of mammals, birds and flowering plants follows.

Molecular clocks and phylogenetic trees calibrated by fossils recover the same broad sequence. Gaps exist—soft-bodied organisms are under-represented, and some intervals are poorly sampled—but the overall order of first appearances is robust. The record demonstrates that life has been continuously present for at least 3.5 billion years, that its complexity and diversity have increased, and that this increase has been repeatedly punctuated by mass extinctions and subsequent recoveries. It supplies the historical evidence for evolution.

title: The Evolution of Plants
paras: Plants originated from freshwater green algae. The closest living relatives are the charophytes. The transition to land required cuticles, stomata, and protected reproductive structures. The earliest fossil evidence of land plants is spores from the Ordovician, about 470 million years ago. Vascular tissue appears in the Silurian. By the Devonian, forests of lycophytes, ferns and progymnosperms existed.

Seeds evolved in the late Devonian. They freed reproduction from the requirement for free water and allowed colonisation of drier habitats. Gymnosperms dominated the Mesozoic. Flowering plants (angiosperms) appear in the Early Cretaceous and radiate rapidly. Flowers and fruits coevolved with animal pollinators and dispersers. By the end of the Cretaceous, angiosperms were the most diverse plant group. They remain so today.

Photosynthetic efficiency, vascular architecture and reproductive strategy have been the principal axes of innovation. Polyploidy is common and has contributed to speciation. The same core genetic toolkit that patterns shoots and roots in mosses operates in flowering plants. The fossil record, comparative morphology and molecular phylogenies converge on a single origin of land plants and on the subsequent sequence of major innovations. Plants transformed the terrestrial surface, altered the atmosphere and created the habitats in which animals evolved.

title: The Evolution of Animals
paras: Animals are multicellular heterotrophs that develop from a blastula. Their closest unicellular relatives are the choanoflagellates. The earliest animal fossils are Ediacaran impressions, about 575 million years old. The Cambrian explosion, beginning 540 million years ago, records the rapid appearance of most extant phyla that possess mineralised skeletons. Molecular clocks place the origin of the major clades somewhat earlier, in the late Neoproterozoic.

Bilaterians—animals with a single plane of symmetry and three germ layers—dominate the subsequent record. Two great branches exist: the protostomes (arthropods, molluscs, annelids and others) and the deuterostomes (echinoderms and chordates). Segmentation, jointed appendages, and a through-gut evolved independently in several lineages. The colonisation of land by arthropods occurred in the Silurian–Devonian. Vertebrates followed in the Devonian. Tetrapods, amniotes and, later, endotherms each opened new ecological possibilities.

Mass extinctions repeatedly reset diversity. The end-Permian and end-Cretaceous events are the most severe. Recoveries produced the characteristic faunas of the following eras. Developmental genetics shows that the same Hox and other regulatory genes pattern the body axes of flies and mice. The morphological disparity of animals therefore rests on a conserved genetic toolkit deployed in different combinations. The fossil record, comparative anatomy and molecular phylogenies converge on a single origin of animals and on the subsequent branching order of the major phyla.

title: Plate Tectonics
paras: The Earth’s lithosphere is divided into rigid plates that move relative to one another. The motions are driven by mantle convection and by the sinking of cold oceanic lithosphere. Divergent boundaries produce mid-ocean ridges and new oceanic crust. Convergent boundaries produce subduction zones, volcanic arcs and mountain belts. Transform boundaries accommodate lateral slip.

The theory unifies continental drift, seafloor spreading and the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes. Magnetic anomalies symmetric about ridge axes record reversals of the geomagnetic field and demonstrate that oceanic crust is created at ridges and destroyed at trenches. The oldest oceanic crust is about 180 million years old. Continental crust is older and is not systematically recycled.

Plate motions have rearranged the continents repeatedly. The assembly and breakup of supercontinents correlate with changes in sea level, climate and biological diversity. The same processes operate today. GPS measurements confirm the velocities predicted by magnetic anomalies and by earthquake slip vectors. Plate tectonics is the surface expression of the Earth’s internal heat engine.

title: The Earth’s Atmosphere and Climate
paras: The atmosphere is a thin gaseous envelope whose composition is maintained by geological and biological fluxes. Nitrogen and oxygen dominate. Trace gases—water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, ozone—control the radiative balance. Incoming solar radiation is partly reflected and partly absorbed. Outgoing long-wave radiation is trapped by greenhouse gases. The resulting surface temperature is approximately 33 K warmer than the effective radiating temperature.

Climate is the long-term statistics of weather. It varies on every timescale. Orbital (Milankovitch) cycles modulate the seasonal distribution of sunlight and pace the Pleistocene ice ages. Volcanic aerosols cool the surface for a few years. Changes in greenhouse-gas concentrations alter the energy budget for decades to millennia. The present rise in carbon dioxide is produced by fossil-fuel combustion and land-use change. It is occurring at a rate unprecedented in the ice-core record.

Feedbacks amplify or damp the response. Water vapour and snow–ice albedo are positive. Clouds and the carbon cycle contain both positive and negative terms. The equilibrium climate sensitivity to a doubling of carbon dioxide is estimated between 2 K and 5 K. The atmosphere and ocean together redistribute heat. The same physical principles govern the climates of other planets that possess atmospheres.

title: Antibiotics and Resistance
paras: Antibiotics are compounds that kill or inhibit bacteria at concentrations tolerable to the host. Most clinical antibiotics are natural products or their derivatives. They target cell-wall synthesis, protein synthesis, nucleic-acid synthesis or membrane integrity. The therapeutic window exists because these targets differ between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

Resistance arises by mutation or by acquisition of resistance genes. Mechanisms include enzymatic inactivation, target modification, efflux pumps and reduced permeability. Resistance genes are frequently carried on plasmids and transposons and spread by horizontal transfer. The same genes occur in environmental bacteria that have never encountered clinical antibiotics. Clinical use merely enriches pre-existing resistance.

The rate of discovery of new antibiotic classes has slowed. Resistance continues to spread. The evolutionary process is ordinary natural selection acting on large bacterial populations with short generation times. Stewardship, combination therapy and the development of new agents are the available countermeasures. The underlying biology is the same biology that governs any host–parasite interaction.

title: The Nervous System
paras: The nervous system transmits and processes information by means of electrical and chemical signals. Neurons generate action potentials—brief, all-or-none reversals of membrane potential produced by voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels. The potential propagates along the axon without decrement. At chemical synapses the arriving action potential triggers calcium influx and vesicle release. Neurotransmitter binds receptors on the postsynaptic cell and opens or closes ion channels.

Synaptic strength is modifiable. Long-term potentiation and long-term depression are cellular correlates of learning. They depend on receptor trafficking, second-messenger cascades and, ultimately, changes in gene expression. Neural circuits implement sensation, motor control, homeostasis and, in larger brains, cognition. The same ionic mechanisms operate from jellyfish to humans.

Glia support, insulate and modulate neurons. Myelination increases conduction speed. The blood–brain barrier isolates the central nervous system from many blood-borne substances. Development of the nervous system requires precise axon guidance and activity-dependent refinement of connections. The adult brain retains limited plasticity. The principles of excitability, synaptic transmission and circuit computation are conserved across animals that possess nervous systems.

title: The Human Microbiome
paras: The human microbiome is the community of microorganisms that live on and inside the body. The majority reside in the gut. Their collective genome contains orders of magnitude more genes than the human genome. Most are bacteria. Archaea, fungi, viruses and protists are also present.

The composition is established in early life and is influenced by mode of birth, diet, antibiotics and environment. It remains relatively stable in healthy adults yet varies among individuals. The gut microbiota ferment otherwise indigestible carbohydrates, produce short-chain fatty acids, synthesise certain vitamins, and compete with pathogens for space and nutrients. They also interact with the immune system, promoting tolerance to harmless antigens and responsiveness to pathogens.

Disruption of the community—dysbiosis—is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, metabolic syndrome, and increased susceptibility to infection by organisms such as *Clostridioides difficile*. Faecal microbiota transplantation can restore a diverse community and cure recurrent infection. Causal links to other conditions remain under investigation.

The microbiome is not an optional accessory. It is an integral part of human physiology. Its metabolic and immunological contributions are measurable. Its composition is heritable only insofar as it is transmitted and selected by the host environment. The nucleotide sequence of the human genome does not encode it.

title: The Human Genome
paras: The human genome is the complete DNA sequence of a human cell. The haploid genome contains approximately 3.2 billion base pairs. About 1.5 percent codes for proteins. The remainder consists of introns, regulatory sequences, transposable elements, and other non-coding DNA. Roughly 20 000 protein-coding genes are present. Many genes produce multiple transcripts by alternative splicing.

The sequence was first completed in draft form in 2001 and in finished form in 2003. Subsequent projects have catalogued common variation. Any two unrelated individuals differ at about one site in a thousand. Most variants are single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Structural variants—insertions, deletions, inversions and copy-number changes—also contribute. The majority of variants are neutral or nearly neutral. A minority affect disease risk or drug response.

Genes are not uniformly distributed. Some chromosomal regions are gene-rich. Others are gene-poor. The mitochondrial genome is a separate circular molecule of 16 569 base pairs that is maternally inherited and encodes 13 proteins of the respiratory chain. Nuclear and mitochondrial genomes together constitute the hereditary material.
