The logic of natural selection is small enough to state in a paragraph and strong enough to organize a science. Individuals vary. Some of the variation is inherited. Individuals with certain heritable traits leave more offspring in a given environment. Those traits become more common. Over time, populations change. Given enough time, and given the way development builds bodies, the changes can be large. The logic does not require progress, purpose, or a direction toward complexity. It requires differential reproductive success. Complexity has increased in some lineages and not in others. Bacteria have remained bacteria, with enormous biochemical sophistication, for billions of years.

The evidence is independent in kind and convergent in result. Fossils show a sequence. They do not show modern animals in the oldest rocks. They show earlier forms, then later forms, with transitional fossils in many lineages: fish with limb-like fins, dinosaurs with feathers, whales with hind limbs, hominins with intermediate brain sizes and bipedal skeletons. Biogeography shows that islands and continents carry the descendants of whoever could get there. Anatomy shows common structure under different uses. Embryology shows related species passing through related stages. Molecular biology shows the same code, shared genes, shared errors, and shared viral insertions. A single lineage explains all of these. Separate creation of each species would have to explain them again, one by one, as coincidences.

Genetics filled the gap Darwin noted. He did not know how traits were inherited or how variation was supplied. Mendel’s work, rediscovered at the start of the twentieth century, showed particulate inheritance. Later work identified the particles as stretches of DNA. Mutation, recombination, and gene flow supply variation. Selection, drift, and the biases of development filter it. The modern synthesis joined Mendel to Darwin. Later work has added regulatory genetics, developmental genetics, and the movement of genes between lineages, especially in microbes. The additions refine the mechanism. They do not replace the filter.

Speciation is the production of separate lineages that no longer freely intermix. It can happen when populations are divided by geography, and it can happen, less simply, without that division. Once separated, populations accumulate differences. Eventually they may be unable to produce fertile offspring together, or they may simply not meet. Species are real lineages. The boundaries can be messy, especially in plants and in microbes, where hybridization and gene transfer are common. Messy boundaries are what a branching process produces. They are not an objection to the process.

Human evolution is the same process applied to one lineage. The fossil and genetic evidence places the human lineage’s split from the chimpanzee lineage several million years ago. Bipedalism, larger brains, stone tools, and later language and culture accumulated. Other hominin species existed and are gone. Some of their genes remain in modern human populations, from episodes of interbreeding. The genetic difference between humans and chimpanzees is small in percentage and consequential in outcome, much of it in regulation rather than in the protein-coding sequence. Nothing in this requires a special biological mechanism for humans. It requires the ordinary mechanism acting on a particular lineage, plus the cultural inheritance that lineage eventually produced.

Evolution is as well supported as any theory in science. It is also, in its details, an active research field. The relative importance of selection and drift, the role of development in biasing variation, the frequency of gene transfer, and the genetic basis of particular adaptations are debated. Debate about details is not doubt about the framework. A reader can treat the framework as settled and the details as the place where new work happens. That is the accurate division.

Resistance is the evolution a person can watch. Bacteria exposed to an antibiotic evolve resistance, by mutation or by acquiring a gene from elsewhere. Viruses evolve as they spread. Tumors evolve under treatment. The process is not confined to the fossil record. It is a present mechanism. Medicine that ignores it produces resistant infections and resistant cancers. Agriculture that ignores it produces resistant pests. The practical importance of evolution is not only that it explains the history of life. It is that it is still running, on timescales that policy and medicine have to respect.

Sexual reproduction is a puzzle the theory has to solve, because it has a cost. An organism that reproduces sexually passes on only half its genes, relative to one that clones. The advantage that pays for the cost is probably the mixing of genes, which produces variety that helps in the presence of parasites and of changing conditions, and which clears harmful mutations. The debate about the exact advantage is ongoing. The existence of the cost is clear. The near-universality of sex among complex organisms suggests the advantage is large. The theory is strong enough to have puzzles of this kind. A weaker theory would not define them so sharply.

Convergence is the evidence that selection can reach similar solutions more than once. Eyes have evolved several times. Wings have evolved several times. Antifreeze proteins in cold-water fish have evolved separately in different lineages. Convergence shows that the space of possible forms is constrained by physics and by development, and that selection finds the workable regions of that space repeatedly. It is not evidence against common ancestry. It is evidence about the power of the filter once ancestry has supplied a lineage. The two together, shared descent and repeated solution, explain both the unity and the rhyming of life.

title: The Human Genome
paras: In 2001 two drafts of the human genome were published. In 2003 the project was declared complete, with reservations. In 2022 the last gaps, mostly difficult repetitive regions, were filled. We now have a continuous sequence of a human genome, a string of about three billion base pairs.

The string is not a blueprint in the way a blueprint specifies every board. It is closer to a recipe that assumes a cell already running. Genes, in the classical sense of protein-coding sequences, are a small minority of the total, on the order of one to two percent. The rest is not junk in the careless sense. Some of it regulates when and where genes are used. Some is structural. Some is the residue of old viruses and old copying accidents. How much of the noncoding DNA has a selected function remains debated. The debate is empirical. It will be settled by experiment, not by preference for tidiness.

What the sequence gave biology was a reference. Variation could be compared to something. Common differences among people, single-letter changes and larger rearrangements, could be catalogued. Disease studies could ask which differences are more common in people with a condition than in people without it. For rare diseases caused by a single broken gene, the method has been transformative. A child with an unexplained disorder can sometimes receive a diagnosis that did not exist as a named gene twenty years ago.

For common diseases the picture is harder. Heart disease, diabetes, and most psychiatric conditions are influenced by many variants of small effect, plus environment. Polygenic scores can rank risk in a population. They are not destinies, and they travel poorly between populations if the underlying studies were narrow. The genome is necessary information. It is not sufficient information.

The human genome also ended a certain kind of vanity. We do not have an unusually large number of genes. We have on the order of twenty thousand protein-coding genes, similar to other animals, fewer than some plants. Complexity, where we have it, comes from regulation, from splicing one gene into multiple products, and from a brain that builds itself by using the genome as a starting constraint rather than a finished diagram.
Reading the genome was the achievement of one generation. Writing it, in living people, is the argument of the next chapter.

Sequencing the genome was a technical achievement and a conceptual correction. The technical achievement was the reading of three billion base pairs with enough accuracy to be useful, first as drafts, then as a finished reference, then as a complete end-to-end sequence including the hard repetitive regions. The conceptual correction was the discovery that gene number did not measure complexity in any simple way. Humans have on the order of twenty thousand protein-coding genes. So do other animals. Some plants have more. Complexity, where it exists, is in the regulation, the splicing, the timing, and the networks, not in a longer list of parts.

Noncoding DNA is the majority of the sequence. Some of it is regulatory: switches that determine when and where a gene is used. Some of it is structural. Some of it is the remains of ancient viruses that inserted themselves and were inherited. Some of it may have no selected function. The fraction with function is disputed, and the dispute depends on what “function” is taken to mean. A sequence can affect a molecular measurement without affecting the organism’s success. The careful claim is that noncoding DNA is a mixture, not a wastebasket and not a hidden second genome of equal importance to the genes. Its importance is real and uneven.

Variation among people is the genome’s other lesson. Any two people differ at millions of sites. Most differences are common, small in effect, and shared across populations in different proportions. Some are rare and consequential in a single gene. The common differences are the raw material of polygenic scores and of adaptation. The rare ones are the raw material of many genetic diseases. Both kinds are inherited. Neither kind supports the older idea that human groups are discrete biological types. Human genetic variation is real, geographically patterned, and small compared with the variation inside any one population. The patterning is what migration and history produce. It is not a set of separate species.

The clinical use of the sequence has been most decisive for rare disease. A child with a severe, unexplained condition can have their genome, or their exome, sequenced and compared with their parents’. A new mutation in a known gene, or a pair of mutations in a recessive gene, can end a diagnostic search that once took years. Treatment does not always follow diagnosis. Sometimes it does. The diagnosis itself is a change in medicine.

For common disease the contribution is statistical. Genome-wide association studies find variants that are more common in people with a disease than in people without it. Each variant usually has a small effect. Together they can predict a fraction of the risk. The fraction is useful for research and, in some cases, for sorting people into higher and lower risk groups. It is not a personal prophecy. Environment, chance, and the limits of the studies intervene. Scores trained in one population often work less well in another, because the pattern of genetic correlation differs. Equity in the data is a scientific requirement, not only a social one.

The genome is a reference and a parts list. It is not a blueprint that specifies the finished body in detail. Development uses the list in a context: a fertilized egg, a womb, a sequence of signals, an environment. Read the list and you do not yet have the person. That limit is not a failure of the project. It is the next subject, and it is why genomics did not replace the rest of biology.

Privacy and ownership are the social edge of sequencing. A genome identifies a person and their relatives. It can reveal disease risk, ancestry, and, in some cases, information the person did not want. Databases that enable research also enable reidentification if they are careless. The scientific value of shared data is large. The harm of careless sharing is real. The balance is a governance problem sitting on top of a measurement revolution. The measurement will not slow down. The governance has to be built at the same speed.

Ancestry and identity should not be confused with the sequence. Genetic ancestry tests report similarities to reference populations. They are useful for genealogy and for the history of migrations. They do not assign a person to a race in any biological sense that withstands scrutiny, because human variation is continuous and overlapping. The tests measure real patterns. The social categories they are sometimes taken to support are coarser than the patterns. Keeping the measurement and the category apart is a service both to the science and to the people who use it.

Editing and sequencing together change what a variant means. A variant of unknown significance, found in a patient, can sometimes be tested in a cell or in an organoid to see whether it disrupts the gene’s function. The test turns a correlation into a mechanism. Mechanism is what makes a diagnosis solid and a therapy conceivable. The genome supplies the variant. The functional test supplies the interpretation. Neither alone is enough for the hardest cases. The combination is the direction of clinical genetics. It is slower than sequencing alone and more decisive.

title: CRISPR and Gene Editing
paras: Bacteria have been at war with viruses for billions of years. One of their defenses is a memory. They store snippets of viral DNA and use them to recognize the virus if it returns. A protein then cuts the viral genome. The system is called CRISPR.

In 2012 Jennifer Doudna, Emmanuelle Charpentier, and colleagues showed that the system could be aimed. A guide sequence could be designed, and the cutting protein, Cas9, would cut a chosen place in a chosen genome. Other laboratories reached the same capability at nearly the same time. Biology acquired an editor.

The editor is not magic. It cuts. The cell repairs the cut. The repair can disable a gene, or, if a template is supplied, sometimes insert a chosen sequence. Newer variants nick a single strand, or change one letter without a full break. The tools have multiplied. The principle remains: a sequence can be addressed.

In research, the effect has been a change of speed. Genes in mice, fish, crops, and cell lines can be altered in weeks rather than years. In medicine, the first wave of therapies edits cells outside the body and returns them. Blood disorders such as sickle cell disease have been treated this way, by editing bone marrow cells so they produce a useful form of hemoglobin. The early results are striking. The cost, the conditioning treatment, and the long-term watch for unwanted cuts are the constraints.

Editing embryos is a different act. In 2018 a researcher announced the birth of children whose genomes had been edited, ostensibly to reduce HIV risk. The experiment was widely condemned as premature, poorly justified, and a breach of norms that the field had stated. The condemnation was not a rejection of the tool. It was a rejection of using a tool, on people who cannot consent, before accuracy, necessity, and oversight were in place.

The line is worth keeping clear. Somatic editing changes a patient's cells and ends with that patient. Germline editing changes descendants. Agriculture sits in a third category, and societies are already arguing it crop by crop. CRISPR did not create these distinctions. It made them urgent.

Gene editing is the point at which biology became, in a practical sense, a writing discipline as well as a reading one. The power is real. The gaps in delivery, specificity, and ethics are also real. A serious account refuses both the miracle story and the ban.

The tool is simple in outline and subtle in practice. A guide RNA matching a chosen sequence is supplied together with a cutting protein, usually Cas9 or a relative. The protein cuts where the guide matches. The cell repairs the cut. If the repair is a quick join, the gene is often disrupted. If a template is provided, the repair sometimes copies the template, inserting a chosen change. Base editors and prime editors, developed later, change letters with fewer double-strand breaks. The menu of editors has grown. Delivery remains the hard part.

Delivery is the difference between a result in a dish and a result in a patient. In a dish, the editor can be put into cells directly. In a body, it must reach the right cells, in the right tissue, in sufficient number, without damaging the rest. Viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, and direct injection are the current methods. Each has limits on cargo, on which tissues it reaches, and on immune response. Many of the first successes have been in blood, in the eye, and in the liver, where delivery is more tractable. Whole-body editing of arbitrary genes is not the present state.

The sickle-cell treatments show both the power and the cost. Cells are taken from the patient, edited so that they produce fetal hemoglobin or so that a repressor of fetal hemoglobin is disabled, and returned after the remaining bone marrow is cleared. Patients have been freed from the crises of the disease. The procedure is intensive, expensive, and not without risk. It is also a proof that a genetic disease can be treated by editing the relevant cells. Other blood and immune disorders are following the same path.

Off-target cuts are the technical objection that has to be measured rather than assumed. An editor aimed at one sequence may cut similar sequences elsewhere. The rate depends on the guide, the editor, and the cell. It can be measured. It has been reduced by better design. It is not zero in every setting. For a therapy, the question is whether the residual rate is small compared with the benefit. For an embryo, the question is stricter, because every cell of the future person, and of their descendants if the change is inherited, carries the result.

Germline editing is the line most countries and most scientific bodies have treated as not yet permissible, outside tightly limited research that does not lead to a birth. The reasons are practical and ethical. Accuracy and long-term effects are not well enough known. The medical need is often addressable by other means, including selection of embryos in cases where that is accepted. The people affected cannot consent. The 2018 births did not meet the standards the field had articulated. The condemnation was an attempt to keep a powerful tool inside rules made in advance, rather than a rejection of the tool.

Agriculture is the third domain. Edited crops can resist disease, tolerate stress, or improve nutrition. Some jurisdictions treat certain edits, those that could have arisen by mutation, more like conventional breeding than like older transgenic methods. Others do not. The biological question and the regulatory question are different. The biological question is what change was made and what it does. The regulatory question is how a society chooses to label and approve it. A guide can state both and should not pretend they are the same question.

CRISPR did not invent the desire to change inheritance. It made the desire cheap and specific. The specificity is the advance. The cheapness is why the ethical and safety questions, which were once hypothetical, now have deadlines.

Somatic editing and enhancement should be distinguished. Treating a disease in a consenting patient’s cells is medicine. Editing an embryo for a trait that is not a disease, or editing a person for advantage rather than for treatment, is a different act. The line is argued. The existence of a difference between treatment and enhancement is clear even where the boundary is not. A therapy for sickle cell is not the same kind of decision as a speculative edit for muscle or for height. Keeping the difference visible is part of using the tool without confusing it with a general permission to redesign people.

Delivery vehicles are a field of their own. Lipid nanoparticles, used in the mRNA vaccines, can carry editors to the liver and to some other tissues. Viral vectors can reach the eye, the nervous system, and muscle, with limits on size and with immune complications. Direct injection works for accessible sites. No vehicle reaches every tissue efficiently. The map of what can be edited in a living person is, for now, a map of delivery as much as a map of genetics. Improving delivery would expand therapy more than improving the editor alone. The editor is ahead of the vehicle.

Equity will determine whether the tool is a general advance or a narrow one. The first therapies are expensive. They require facilities. They will reach patients in rich health systems before they reach patients elsewhere, unless deliberate provision is made. The science does not make the provision. Institutions do. A chapter that celebrates the cure of sickle cell in a trial and omits the question of who receives it describes a result and not a change in the burden of the disease. Both belong in the account. The result is real. The burden shifts only when the result is delivered.

title: Synthetic Biology
paras: If editing changes an existing text, synthetic biology asks whether the text can be written from scratch, or joined in combinations nature did not try.

The field has several layers. At the bottom is DNA synthesis. Machines build genes to order. What once had to be cloned from an organism can be specified in a file and delivered in a tube. The cost has fallen for decades. The consequence is that design can be tested rather than merely described.

Above that is the rearrangement of pathways. Yeast has been engineered to produce a precursor of a malaria drug. Bacteria have been engineered to make fuels, flavors, fabrics, and industrial enzymes. The successes are specific. A pathway that works in a flask may fail in a tank. Biology is not a circuit board, even when it is drawn as one. The drawing is useful anyway. It forces the designer to name the parts.

At a further level, researchers have built cells with synthetic genomes. A bacterium has been run on a genome synthesized in the laboratory, reduced toward a minimal set of genes. The minimal cell still contains genes whose functions are not fully known. Even the smallest life is not yet a fully understood machine. That is an important result, not a failure of the project.

Synthetic biology also includes codes nature did not use. Expanded genetic alphabets, with more than four letters, have been made to function in cells. Nonstandard amino acids have been inserted into proteins. These are proofs that the particular code we inherited is not the only workable one. They are also tools, for proteins with functions ordinary proteins cannot have.

The risks follow the capabilities. A sequence that can be ordered can be misused. The practical barriers, expertise, delivery, and the tendency of engineered organisms to lose against wild ones, are higher than thrillers suggest and lower than complacency assumes. Screening of orders, and a culture of accountability in the laboratories that do the work, are the present defenses. They will need to scale with the tools.

The scientific point is quieter. Life is a material system. Its parts can be listed, synthesized, and recombined. The listing is incomplete. The recombination has already left the page and entered factories and clinics. the earlier guides. It is no longer young.

The enabling change is the fall in the cost of reading and writing DNA. Sequencing now costs a tiny fraction of what it cost at the end of the Human Genome Project. Synthesis of genes, and of whole small genomes, is a commercial service. A design can be a file. The file can be ordered. The distance from idea to test has collapsed for any project that lives in a microbe or a cell line. That is the practical meaning of synthetic biology.

Pathway engineering is the workhorse. A cell has a metabolism. A pathway is a sequence of enzymatic steps from a starting material to a product. If the enzymes exist somewhere in nature, their genes can be moved into a production host, usually a yeast or a bacterium, and tuned. If they do not exist, they can sometimes be designed or evolved. The antimalarial precursor artemisinin, flavors, fragrances, and industrial chemicals have been made this way. The successes are real. So are the failures, which are less famous. A pathway that works in a flask can poison its host, or cost too much feedstock, or lose to an existing chemical process. The field is an industry as well as a science. Industries count costs.

Minimal cells test how much of a genome is required for life under comfortable laboratory conditions. A bacterial genome can be reduced, synthesized, and used to boot a cell. The reduced genome still contains genes of unknown function. Life, even pared down, is not yet a fully annotated machine. The result is a limit on our understanding and a tool for studying what the remaining genes do. It is not a cell built from first principles out of nonliving parts. That harder goal remains ahead.

Expanded alphabets and nonstandard amino acids show that the particular code we inherited is contingent. Cells have been made to use six-letter DNA and to incorporate amino acids that nature does not use. The purpose is usually a better protein for a particular job, or a cleaner biological system that cannot easily exchange genes with the wild. Containment by dependence on a synthetic nutrient is one proposed safety measure. It is a measure, not a guarantee. Evolution is patient.

Safety and misuse are part of the subject because the tools are widely available. Ordering a pathogen’s genome is restricted and screened by responsible suppliers. Not every supplier is responsible, and not every sequence reveals its purpose. The practical barriers to harm remain significant: expertise, equipment, delivery, and the fact that engineered organisms are often fragile. The barriers are lower than they were. Governance has been a mix of self-regulation, screening, and law. It will have to keep pace with cheaper synthesis and with automated design. The scientific opportunity and the governance problem grew from the same cause.

Synthetic biology’s place in a guide is as the writing side of the reading revolution. We can sequence life. We can, in increasing measure, specify changes and build new pathways. We cannot yet design a cell from scratch with the reliability of an engineer designing a bridge. The gap is the size of the remaining mystery of living systems. It is also a gap that narrows with each working pathway and each booted genome.

Automation is the next practical change. Design software, robotic liquid handling, and automated testing let a small team run a cycle of design, build, and measure that once required a large one. The cycle is the method. Faster cycles mean more of the design space can be searched. They also mean that the limits of understanding become clearer: a design that fails does so for a reason in the cell, and the reason is often a regulation, a toxicity, or a burden that the design did not include. Synthetic biology teaches the complexity of cells by trying to write them. The failures are data.

Biosafety levels and screening are the present controls. Laboratories are classified by the hazard of the organisms they handle. DNA synthesis companies screen orders against lists of dangerous sequences. The controls are imperfect and useful. They raise the cost and the visibility of misuse. They do not make misuse impossible. As synthesis moves into more hands and more automated settings, the controls have to move too. The alternative is a capability that grows faster than the practice of watching it. Watching is less exciting than designing. It is part of the same subject if the subject is to remain a public good.

Standards and parts registries are the attempt to make biology more like engineering. Catalogued parts, with measured behavior, can be combined with less surprise. The attempt has helped. Biology’s context dependence has limited it. A part that works in one strain, in one condition, may fail in another. The limit is not a reason to abandon standards. It is a reason to measure context as part of the standard. Synthetic biology matures as it records its failures of transfer and designs around them. Maturity looks like better annotation, not like the end of surprises.

title: Neuroscience
paras: The brain is an organ of about eighty-six billion neurons, supported by a comparable population of glial cells, wired by connections that number in the tens of trillions. It is not a computer in any simple sense. It is the organ that makes computation, perception, memory, and movement out of cells.

A neuron signals by electrical pulses and chemical synapses. The pulse, the action potential, is a brief reversal of voltage across the membrane, driven by channels that open and close. At the synapse, the pulse becomes a chemical message. The receiving cell adds the messages up. If the sum crosses a threshold, it fires. Learning, in many cases, is a change in the strength of these connections. The phrase "cells that fire together wire together" is a slogan with a real mechanism behind it.

The map of regions is older than the mechanism. Damage taught it. A stroke in one place removes speech. Damage in another removes the ability to form new memories while sparing old ones. Modern imaging watches healthy brains at work, with the caveat that blood flow is not thought, and that a lit region is a correlation. The map is useful and incomplete. Functions are distributed. The same task can recruit different patterns in different people.

The great technical change is the ability to record and to perturb. Electrodes listen to hundreds or thousands of cells at once. Optogenetics, in animals, makes chosen neurons sensitive to light, so a circuit can be switched on or off rather than merely watched. The difference between watching and switching is the difference between a story and a test.

Disorders keep the field honest. Alzheimer's disease spreads abnormal proteins through characteristic networks, and disease-modifying treatments have only begun to slow it, not reverse it. Depression is not a simple shortage of one chemical, though chemicals matter. Parkinson's disease is, in part, the loss of a particular population of dopamine neurons, which is why replacing the signal helps movement and does not restore the whole person. The brain is not one problem. It is many systems sharing a skull.

Neuroscience can say, with confidence, that thought is what brains do, and that brains are physical. It cannot yet say how a pattern of firing becomes the experience of red, or of pain, or of understanding a sentence. That gap has its own chapter. It should not be used to smuggle mystery into the parts we can measure. The measurable parts are already the most complicated objects science has tried to map.

The neuron is the signaling unit, and its signal is better understood than the system it belongs to. At rest, the inside of the cell is negative relative to the outside. Channels in the membrane, selective for particular ions, open and close. A sufficient input opens sodium channels, sodium enters, the voltage reverses briefly, and the reversal travels along the axon. At the synapse, the arrival of the pulse triggers the release of neurotransmitter. The receiving cell’s response depends on which transmitter and which receptor. Some inputs excite. Some inhibit. The cell sums them. Learning changes the strengths and the numbers of these connections. The summary is accurate and incomplete. Modulation, timing, and the identity of the cells matter as much as the bare on and off.

Maps of function came first from damage. Broca’s area and Wernicke’s area entered the vocabulary because injury there disrupted speech in different ways. The hippocampus entered the study of memory because a patient who lost both, in an operation for epilepsy, could not form new episodic memories and could still learn some skills. The cases were cruel and informative. Imaging later showed which regions are active, on average, during which tasks in healthy people. Activity is a correlation. It does not, by itself, prove that the region is necessary. Necessity is tested by disruption. Disruption in humans is limited to what disease, surgery, and careful noninvasive methods allow. In animals it can be precise.

Optogenetics made disruption precise in animals. A gene for a light-sensitive channel is inserted into chosen neurons. Light delivered to the tissue switches those neurons on or off. A behavior can be started or stopped by the switch. The method has linked particular cell types to fear, thirst, movement, and memory retrieval in mice. It is not a human therapy in any ordinary form. It is a research instrument that turned correlation into a stronger kind of evidence.

Recording has scaled. Arrays now listen to hundreds or thousands of neurons at once. The data are large. The interpretation is the bottleneck. A pattern of firing is not yet a content. Decoding work can predict, from the pattern, which stimulus was shown or which movement is about to occur, with imperfect accuracy. Prediction of that kind is evidence that the information is present in the recorded cells. It is not a reading of thought in the ordinary sense. The gap between a decoded variable and a subjective report remains.

Disease keeps the claims modest. Neurodegenerative diseases show that particular proteins, misfolded and spreading, can dismantle particular systems. Parkinson’s disease shows that replacing a missing chemical signal can restore movement for a time and does not restore the lost cells. Depression and schizophrenia show that the chemistry matters and that no single chemical account covers the patients. The brain is not one organ in the way the liver is one organ. It is many systems. A treatment that helps one system can leave the others untouched. That is a reason for precision and a reason against slogans.

The physical basis of thought is not in serious doubt among neuroscientists. Thought depends on the brain. Change the brain in particular ways and thought changes in particular ways. What remains open is the mapping: which patterns constitute which mental operations, how development wires the patterns, and how the patterns relate to conscious experience. The open questions are large. They sit on top of a base that is already physical, cellular, and, in increasing measure, testable.

Development is the part of neuroscience that a focus on the adult brain understates. The brain wires itself. Genes set the outline. Activity, before and after birth, refines the connections. Critical periods exist, during which certain skills are acquired more readily. Deprivation during a critical period has lasting effects. The wiring is not a readout of a fixed plan. It is a plan that expects input. That fact connects neuroscience to pediatrics, to education, and to the effects of early environment, without reducing any of those to a slogan about plasticity. Plasticity is real and bounded. The bounds are part of the science.

Memory is not a single store. Working memory holds a little information briefly. Episodic memory records events and depends heavily on the hippocampus for formation. Semantic memory holds facts and becomes partly independent of the hippocampus over time. Skill memory lives in other circuits. The distinctions are supported by patients who lose one and keep another. They matter for education, for dementia, and for the design of any interface that claims to match how people learn. A single word, memory, covers several systems. The systems fail separately and are studied separately.

Brain-computer interfaces are the applied edge. Electrodes decode intended movement and allow a paralyzed person to control a cursor or a robotic arm. The decoding is imperfect and improving. The clinical benefit, for some patients, is already real. The interface is not a reading of private thought in general. It is a reading of specific, trained signals related to a task. Keeping the specificity in view prevents both the understatement of a real assistive technology and the overstatement of a general mind-reading. The technology does what it is trained to do. That is enough to matter.

title: Consciousness
paras: Consciousness is the fact that there is something it is like to be you. A camera does not, so far as we know, have a point of view. You do. Explaining the point of view is the problem.

The easy problems, which are not easy, are the functional ones. How does the brain discriminate, integrate, report, and control? These can be studied. The hard problem, as the philosopher David Chalmers named it, is why any of that functioning is accompanied by experience. A complete diagram of the visual system would not, by itself, seem to explain why seeing red feels like something.
Science has not solved the hard problem. It has narrowed the easy ones.

Some contrasts are reliable. Certain patterns of cortical activity accompany conscious perception, and others, under masking or distraction, do not, even when the sense organ received the stimulus. Anesthesia has signatures. Sleep stages have signatures. Patients with disorders of consciousness can sometimes be distinguished, by brain activity, from patients who appear unresponsive and are. These are correlations with report and behavior. They are precious. They are not a theory of feeling.

Competing theories make different bets. Global workspace theories say a content becomes conscious when it is broadcast widely through the cortex for use by many systems. Integrated information theories say consciousness tracks a particular kind of internal causal structure, and try to quantify it. Higher-order theories say a state is conscious when the brain represents itself as being in that state. Predictive-processing accounts fold experience into the brain's work of guessing the causes of its inputs. The theories are testable at the edges. None is established.

Two cautions follow. First, consciousness is not a license to ignore mechanism. Whatever experience is, in humans it depends on particular brain processes, and those processes can be disrupted in particular ways. Second, the unsolved problem is not evidence for a particular doctrine. It is evidence that the problem is unsolved. A guide written now should say so without embarrassment. the earlier guides. He could not close this question. Neither can we.

A useful distinction separates access from experience. Access consciousness is the availability of information for report, for reasoning, and for the control of action. Experience is the fact that there is something it is like to have the information. The two usually travel together in healthy people. They can be pulled apart in experiments and in clinical cases. A stimulus can influence behavior without being reportable. A patient can show brain responses consistent with awareness and be unable to move or speak. The distinction does not solve the hard problem. It makes the experimental subject less muddy.

Correlates of consciousness are the empirical foothold. When a subject reports seeing a stimulus, certain cortical patterns are present. When the same stimulus is presented but masked or missed, those patterns are absent or reduced, even though earlier sensory areas may still respond. The timing and the spread of activity matter. Theories differ on which feature is decisive. Global workspace theories emphasize broadcast. Integrated information theories emphasize a structural property. Higher-order theories emphasize a representation of the representation. Each makes predictions. Adversarial collaborations have begun to test them against the same experiments. That is the right method. It is too early to declare a winner.

Anesthesia and sleep are natural experiments. Under general anesthesia, report and the associated cortical patterns cease, and they return together. Different anesthetics act by different molecular routes and converge on similar network effects. Sleep stages show that behavior and experience can dissociate: in some stages people dream and in some they do not, and the brain signatures differ. Disorders of consciousness after injury show a spectrum from unresponsive wakefulness to states in which communication is possible through brain activity even when movement is not. These findings matter clinically. They also constrain theory. A theory of consciousness that cannot say why anesthesia abolishes it is incomplete.

The hard problem remains a problem about explanation, not about evidence that experience exists. Experience exists for the reader. The question is why any physical process should be accompanied by it, and whether a future theory will close the question or dissolve it. Some philosophers argue that the question is misconceived. Some neuroscientists argue that a sufficiently detailed account of access and of self-modeling will leave no further question that has an empirical grip. The argument is open. What is not open is the dependence of human experience on the brain. Damage, drugs, stimulation, and development all demonstrate the dependence. A theory that ignored them would not be a theory of this phenomenon.

Nonhuman consciousness is a related and unsettled question. Many animals have nervous systems that support learning, perception, and flexible behavior. Whether and where experience accompanies those capacities is inferred from anatomy, behavior, and, increasingly, from comparative neuroscience. The inference is not certainty. It is strong enough, for mammals and birds in particular, that welfare decisions already treat them as experiencing subjects. The guide’s claim is limited. Consciousness in humans is tied to measurable brain processes. Those processes have relatives in other animals. The hard problem is unsolved in every species, including ours.

The clinical stake keeps the subject from being only philosophical. Decisions about withdrawing care, about anesthesia, and about the treatment of infants and of nonhuman animals all assume something about the presence of experience. Better correlates make those decisions better informed. They do not make them automatic. A signature of awareness in an unresponsive patient changes what the family and the physicians know. It does not by itself say what should be done. The science improves the information. The decision remains a decision. Confusing the two helps neither.

Report is the usual measure and a limited one. Adults who can speak are the easiest subjects. Infants, nonhuman animals, and patients who cannot move require other measures: behavior, physiology, and neural signatures validated against report in those who can report. The extension is uncertain and necessary. A science of consciousness confined to verbal adults would miss most of the subjects who have nervous systems. The correlates established in adults are the bridge. Crossing the bridge carefully is the work. Refusing to cross it leaves the science narrower than the phenomenon.

The study of consciousness has attracted theories that outrun their tests. The corrective is the same as in any science. A theory must say what would count against it. Several current theories have begun to do so, and to be tested in shared experiments. The outcome of those experiments will retire some claims. It will not, by itself, solve the hard problem. Retiring claims is progress. A field that cannot retire claims is not yet a science. The presence of adversarial tests is a sign that this field is acquiring the habit. The habit matters more, at this stage, than any single theory’s success.

title: Aging and Longevity
paras: Aging is not a single disease. It is the rising risk of many diseases, and the slow loss of repair.

Cells accumulate damage. DNA picks up errors. Proteins misfold. Mitochondria, the cell's power stations, falter. Telomeres, the caps on chromosomes, shorten in many tissues. Stem cells deplete. Chronic, low-grade inflammation rises. These processes are measured. They are not yet a unified theory. They are a list with overlaps.

The list is encouraging, because lists can be tested. Animals with altered single genes live substantially longer. Nutrient-sensing pathways, including those involving insulin and a regulator called mTOR, affect lifespan in yeast, worms, flies, and mice. Rapamycin, a drug that damps mTOR, extends life in mice. Whether it does so usefully in humans, at a dose that does not cost too much immunity, is not settled. Caloric restriction extends life in many species and has mixed, modest results in primates. Metformin, a diabetes drug, is under study for broader effects on aging. The studies are the right response. The marketing that leaps ahead of them is not.

Senescence is a particular target. Cells that have stopped dividing but refuse to die secrete inflammatory signals. Drugs that clear such cells, called senolytics, improve health in old mice. Human trials are early. Reprogramming is another target. Factors that can turn an adult cell back toward an embryonic state can, in partial doses, reverse some signs of age in animal tissues. The risk is cancer, or the loss of cell identity. The dose is the problem.

Human lifespan has already changed, mostly for other reasons. Clean water, vaccines, antibiotics, and surgery added decades to life expectancy where they arrived. Further gains will be slower if they depend on postponing the diseases of age rather than on preventing infection in childhood. The honest goal of the field is healthspan, years lived without disability, more than a fantasy of indefinite life. Indefinite life is not a result anyone has. Slower aging, in some tissues, under some interventions, is a result in animals. That is enough to make the field serious, and not enough to make promises.

Aging can be described as the accumulation of damage plus the decline of maintenance. Cells suffer mutations. Some mutations are harmless, some kill the cell, and some push the cell toward cancer. Proteins misfold and aggregate. Mitochondria become less efficient and more productive of damaging byproducts. Telomeres shorten in tissues that divide, limiting further division. Stem-cell pools shrink. The immune system becomes less precise and more inflammatory. Epigenetic marks, which help cells remember their identity, drift. Each of these is documented. Their relative contributions differ by tissue and by species. No single lesion is “the cause” in the way a single bacterium is the cause of tuberculosis.

Comparative biology is a source of clues. A mouse lives two or three years. A naked mole-rat of similar size lives decades and rarely develops cancer. A bowhead whale lives two centuries. Some of the difference is size and metabolic rate. Some of it is specific protections: better DNA repair, different immune strategies, membranes less prone to oxidation. The protections are genetic and, in principle, intelligible. They have not yet been copied into a therapy for humans. They show that lifespan is not a fixed law of biochemistry. It is a trait, and traits can differ.

Interventions in laboratory animals are the other source. Mutations in nutrient-sensing pathways extend life in short-lived species. Rapamycin extends life in mice even when started late. Senolytic drugs, which clear senescent cells, improve health measures in old mice. Partial reprogramming with factors that can reset cell identity has reversed some age-related changes in animal tissues, with a risk of cancer or of loss of cell type that has to be managed. These results are why the field is active. They are results in animals, under controlled conditions, often with tradeoffs. Translation is the unsolved step.

Human evidence is slower and more important. Life expectancy rose mainly because fewer people died young. The maximum human lifespan has not shown a comparable rise. Centenarians exist and are studied. Their genetics and habits are informative and not yet a recipe. Caloric restriction and related diets improve some risk markers in people and have not been shown to extend maximum lifespan. Metformin, rapamycin, and other candidates are in trials aimed at healthspan. The trials are the correct next evidence. Marketing that precedes the trials is not evidence.

The practical conclusion is modest and still large. Some processes of aging are modifiable in animals. Some diseases of aging are already modifiable in people by ordinary medicine: blood pressure, lipids, smoking, vaccines, cancer screening. Further modification of the underlying processes is a research program with animal proof-of-concept and incomplete human proof. The goal that matches the evidence is more years of health, not a promise of indefinite life. Indefinite life is a speculation. Slower aging is a hypothesis with enough support to be worth testing carefully.

Inequality belongs in any honest chapter on longevity. Life expectancy differs by country, by income, and by access to ordinary medicine by amounts that dwarf the effect of any anti-aging supplement on the market. The largest available gains, globally, are still in infection control, in maternal care, in smoking reduction, and in the management of blood pressure and diabetes. Research on the biology of aging may add further gains. It does not replace the gains that public health already knows how to deliver. A reader should hold both projects in view. They are not rivals. They operate on different parts of the same curve.

Biomarkers of aging are an attempt to measure the process rather than the calendar. Epigenetic clocks, built from methylation patterns, predict mortality better than age alone in some studies. Other markers use proteins, inflammation, or physical function. None is yet a replacement for tracking actual disease and death in a trial. A clock that moves in response to an intervention is a hint. A trial that shows fewer heart attacks, or a longer life, is a result. The field is rich in hints and poorer in results of the second kind. The distinction should govern the headlines.

The tradeoff with cancer is structural. Mechanisms that allow cells to divide and repair also allow cells to divide when they should not. Mechanisms that suppress tumors, such as senescence and apoptosis, contribute to aging. An intervention that pushes on one side of the tradeoff must watch the other. Some of the most promising aging interventions are being studied with cancer surveillance built in. The surveillance is not a bureaucratic addition. It is a recognition of the biology. A longer life bought with a large increase in cancer would be a different kind of result. The field is looking for interventions that improve the whole, not only the marker.

title: The Microbiome
paras: You are not only your cells. You are an ecosystem.

The gut alone holds trillions of bacteria, with fungi, viruses, and archaea in attendance. Skin, mouth, and lungs have their own communities. The genes in these microbes outnumber the genes in the human genome by a large factor. For a long time medicine treated this fact as contamination. It is closer to an organ.

The community helps digest what we cannot, trains the immune system, and produces molecules that enter the blood. Mice raised without microbes have abnormal immune systems and abnormal guts. Transfer the microbes, and some of the abnormalities change. In humans, recurrent infection with Clostridioides difficile, a bacterium that overruns a gut after antibiotics, can be cured by transferring stool from a healthy donor. The cure is unglamorous and real. It is the clearest proof that a microbial community can be a medicine.

The rest of the claims need sorting. Associations are everywhere. People with obesity, diabetes, autism, depression, and inflammatory bowel disease have, on average, different gut communities from people without those conditions. Difference is not cause. Diet changes the community in days. Illness changes it. Drugs change it. A microbe that marks a disease may be a passenger.

Cause is being tested. Specific strains affect specific pathways. Some gut bacteria modify drugs, including a common cardiac medicine, so that the drug's effect depends on who is living in the patient. Others produce short-chain fatty acids that influence metabolism and immune cells. The phrase "the microbiome" hides this specificity. A serious result names a microbe, a molecule, and a host response.

Antibiotics are the blunt history of the subject. They save lives and strip communities. The recovery is usually good and sometimes not. The long project is more precise: add the missing organism, feed the useful one, stop feeding the harmful one, and leave the rest alone. Microbiome science is past the stage of discovering that the organisms are there. It is at the stage of learning which ones matter, and when.

The community in the gut is the best studied because it is the largest and the most accessible. It is dominated by bacteria, with important contributions from archaea, fungi, and viruses that infect the bacteria. Its composition varies along the gut, between people, and within a person over time. Diet is the fastest lever. A change in fiber intake changes the community within days. Antibiotics change it within hours. Illness, travel, and drugs change it. A single sample is a snapshot, not a fate.

What the community does is specific, and specificity is the cure for hype. Some bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids, which feed the cells lining the colon and influence immune signaling. Some modify bile acids. Some synthesize vitamins. Some inactivate drugs, and some activate them. A cardiac drug, digoxin, is inactivated by a particular gut bacterium in some people, which changes the drug’s effect. That is a precise, actionable finding. “The microbiome affects health” is a slogan. A named organism, a named molecule, and a named host response is a result.

Fecal microbiota transplantation proved that a community can be a treatment. In recurrent C. difficile infection, the normal community has been damaged, often by antibiotics, and a pathogen occupies the niche. Transferring a healthy donor’s community restores resistance and cures most such patients. Defined consortia of cultured bacteria are being developed to do the same job more cleanly. The success is a proof of principle. It does not imply that transferring communities will cure unrelated diseases. Trials in other conditions have been mixed. The principle is real. The indications are narrow until shown otherwise.

Associations with obesity, diabetes, autism, depression, and autoimmune disease are widely reported and hard to interpret. People with these conditions often have different average communities. Diet, medication, and the disease itself can produce the difference. Establishing cause requires intervention or a mechanism, preferably both. Some mechanisms are emerging. Others will not emerge, because the association was a passenger. The field is in the stage where the passenger count is being reduced.

The hygiene observation belongs here. Populations with less exposure to diverse microbes in early life have more allergic and autoimmune disease. The observation is epidemiological. The mechanism is probably a matter of immune education: the developing immune system expects certain microbial signals and behaves differently without them. The practical implication is not a return to unmanaged infection. It is a more precise understanding of which exposures train the immune system and which only cause harm. That understanding is incomplete. It is far enough along to be part of pediatrics and of the design of future interventions.

The microbiome is an organ in the functional sense. It contributes to digestion, immunity, and drug response. It is not an organ in the anatomical sense, and it is not a second brain, despite the existence of real gut-brain signaling. Treating it as a partner rather than as dirt was the conceptual change. Treating it with the same demand for mechanism that the rest of medicine requires is the present task.

Diet is the intervention a person can actually control. Fiber feeds the bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids. A varied plant diet tends to support a more varied community. The tending is not a guarantee of any particular health outcome. It is a lever with evidence behind it, unlike many of the commercial tests that classify a person’s microbiome and sell a tailored cure. Most such tests are ahead of the evidence. The research is real. The retail interpretation is often not. The difference is the ordinary one between a field in progress and a market in a hurry.

Early life is when the community is assembled. Birth mode, feeding, antibiotics, and environment shape the first colonists. The assembly influences immune development. The influence is real in animal studies and supported in human epidemiology. It is not a script. Children differ. The practical implication is caution with unnecessary antibiotics in infancy and attention to the conditions of early feeding, not a rigid protocol sold as optimization. Assembly is a window. Windows are not machines.

Causality runs both ways. The community affects the host. The host’s diet, immune system, and drugs affect the community. Cross-sectional studies cannot sort the directions. Longitudinal studies and interventions can. The field has moved toward both. A result that includes a time course, or a transfer, or a metabolite traced from microbe to host effect, is a result that can support a direction. A result that is a single comparison of two groups is a result that cannot. Readers can apply the distinction themselves. It removes a large fraction of the overclaimed literature at a stroke.

title: Precision Medicine
paras: Medicine spent a century learning the average patient. Precision medicine asks what differs in this one.

The differences are genetic, metabolic, microbial, and biographical. A cancer is not only a tissue of origin. It is a set of mutations. Lung cancers with a particular altered gene can be treated with a drug aimed at that alteration, and the response can be dramatic, until resistance emerges. The pattern has repeated for other genes and other tumors. Matching drug to mutation is the clearest success of the idea.

Immune therapies are the other clear success. Checkpoint inhibitors release a brake on immune cells, which then attack tumors that had been invisible to them. They cure some patients with cancers that were uniformly fatal, help others for a time, and do nothing for many. The difference is partly the tumor's mutations, which provide targets, and partly the immune context. Reading both is the work.

Beyond cancer, precision is uneven. Pharmacogenomics can warn that a patient will process a drug too slowly or too quickly. Rare-disease sequencing can end a diagnostic odyssey. Polygenic risk scores can, in some populations, identify people at high risk of heart disease who look ordinary by older measures. Wearable sensors and repeated blood tests promise a medicine of trajectories rather than annual snapshots. Most of that promise is still infrastructure.

mRNA medicine belongs in this chapter. The vaccines against COVID-19 demonstrated that a genetic instruction, packaged in lipid droplets, can be designed in days once a viral sequence is known, and manufactured as a platform rather than as a bespoke organism. The same platform is being aimed at other infections and at cancer antigens personal to a tumor. The demonstration was public and global. It is easy to forget how implausible it would have sounded in a science guide written in 1984.

Precision medicine has a failure mode. It can become expensive stratification without better outcomes, or data without a decision. A sequence is not a treatment. The standard to hold is the old one. Does the patient live longer, or live better, than under the previous care? Where the answer is yes, the approach has earned its name. Where the answer is not yet, it remains a research program with good tools.

Cancer is where precision has changed outcomes most clearly. A tumor is sequenced. A driver mutation is found. A drug aimed at the protein that mutation alters is given. In cancers with the right driver, the response can be rapid. Resistance almost always follows, because the tumor is a population of cells and selection applies. The next drug, or a combination, may answer the resistance for a time. The pattern has turned some diagnoses that were uniformly fatal into chronic or, in a minority of patients, curable diseases. It has left other cancers, without a usable driver or without a drug, where they were. Precision here means matching, not magic.

Immunotherapy is the other transformation. Checkpoint inhibitors remove a brake that tumors exploit. The immune system, once released, can clear cancers that had resisted everything else. It can also attack healthy tissue. Biomarkers, including the number of mutations in the tumor and the expression of certain proteins, predict response imperfectly. Cell therapies that engineer a patient’s own immune cells to recognize a cancer antigen have produced lasting remissions in some leukemias and lymphomas. They are complex to make and not yet general. The direction is clear. The immune system is a drug target and a drug.

Pharmacogenomics is quieter and already useful. Variants in genes that metabolize drugs change the dose a patient needs, or the risk of a severe reaction. Testing before prescribing is standard for some drugs and some ancestries where a dangerous variant is common. The principle extends further than the current testing. Implementation, not knowledge, is often the limit.

mRNA is a platform in the precise sense. The payload is an instruction. The delivery is a lipid droplet. Change the instruction and, in favorable cases, you change the protein the body temporarily makes. Vaccines were the first global proof. Therapeutics that replace a missing protein, or that present cancer antigens particular to a patient’s tumor, are in development. The platform does not remove the need for the right target. It shortens the path from target to candidate.

The limits are as important as the wins. Most common diseases are not single-gene diseases. A polygenic score can stratify risk and cannot yet dictate a unique treatment for each person. Data can accumulate without a decision attached. Cost can confine a therapy to the wealthy unless systems are built to do otherwise. Precision medicine earns its name when the extra information changes what is done and the change helps the patient. By that standard it has earned the name in parts of oncology, in rare disease, in drug safety, and in vaccines. It is still earning it everywhere else.

Data integration is the unfinished infrastructure. A patient’s genome, records, images, and wearable data are usually in different systems. Combining them safely and usefully is an engineering and a governance task. Where it has been done, rare-disease diagnosis has improved and research has accelerated. Where it has not, precision remains a set of separate tests. The science has outrun the plumbing. The plumbing is not glamorous. It is what turns a result in a paper into a result in a clinic.

Rare disease is where sequencing has already changed the standard of care. Many children with suspected genetic conditions now receive a sequencing test as part of diagnosis rather than as a last resort. The yield is substantial. A fraction of diagnoses lead to a change in treatment. A larger fraction lead to an end of uncertainty and to better counseling. The change is quiet compared with a new cancer drug. It is a change in what medicine considers ordinary. Ordinary sequencing for unexplained serious disease is the precision medicine that has most clearly arrived.

Prevention is the precision that scales. Identifying people at high genetic risk of heart disease, and treating the risk before the disease, changes outcomes for a population. The identification is imperfect. The treatment is often an ordinary drug. The combination is precision in the sense that the information selects who benefits most from an intervention that could not be given to everyone. This form of precision is less dramatic than a gene therapy and more consequential in total lives. A balanced account includes it. Drama is not the measure. Lives and years of health are.

title: Climate Science
paras: Climate is weather averaged, and the average is moving.

The basic mechanism is old and solid. Certain gases, among them carbon dioxide and methane, absorb infrared radiation that the Earth's surface emits. Add more of them, and the surface must warm until the energy leaving the planet again balances the energy arriving from the Sun. Svante Arrhenius calculated the effect of carbon dioxide in the 1890s. The calculation has been refined, not repealed.

What has changed is the amount of the gases and the quality of the record. Carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 parts per million before the industrial use of coal, to about 420. The rise is measured in the air and matched, by isotopes, to the burning of fossil fuels. Global average surface temperature is now roughly 1.2 degrees Celsius above the late nineteenth-century baseline, with individual recent years higher. The ocean has taken up most of the added heat. Glaciers and ice sheets have lost mass. Sea level has risen. The timing and the pattern, warmer nights, a warming troposphere, a cooling stratosphere, match the greenhouse account and do not match the alternatives that have been checked, including changes in the Sun.

Models are not the foundation. They are the projection. The foundation is the physics of radiation, the measured rise in greenhouse gases, and the observed heat. Models that include those factors reproduce the past century. Models that omit human emissions do not. The remaining uncertainties are real and narrower than the public argument often suggests. How much warming a doubling of carbon dioxide produces is constrained to a range, not a point. How clouds will respond is the largest piece of that range. How fast ice sheets will add to sea level is the largest practical uncertainty for coasts.

Impacts scale with the warming. More intense heat waves, heavier rainfall in wet storms, deeper drought in some dry regions, and higher seas are consequences already under way, not only forecasts. Ecosystems shift. Crop regions shift. The size of the harm depends on emissions still to come and on adaptation already possible.

Climate science is not a mood. It is a branch of physics and Earth history with a policy consequence. The consequence is that the carbon added to the air stays for centuries, and that the cheaper time to avoid an emission is before it is made. Disagreement about policy does not reopen the energy balance of the atmosphere.

The energy balance can be stated simply. The Earth receives energy from the Sun, mostly in visible light. It emits energy to space as infrared radiation. If the energy in exceeds the energy out, the planet warms until the two balance again. Greenhouse gases intercept part of the outgoing infrared and return some of it downward. More greenhouse gas means a higher surface temperature at the new balance. This is physics measured in the laboratory and observed in the atmosphere. It is not a model. Models are what you build when you want to know how much, how fast, and where.

Carbon dioxide is the dominant control over long periods because it stays in the air for centuries and because the oceans and rocks exchange it slowly. Methane is more potent per molecule and shorter-lived. Nitrous oxide and some industrial gases add smaller amounts. Water vapor is a strong greenhouse gas and a feedback rather than a driver: warmer air holds more of it, amplifying a warming started by the others. Aerosols from pollution cool the planet slightly by reflecting sunlight, and they are a reason the observed warming is not even larger. As aerosols are reduced for the sake of lungs, some masked warming can appear.

The rise in carbon dioxide from about 280 to about 420 parts per million is measured directly, in the modern record, and in ice cores for the preindustrial baseline. The isotopic composition of the added carbon matches fossil carbon, not volcanic carbon. Volcanoes emit carbon dioxide. Human activity currently emits on the order of a hundred times more. The source is not in serious doubt among the people who measure it.

The observed warming of about 1.2 degrees Celsius, with recent years higher, is measured by thermometers, by ocean buoys, and by satellites, after the known corrections for instrument changes and for urban effects. The corrections are a source of public confusion and a normal part of measurement. Independent analyses converge. The ocean’s heat content, which is the largest reservoir, has risen steadily. Ice has lost mass. Sea level has risen through thermal expansion and through the addition of meltwater. These are the fingerprints. They match the greenhouse account. They do not match a change in the Sun, which has not supplied the extra energy, or a rearrangement of heat without a net gain.

Models are tested by their ability to reproduce the past when given the past’s emissions, volcanic eruptions, and solar changes, and by their ability to fail when the human emissions are omitted. They pass the first and fail the second in the expected way. Their projections for the future depend on emissions. Continued high emissions lead to warming well above two degrees by late century. Rapid cuts lead to less. The range within any one emissions path comes mainly from clouds, from aerosols, and from the carbon cycle’s feedbacks. The range is a reason for humility about the exact number. It is not a reason for expecting no further warming.

Impacts are already measured. Heat waves are hotter and more frequent. Heavy rainfall is heavier in many regions, because warmer air holds more water. Drought risk rises in regions where evaporation increases more than rainfall. Sea level rise is accelerating slowly. Ecosystems are shifting toward the poles and uphill. None of this requires a model to notice. Attribution studies, which ask whether a particular event was made more likely by the warming, now regularly find that it was. The science of impacts is no longer only a forecast. It is a mixture of forecast and record.

The policy implication is separate from the physics and follows from it. Because carbon dioxide accumulates, the total emitted over time matters more than the rate in any one year. Because the ocean and the ice are slow, warming and sea level continue after emissions fall. Early reduction costs less total damage than late reduction, on the standard economic comparisons. Disagreement about the pace, the tools, and the fairness of reduction is a political disagreement. It does not reopen the energy balance.

Tipping points are the part of the subject that most exceeds a smooth projection. A tipping point is a threshold beyond which a system moves to a new state and does not easily return. Ice sheets, the Atlantic circulation, the Amazon forest, and permafrost carbon are the systems discussed. Some thresholds are better constrained than others. None is a reason to ignore the smooth projection, which already contains serious impacts. They are a reason to treat the smooth projection as a lower description of risk rather than as a complete one. The existence of thresholds is a property of the systems. Their exact locations are uncertain. Both facts belong in the account.

Carbon budgets translate the physics into a quantity a policy can use. For a given chance of staying below a temperature threshold, there is a remaining amount of carbon dioxide that can be emitted. The budgets are uncertain and usable. They say that continuing at the present rate exhausts a 1.5-degree budget quickly and a 2-degree budget over a longer, still limited, period. The exact year is less important than the direction. A budget is the kind of object this book has favored: a measurement converted into a constraint. Disagreement about how to meet the constraint is expected. Disagreement about whether the constraint exists is a disagreement with the measurement.

Adaptation and mitigation are both required by the lags. Mitigation reduces future warming. Adaptation reduces harm from warming already in train and from warming still to come. Cities, agriculture, and coasts can be adapted, at a cost, up to a point. The point depends on how much warming is allowed. Adaptation without mitigation eventually meets changes that are hard to adapt to. Mitigation without adaptation leaves people exposed to changes already locked in. The two are complements. Treating them as rivals is a rhetorical choice, not a scientific one. The science supplies the lags that make both necessary.

title: Biodiversity
paras: Life has been pruned before. The fossil record holds several mass extinctions, the most famous of which ended the non-bird dinosaurs sixty-six million years ago. The present loss is different in cause and in speed. It is driven by a single species changing habitats, climates, and the movement of other species.

The numbers should be handled carefully. Documented extinctions of birds, mammals, and amphibians are far above the background rate inferred from fossils. Many more species are in decline without yet being gone. Insect declines are severe in some monitored places and poorly known in most. The honest statement is not that a single percentage captures the crisis. It is that populations are shrinking across many groups, that habitat loss is the largest current driver, and that climate and exploitation add to it.

Biodiversity is not only a list of species. It is variation within species, and the workings of communities. A forest is not a set of trees. It is pollination, predation, decay, and soil. Remove a function and the list of remaining names misleads. Fisheries collapse when the large fish are gone even if the water still holds life. Soils fail when the community under them is simplified.

Conservation has successes, and they are specific. Species have returned where hunting was limited and habitat restored. The ozone layer, a different problem, is healing because the chemicals that destroyed it were restricted, a reminder that global agreements can work when the substitute exists. Protected areas help and are not enough if the surroundings are emptied. The deeper difficulty is that human land use and wild habitat are drawing on the same surface.

A guide's job is not to preach. It is to state the mechanism. Extinction is permanent on human timescales. Evolution will fill gaps, over millions of years, with different creatures. The interval between is the interval in which we live. The species and the functions lost in that interval are a choice, in the limited sense that the drivers are human, even when no one intended the loss.

The background rate of extinction, inferred from the fossil record, is low. The documented rate for well-studied groups over the last few centuries is much higher. Amphibians, with their permeable skins and their dependence on both land and water, have suffered especially. Large mammals and birds have suffered where they were hunted or where their habitat was converted. Many invertebrates are declining in monitored places and unmonitored in most places. The phrase “sixth mass extinction” is a warning about trajectory, not a claim that the losses already equal the great fossil die-offs. The trajectory, if continued, points that way. It has not arrived.

Habitat loss is the largest present driver on land. Forests are cleared for crops and pasture. Wetlands are drained. Grasslands are plowed. Fragmentation leaves patches too small for species that need room. In the sea, fishing pressure and habitat damage from trawling and from coastal development play the corresponding role. Climate change adds a driver that habitat protection alone cannot cancel: a species may lose the climate it requires even inside a park. Exploitation, pollution, and invasive species add further pressure, dominant in some places and secondary in others.

The value of biodiversity is argued in several currencies. One is instrumental: pollination, fisheries, soil, and the chemical library of possible medicines. One is insurance: variety makes a system more likely to contain a member that can handle a new stress. One is scientific: each lineage is a history, and extinction deletes the history. One is ethical, and sits outside science. A guide can note that the first three are empirical claims with evidence behind them, and that the fourth is a judgment societies make. The empirical claims do not require the ethical one to be real. The ethical one does not require the empirical ones to be felt.

Successes show that decline is not a law. Species have recovered where hunting stopped and habitat returned. The bald eagle, the wolf in parts of its range, and various whales are examples, each with caveats. The ozone agreement shows that a global pollutant can be restricted when the science is clear and the substitutes exist. Protected areas work better when they are large, connected, and actually protected. Restoration works better when the driver has been reduced. These are design lessons, not consolations. They say that the outcome is sensitive to what people do.

The deeper tension is land. Food for eight billion people requires land or a large increase in yield per area, or both. Yield increases have spared land relative to what would otherwise have been needed. Further sparing, through yield, diet, and waste reduction, is the arithmetic of having both agriculture and wild habitat. The arithmetic can be done. It is not automatic. Biodiversity science is, at bottom, the measurement of what is being lost and of what the losses do, so that the arithmetic is not done in ignorance.

Extinction debt is a concept the numbers require. A habitat reduced below the size a species needs may still hold the species for a time. The loss appears later, when the remaining population fails to replace itself. Counts of species present today can therefore understate the effect of habitat loss already done. The debt is not a reason for despair about every damaged place. It is a reason to restore and to connect habitats sooner rather than later, while the species are still there to be saved. Lag cuts both ways. Damage can be slow to appear. Recovery can be real if the conditions are returned.

Invasive species are a driver that globalization amplified. Organisms moved by trade and travel encounter communities that have not adapted to them. Some fail. Some become problems. Islands have suffered most, because their species evolved without the new arrivals. Prevention is cheaper than removal. Removal works in some cases, especially on islands, and fails in others. The subject is a branch of ecology with a customs office. Treating it as either hopeless or trivial misreads the record, which contains both expensive failures and clear successes.

Genetic diversity within species is the part of biodiversity least visible and most useful. A species with little genetic variety is brittle. A species with a range of variants is more likely to contain one that tolerates a new disease or a new climate.
