Conservation that saves a species as a few individuals, without regard to variety, saves less than it appears to. Seed banks, captive breeding that manages relatedness, and protection of populations across a species’ range are the responses. The responses are technical. They follow from the same population genetics that explains evolution. Conservation is applied evolution, practiced in reverse, against a loss.

title: Oceans and Ecosystems
paras: Most of the living surface of the planet is ocean. Most of that ocean is poorly visited.

The sea is not a uniform bath. It is structured by light, temperature, and nutrients. Photosynthesis happens in the sunlit top. Below a few hundred meters, food falls or swims. The deep ocean is cold, dark, and inhabited. Hydrothermal vents support communities that run on chemical energy rather than sunlight, a reminder that life's energy source is broader than the textbook diagram.

Currents move heat. The overturning circulation carries warm water north in the Atlantic and returns cold deep water south. A slowdown would shift climates around the basin. Whether a slowdown is under way, and how far it might go, is an active measurement problem, not a settled catastrophe. The measurement is worth doing because the circulation is a hinge.

Two chemical changes are settled. The ocean is warming, and it is acidifying. Carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater forms carbonic acid. The pH of surface waters has dropped, a small number with a large effect on organisms that build shells of calcium carbonate. Corals bleach when heat drives out their symbiotic algae. Reefs can recover from mild events and fail under repeated ones. Fisheries depend on temperatures and on management. The same species can be stable under one regime and collapsing under another.

Ecosystems on land obey the same kind of rule. They are networks, not scenery. A change in one population propagates. Reintroducing a predator can change a river, as wolves in Yellowstone illustrated, though the story is more tangled than the first telling. Removing a forest changes rainfall downwind. The lesson of ecology is connection with limits. Not everything is connected to everything else with equal strength. The connections that matter can be found.

The ocean's practical importance is easy to understate because it is opaque. It is the largest carbon sink after the geological ones, a source of food for billions of people, and the driver of coastal weather. Studying it used to mean ships and nets. It now also means satellites, autonomous floats, and genetic surveys of seawater. The planet's dominant habitat is finally being measured at something like the scale it occupies.

The ocean’s layers are set by density. Warm water sits on cold water. Fresh water sits on salt water. The boundaries between layers limit the upward mixing of nutrients and the downward mixing of oxygen. Most of the ocean’s productivity happens where nutrients reach the sunlit surface: in upwelling zones, in high latitudes in season, and near coasts. The open tropical ocean is often a desert by comparison, blue because it is empty. Productivity is not uniform, and fisheries follow the productive places.

The biological pump is the ocean’s way of moving carbon. Phytoplankton take up carbon dioxide. Some of the resulting organic matter sinks. A fraction reaches the deep sea and stays there for centuries. The pump is a part of the carbon cycle and a part of the climate system. Its strength depends on the plankton community, on nutrients, and on temperature. How it will change as the ocean warms and stratifies is a research question with a large lever attached.

Acidification is the chemical twin of warming. Dissolved carbon dioxide lowers pH and reduces the availability of the carbonate ions that many organisms use to build shells and skeletons. Corals, mollusks, and some plankton are the groups of concern. The effect is measurable in the water and in experiments. It is not uniform, because temperature, nutrients, and the organism’s biology modify it. Reefs under combined heat and acidity are the clearest warning. A reef can recover from a mild bleaching. Repeated severe bleaching, with slower calcification, is a different prospect.

Fisheries are an ecological and an economic system. A stock can be harvested sustainably if the take stays below the stock’s production. Many stocks are managed near that line. Some are past it. The data for good management exist in some fisheries and not in others. Illegal and unreported fishing is a measurement problem as much as a policing problem. Aquaculture supplies a growing share of the fish people eat, with its own issues of feed, waste, and disease. The ocean as a food source is not exhausted. It is unevenly and often poorly governed.

Land ecosystems obey parallel rules. Energy enters through photosynthesis. It moves through food webs. Nutrients cycle. Disturbance, from fire, storm, or herbivory, resets succession. Remove a top predator and the herbivores may increase and the plants decline, or the effect may be weak, depending on the web. The Yellowstone wolf example is real and was oversold as a simple cascade. Real cascades are common. Simple ones are rarer. The lesson is to measure the connections rather than to assume them.

The practical upshot is that the ocean and the land are not backdrops. They are systems with rates. Exceed the rate of renewal and the stock falls. Change the temperature and the chemistry and the rates change. The measurements of those rates, from floats, from satellites, from long-term plots, are the evidence base for every later argument about what can be taken and what has to be left.

Oxygen is the quiet variable. Warming reduces the solubility of oxygen in seawater and can strengthen the stratification that limits mixing. Low-oxygen zones have expanded in some regions. The expansion affects fisheries and the chemistry of the deep. It is less visible than bleaching or than storms, and it is measured. The ocean’s health is not one indicator. Temperature, acidity, oxygen, nutrients, and exploitation move together and separately. Managing one while ignoring the others produces surprises. The system rewards attention to the set.

Coral reefs are the ecosystem where several stresses meet in public. Heat causes bleaching. Acidity slows the building of skeletons. Fishing and pollution reduce resilience. A reef under one stress may recover. A reef under several may not. The decline of many reefs is documented. The survival of some, in places where local stresses are low or where the corals are naturally more tolerant, is also documented. The difference is a map of what still responds to local protection and what will require the global temperature to stabilize. Both kinds of place exist. Policy that treats them as one place will mistreat one of them.

Long-term ecological research sites are the reason some trends are known rather than guessed. Plots and transects observed for decades show changes that a single survey cannot. The value of the record grows with its length. Interruptions for budget reasons create gaps that cannot be filled later. The infrastructure of observation is part of the science. It is less photogenic than a discovery. It is what makes the discovery of a trend possible. A society that wants to know whether its ecosystems are changing has to keep the measurements going. The knowledge is not a stock. It is a practice.

title: Renewable Energy
paras: Energy is the constraint under every other civilization. The modern world was built on stored sunlight, coal and oil and gas, burned faster than it was buried. The next energy system, if it is to last, has to live on flows.

The flows are large. Sunlight arriving on Earth exceeds human energy use by many thousands of times. Wind is sunlight converted into motion. The engineering problem is not a shortage of energy. It is collection, conversion, storage, and the materials to do those things.

Solar and wind have crossed a threshold. Their costs fell for decades, and in many places they are the cheapest new electricity. The limit is no longer the panel. It is the hour when the panel is dark, and the distance between a windy plain and a city. Batteries have fallen in cost as well, enough to shift a few hours of demand. They are not yet a general solution for seasons. A winter of low wind is not a battery problem of the ordinary kind.

Other pieces exist at different stages of maturity. Hydroelectric dams are old and effective, and most of the best sites are taken. Nuclear fission provides steady power with a small land footprint and a waste problem that is political as much as technical. Existing plants are among the largest low-carbon sources already running. New designs promise smaller size and passive safety. They have to arrive on time and on budget, which the recent record makes a fair demand. Geothermal power is local and promising where the crust cooperates. Hydrogen is a way to store energy, not a source. It is only as clean as the energy used to make it.

Materials set the other constraint. Turbines need magnets and steel. Batteries need lithium, nickel, graphite, and other elements, in amounts that can be mined but not casually. Recycling will matter more as the stock grows. A renewable system is a mining and manufacturing system with a different profile, not a system without industry.

The transition is therefore an engineering project with a deadline set by the climate chapter. The tools are further along than a reader of 1980 would have been told to expect. They are not, by themselves, a completed replacement. The remaining work is grid, storage, industry, and the willingness to build.

Solar and wind became cheap for ordinary industrial reasons. Manufacturing scale, learning by doing, and competition drove the cost of panels and turbines down by large factors over two decades. In many regions they are now the cheapest source of new electricity. That fact is the foundation of the present transition. It does not, by itself, solve nights, winters, or industrial heat.

Variability is the engineering problem. A grid must balance supply and demand continuously. Wind and sun do not follow demand. Over short periods, batteries, flexible demand, and existing hydro and gas plants can balance them. Over long periods, especially in climates with dark winters, the balancing is harder. Options include long-distance transmission, overbuilding and curtailment, hydrogen or other fuels made from surplus electricity, geothermal where it exists, nuclear, and storage beyond batteries. Each option has a cost and a maturity. A serious plan uses several. A plan that relies on one is fragile.

Nuclear fission is the existing low-carbon source that does not depend on weather. Existing plants are valuable for that reason. New plants have been slow and expensive in some countries and faster in others. The difference is largely institutional. Waste is a real issue and a bounded one: the volume is small, the technology for storage exists, and the political path for permanent repositories has been the obstacle. Accident risk is real and, in the record of modern designs, small compared with the air-pollution deaths of fossil generation. These comparisons do not settle policy. They are the factual background of the settlement.

Materials are the hidden schedule. Electrifying transport and expanding wind and solar increases demand for copper, lithium, nickel, rare earths, and steel. The quantities are large and mineable. Opening mines is slow. Recycling will matter more as the stock of batteries and turbines grows. Dependence on a few countries for processing is a strategic fact as well as a geological one. A renewable system is a materials system. Treating it as weightless is a mistake.

Efficiency is the other half. The cheapest energy is the energy not used. Buildings, industry, and vehicles have large remaining efficiency gains, some of them economical already. Electrification helps because electric motors and heat pumps are more efficient than combustion for the same service. Demand will still grow in many places as people gain access to energy they do not now have. The transition is a race between the growth of clean supply and the growth of total demand. Both numbers are measurable. The race is not metaphorical.

The state of the art is that the tools for a largely decarbonized electricity system exist, that the tools for industry, aviation, and shipping are less mature, and that the pace is set by building, by grids, and by policy rather than by a missing invention. Invention would help. It is not the only thing required.

Storage deserves a clearer accounting. Lithium-ion batteries have fallen in cost and dominate short-duration storage. They are a poor fit for storing energy across seasons. Pumped hydro is excellent where the geography exists. Hydrogen, made by electrolysis and stored, can serve long duration and can supply industry, at a cost in efficiency. Thermal storage and other chemistries are in development. The portfolio is the point. A grid with wind, solar, batteries, transmission, and a firm source, whether nuclear, hydro, or gas with capture, is a different engineering object from a grid of any one of these. The object can be built. Its cost and its reliability depend on the mix and on the place.

Transmission is as important as generation. A windy or sunny region far from cities is useful only if the electricity can be moved. Building transmission is slow, because of permits, land, and local opposition. The technology is ordinary. The implementation is the constraint. A transition plan that counts generation and omits wires will underperform. The wires are part of the machine. So are the markets and the operators that balance them. The engineering is socio-technical. Describing only the turbine describes a component.

Industry is the harder decarbonization. Cement, steel, chemicals, and aviation require high temperatures or dense fuels. Electricity and efficiency can do part of the work. Hydrogen, made cleanly, can do part. Carbon capture can do part, where the stream is concentrated. The mix differs by industry. None of these sectors is as far along as electricity generation. Their lag is a reason the electricity transition is not the whole transition. It is also a reason to start with the sectors that are ready while the others are prepared. Sequence is a strategy. Waiting for every sector to be ready is not.

title: Sustainability
paras: Sustainability is a word asked to do too much. In this book it means a practical question. Can a civilization of billions maintain food, water, energy, and a living biosphere without spending down the conditions that make those things possible?

Some accounts are encouraging. Farm yields rose faster than population in the late twentieth century. Air and water in many rich countries are cleaner than in 1970. The area of land needed to feed a person has fallen. These are not illusions. They are the result of fertilizer, breeding, sewage treatment, and rules.

Other accounts are warnings. Groundwater is being pumped faster than it recharges in major farming regions. Topsoil is lost where farming leaves it bare. Fisheries are harvested near or past their limits. Nitrogen and phosphorus, freed by fertilizer, create dead zones where rivers meet the sea. The carbon account is the largest open bill.

A sustainable system is not a return to a smaller past. Eight billion people cannot live on medieval yields. It is a set of loops. Nutrients returned to fields. Materials recycled where recycling saves more than it costs. Energy from flows rather than from a single inheritance of fossil carbon. Cities dense enough that land remains for other uses. None of these loops is mysterious. All of them are incomplete.

Technology helps and does not absolve. A more efficient engine can lower fuel use, or it can be used to travel more. Both outcomes occur. The name for the second is the rebound effect, and it is a reason to count total use, not only use per device. Counting is the unglamorous core of the subject. A society that does not measure its aquifers will empty them by surprise.

The scientific content of sustainability is therefore ecology plus thermodynamics plus demography. Energy is conserved and degraded. Populations consume. Ecosystems have rates of renewal. Exceed the rate, and the stock falls. The politics of who sacrifices what sits on top of that arithmetic. The arithmetic remains if the politics fails.

Carrying capacity is a useful phrase and a bad number. There is no single headcount the Earth can support, because the count depends on technology, diet, and distribution. A population living on grain and vegetables uses less land than the same population living on grain-fed meat. A population with high yields uses less land than a population with low yields. The useful question is not a magic number. It is whether the particular system in use is within the renewal rates of the resources it draws on.

Several systems are not. Groundwater in major agricultural regions is being depleted. The depletion is measured by wells and by satellites that weigh the water. Topsoil is lost where tillage and bare seasons leave it exposed. Fisheries in many places are harvested at or beyond their production. Nitrogen fixed by industry for fertilizer exceeds natural fixation and ends in rivers and coastal dead zones. These are stock-and-flow problems. They have the same structure as a bank account drawn down faster than the deposits.

Other trends have improved. Air pollution in many rich countries is lower than fifty years ago. Deforestation has slowed in some regions and reversed in a few. The land used per person for food has fallen. Poverty, measured by consumption, has fallen in large parts of the world over the same decades that population rose. The improvements came from technology, from rules, and from wealth. They are evidence that trajectories can bend. They are not evidence that every trajectory bends by itself.

Rebound deserves a clear statement. When a service becomes cheaper in energy or in materials, people often use more of it. Lighting became so efficient that total lighting grew. Efficient cars can be driven more. The rebound does not always cancel the gain. It often reduces it. Counting the total, not the efficiency alone, is the correction. A sustainability metric that ignores rebound will overstate progress.

Justice is not a scientific variable and affects every practical plan. The people who have emitted the least are often the most exposed to climate harm and the least able to pay for adaptation. A transition that ignores that fact may be physically possible and politically impossible. A guide can note the constraint without pretending to settle the distribution. The physical constraints remain either way: the carbon budget, the aquifers, the fish stocks, the soil. Negotiation does not enlarge them. It allocates them.

The scientific core of sustainability is therefore unromantic. Measure the stocks. Measure the flows. Do not draw the stocks down faster than the flows refill them, if you want the stocks later. Technology can improve the flows and reduce the draw. It has done so repeatedly. It has not repealed the accounting.

Circular economy is a useful aim and a sloppy slogan. Some materials, like aluminum, are recycled profitably and well. Others, like many plastics and mixed electronics, are recycled poorly or not at all, because the physics and the economics do not favor it. Designing products for disassembly, keeping materials in known streams, and accepting that some uses are dissipative and should be minimized, is the practical content. A circle drawn on a slide is not a materials policy. A measured recovery rate is. Sustainability, again, is accounting. The accounting can include ambition. It cannot include a circle that violates the second law or the market as it actually is, without saying so.

Population is part of the accounting and not the whole of it. Impact is population times affluence times technology, in the old identity. All three terms move. Population growth is slowing. Affluence is rising in many places, which raises impact and also pays for cleaner technology. Technology can raise or lower impact per person. The identity does not pick a villain. It says that a plan which addresses only one term will be surprised by the others. Sustainability arithmetic is multiplication. Changing one factor helps. Ignoring a growing factor undoes the help.

Measurement is the unglamorous prerequisite. Aquifers, fish stocks, soil carbon, and material flows can be managed only if they are measured. In many places they are not, or are measured too coarsely to guide a decision. Investing in the measurement is less satisfying than announcing a goal. It is what makes a goal checkable. Sustainability goals that cannot be checked against a stock and a flow are aspirations. Aspirations have a use. They are not a substitute for the account. This book has preferred the account. The preference applies here with particular force.

title: Artificial Intelligence
paras: Machines that perform tasks once called intelligent are no longer a speculation. They are a deployed technology, and an unfinished science.

The modern wave rests on a simple idea with an expensive realization. A network of simple units, trained on examples, can learn a function too complicated to write by hand. Given enough data and enough computation, such networks recognize speech, classify images, fold proteins, and generate language. The protein result deserves a sentence of its own. Systems trained to predict the shape of a folded protein, notably AlphaFold, solved a fifty-year problem well enough to change daily work in biology.

Language models are the public face. They are trained to predict the next piece of text. From that training they acquire, as a side effect, a useful facility with questions, summaries, code, and translation. The facility is not understanding in the human sense, and the disclaimer is not an insult. A model can produce a fluent falsehood, because fluency is what the training rewarded. It can also produce a correct proof or a working program. Users have to supply the judgment the training did not guarantee.

The limits are as important as the feats. Models fail at tasks that require a stable model of the world over long chains of action. They absorb the biases of their data. They consume large amounts of energy and data to train. They do not, on present evidence, set their own goals. A system that acts, rather than only replies, raises a different problem: keeping the action inside the bounds a person intended. That problem is engineering and governance, and it is already practical wherever automated systems trade, drive, or diagnose.

Artificial intelligence is not a single threshold waiting in the future. It is a set of capabilities that have been arriving, one task at a time, for seventy years, and quickly in the last fifteen. The scientific question still open is whether prediction at scale, plus tools, is enough for the flexible competence humans recognize in each other, or whether something structural is missing. The social question is how to use a tool that writes, sees, and recommends, without confusing its output for a source of record.

The revival of neural networks after a long winter is a story of data, hardware, and a few algorithmic ideas. Networks of simple units had been studied for decades. They became dominant when large labeled datasets, fast parallel hardware, and training methods that worked at scale arrived together. Image recognition crossed human-level accuracy on certain benchmarks. Speech recognition became good enough for daily use. Protein structure prediction, in the form of AlphaFold and its successors, solved a problem that had resisted fifty years of other methods. The pattern is that a task with a lot of examples and a clear measure of success can often be learned.

Language models extended the pattern to text. Trained to predict the next token, they acquire abilities that look like knowledge: answering questions, writing code, translating, summarizing. The abilities are real and uneven. A model can produce a correct explanation of a standard topic and a fluent error on a less standard one. It does not have a reliable internal marker for which is which. Users supply the marker, or they do not. Systems that retrieve from a trusted source, or that use tools to check a calculation, reduce the problem. They do not abolish it.

The limits are structural as well as temporary. Models trained on text have no direct contact with the physical tests that correct human belief. They can describe an experiment. They cannot run one unless connected to instruments. Long chains of reasoning accumulate errors. Novelty that lies outside the training distribution is handled less well than interpolation inside it. These limits may move. They are the reason current systems are powerful assistants and unreliable authorities.

Learning from human feedback and from other models has been used to make the outputs more helpful and less harmful by ordinary standards. The methods work imperfectly. They can be evaded. They encode the judgments of the people who supplied the feedback. A system aligned with one set of judgments is not aligned with every set. Alignment, in the practical sense, is the problem of keeping a capable system inside the bounds its operators intend. It becomes more important as systems gain tools and act, rather than only reply.

The effect on work is already measurable in some tasks and speculative in others. Programming, drafting, translation, and customer support have seen real productivity changes. Physical trades, care work, and any job whose bottleneck is a body or a relationship have seen less. Forecasts of wholesale replacement have been early before. Forecasts of no effect are already false. The accurate statement is that a class of cognitive tasks has become cheaper, and that the rearrangement of jobs around that fact is underway and unfinished.

The scientific question and the social question should not be fused. The scientific question is what these systems can and cannot do, and what architectures and training methods change the boundary. The social question is how to use, regulate, and distribute a technology that writes and recommends at scale. Both are open. Neither is settled by calling the technology intelligent or by refusing to.

Evaluation is the unglamorous core. A model’s performance on a benchmark is a fact about that benchmark. It is not a general intelligence quotient. Benchmarks saturate. Models overfit to them. New benchmarks are written and saturate in turn. The meaningful tests are the ones that resemble the use: a coding task with a real codebase, a medical question checked against a source, a plan executed by a robot. Narrow tests produce narrow claims. The field has sometimes advertised the narrow test as the general claim. Readers should demand the use case. The use case is where the limits appear.

Open and closed models are a practical division. Some systems are released with weights that others can run and modify. Some are available only through an interface. The division affects research, safety, and concentration of capability. Open release spreads benefit and spreads the chance of misuse. Closed release concentrates both. Neither is a complete answer. The existence of the division is a fact about the present industry. Regulation that ignores it will misfire. A reader does not need to settle the argument to notice that the argument is about deployment, not only about capability.

Energy and data are the material constraints. Training large models consumes electricity and requires large collections of text, images, or other inputs. The electricity can be supplied more or less cleanly. The data raise questions of consent, of copyright, and of representation. Neither constraint is a reason the technology will stop. Both are reasons its growth has costs that should be counted. A description of capability that omits the electricity and the data describes a software abstraction. The system is a physical and a social object. The object has a footprint. The footprint belongs in the chapter.

title: Robotics
paras: A robot is a machine that senses and acts in the physical world. The definition is plain. The execution is where intelligence meets friction, lighting, and a floor that is not the floor in the diagram.

Industrial robots have been mature for decades. In a painted cage, with parts presented at known positions, an arm repeats a weld more accurately than a person and does not tire. The cage is the clue. The hard problem is the unstructured world: a home, a street, a warehouse where the box has moved.

Progress has come from better sensing and from learning. Cameras and depth sensors became cheap. Reinforcement learning and imitation learning let a robot practice a grasp rather than follow a script for every object. Warehouses use mobile robots in large numbers. Surgical robots extend a surgeon's hands. Autonomous cars have driven paying passengers in limited cities and have also failed in ways that justify the limits. Legs have improved. Humanoid robots can walk, recover from a shove, and manipulate objects in demonstrations. Demonstrations are not deployments. Hands are still worse than yours.

The gap is instructive. Reasoning about a photograph leapt forward. Reasoning about a cabinet door, a cable, and a slightly wrong belief about where the door is, remains expensive and brittle. The physical world does not offer a clean next-token prediction. It offers contact.

Robotics matters because most of the economy is physical. Care, construction, harvesting, and disaster response happen in places software cannot go alone. The likely path is not a sudden replacement of every manual job by a general humanoid. It is a succession of narrow machines that become less narrow. The succession is under way. It should be described at the speed of the machines that actually run, not at the speed of the videos.

Industrial robotics is the existence proof that machines can do physical work reliably. In automotive plants and electronics factories, arms weld, paint, and place parts with repeatability a person cannot match. The conditions are the secret. The workspace is controlled. The parts are fixtured. The exceptions are rare. Move the same arm into a kitchen, and the exceptions become the job.

The unstructured world is hard for reasons that are easy to underestimate. Objects vary. Lighting varies. A grasp that works on a rigid box fails on a soft bag. A door that is slightly ajar is a different problem from a door that is latched. Small errors in position compound. A robot that is ninety-nine percent reliable at each step of a ten-step task fails often. Human environments were built for human hands and human tolerance of variation. They are not neutral test tracks.

Progress has come from learning and from better sensors. Cameras became cheap and good. Depth sensors became ordinary. Simulation let robots practice millions of grasps. Imitation learning let them copy human demonstrations. Warehouses now use mobile robots to move shelves, and increasingly to pick items. The picking is narrower than a person’s, and it is deployed. Surgical robots translate a surgeon’s movements to smaller, steadier ones. They do not operate alone. Autonomous vehicles have operated in limited domains and have struggled at the edge cases that driving contains in abundance. Legs have improved enough for impressive recovery from disturbance. Hands remain behind.

Humanoid form is a choice, not a requirement. A humanoid can use spaces and tools designed for people, which is an advantage if the goal is to enter those spaces without rebuilding them. A specialized machine is usually better at a single task. Most successful robots have been specialized. Whether general humanoids become economical depends on whether their generality is worth their complexity. The answer is not yet in. Demonstrations are not the answer. Cost per reliable task is the answer.

The near future is more likely to be a proliferation of narrow robots than a sudden population of general ones. Inspection drones, warehouse movers, agricultural machines, delivery vehicles in constrained areas, and laboratory automation are the present growth. Each extends the domain of reliable physical automation a step. The steps are the story. A guide that describes only the video of a humanoid folding a shirt, and not the machines already running a shift, has the proportions backward.

Safety in robotics is physical. A software error in a chatbot produces a bad paragraph. A software error in a moving machine can produce an injury. The standards for industrial robots, for surgical robots, and for autonomous vehicles are accordingly stricter, and the deployment is accordingly slower. The slowness is not only technical caution. It is the correct matching of speed to consequence. A guide that celebrates laboratory agility and omits the safety case has described a demonstration, not a technology that shares a room with people.

Warehouses are the clearest present success outside the classic factory. Mobile robots move goods. Picking robots, narrower than people, handle a growing fraction of items. The environment was built to suit the machines, with barcoded bins and flat floors. Suiting the environment is a legitimate strategy. It is how factories have always worked. The home, which cannot be rebuilt for the robot, remains harder. Success in structured spaces and difficulty in unstructured ones is the pattern. The pattern tells you where the next deployments will be.

Maintenance is the hidden labor. Robots in real environments need supervision, repair, and the handling of exceptions the design did not cover. The labor is less than the labor replaced, in the successful deployments, and it is not zero. Automation changes work as much as it removes it. The change can be toward higher-skill supervision or toward more fragmented tasks. The outcome depends on how the work is organized, not only on the machine. A forecast that counts only the machine will miscount the jobs. The jobs are the machine plus the people who keep it running and who handle what it cannot.

title: Quantum Computing
paras: A classical computer stores bits, each a zero or a one. A quantum computer stores qubits, which can be placed in combinations of zero and one, and entangled with one another. The point is not that a qubit holds both values in a way you can read out. A measurement still yields a zero or a one. The point is that the computation can explore amplitudes, and amplitudes can cancel.

For most tasks, this buys nothing. Adding a column of numbers does not need amplitudes. For some tasks, the cancellation is the algorithm. Peter Shor showed in 1994 that a large enough quantum computer could factor large numbers efficiently, which would break widely used forms of encryption. Lov Grover showed a faster way to search unstructured lists. Chemistry and materials problems, which are quantum systems being simulated badly on classical machines, are the application most scientists actually want.

The machines exist, and they are early. Qubits are made from superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photons, and other physical systems. They decohere. Noise spoils the amplitudes. Error correction, the encoding of one logical qubit in many physical ones, is required for the famous algorithms and has only begun to be demonstrated at interesting scales. A device with a few hundred noisy qubits can do impressive physics. It cannot break the internet. Claims that it can are a sign to read the paper.

Cryptography has already responded. Standards for encryption believed to resist quantum attack are being adopted, because data stolen now could be stored until a future machine exists. That is the correct order. Prepare for the capability before the capability arrives.

Quantum computing is often sold as a faster computer. It is better sold as a different computer, useful where interference is an advantage, irrelevant where it is not. If the engineering succeeds, the first deep consequences will likely be in the simulation of molecules and materials, the subject of an earlier chapter, rather than in a general replacement of the laptop.

The advantage of a quantum computer is interference. Amplitudes for wrong answers cancel. Amplitudes for right answers add. For this to help, the problem must have a structure that an algorithm can exploit. Factoring has such a structure, which is why Shor’s algorithm matters to cryptography. Searching an unstructured list has less, which is why Grover’s algorithm offers only a square-root speedup. Simulating a quantum system has the structure by definition, which is why chemistry and materials are the applications scientists emphasize.

Building the machine is a fight with noise. A qubit is a physical system, and physical systems interact with their surroundings. The interaction leaks information and destroys the amplitudes. Error correction encodes one logical qubit in many physical qubits so that errors can be detected and fixed faster than they occur. The overhead is large. A useful error-corrected machine requires many physical qubits per logical qubit, with error rates below a threshold. Recent experiments have demonstrated error correction that improves as the code grows, which is the necessary direction. They have not yet produced a machine that runs Shor’s algorithm on cryptographically relevant numbers.

Cryptography has not waited. Public-key systems based on factoring or on related problems are vulnerable in principle to a large quantum computer. New systems, based on problems believed to resist quantum attack, have been standardized and are being adopted. The migration is slow because it touches everything that authenticates and encrypts. It is underway because data recorded today can be stored and decrypted later. The correct engineering response precedes the machine.

The phrase “quantum supremacy” or “quantum advantage” has been used for demonstrations in which a quantum device performed a particular task faster than a classical computer. The tasks were chosen to suit the device. They were real comparisons and not, by themselves, useful computations. The useful threshold is a calculation that someone wanted for an independent reason, done better than by any classical method. That threshold has not been clearly passed for a commercially relevant problem. It is the threshold that matters.

Quantum computing is therefore best understood as a new kind of instrument, powerful where interference helps and irrelevant where it does not. If the engineering succeeds, the first deep scientific returns are likely to be in the simulation of molecules, materials, and perhaps nuclear physics. Those are returns worth having. They are not a general replacement of classical computing. Most of what computers do will remain classical, because most of what computers do does not need amplitudes.

The classical competition should not be underestimated. Algorithms and hardware for classical simulation of quantum systems improve. A claimed quantum advantage has to beat the best classical method, not a naive one. Several early claims were later matched or approached classically. The race is real. It is a reason to be precise about what has been shown. It is also a reason the useful applications, when they come, will be in problems where the quantum structure is essential and the classical simulation is genuinely hard, not in problems where a cleverer classical programmer had not yet looked.

The qubit zoo is a sign of an early technology. Superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons, and spins in solids are all in use. Each has advantages in speed, in connectivity, or in stability. None has won. A mature technology usually settles on one or two platforms. Quantum computing has not settled. The unsettled state is a reason for parallel investment and a reason not to treat any one company’s roadmap as the field’s. Roadmaps are plans. The platforms are the evidence. The evidence is still a competition.

Education and workforce are part of the timeline. A technology that requires specialists in physics, in engineering, and in the algorithms will be limited by how many such people exist. Programs to train them are part of the investment. The timeline for useful machines is set by error rates and by scale, and also by whether the people who can build and use the machines are available. Neither factor should be omitted. Hardware roadmaps that ignore the workforce describe a laboratory success. A field is a laboratory plus a community that can reproduce and extend it.

title: Biotechnology
paras: Biotechnology is the use of living systems, or their parts, as technology. Fermentation is the old version. The new version reads and writes cells.

The reading side produced the genome projects, the microbiome surveys, and the rapid sequencing of pathogens. A virus can now be identified, and its spread tracked by its mutations, on a schedule that public health of the twentieth century would not have recognized. The writing side produced recombinant drugs, engineered crops, monoclonal antibodies, cell therapies, and the mRNA platforms already mentioned. Insulin for diabetics has long been made by engineered microbes rather than taken from animals. The precedent is easy to overlook because it works.

Antibodies deserve a place beside CRISPR in any current guide. A monoclonal antibody is a chosen immune protein, manufactured, aimed at one target. Such antibodies treat inflammatory disease, cancer, and infection. They are expensive to make and precise in action. They are what drug discovery looks like when the target is known.

Cultured meat, engineered organs, and gene drives are at earlier stages. Gene drives, which bias inheritance so a trait spreads through a wild population, could in principle reduce the mosquitoes that carry malaria. They could also be difficult to recall. Trials have been cautious, and should be. Organoids, miniature tissues grown from stem cells, already let researchers study organs that cannot be biopsied at will, including regions of the brain. They are models, not miniature people. The distinction matters and should be kept.

Biotechnology's pace is set by a fortunate fact. Cells already solve problems of manufacture that factories find difficult. Persuading a cell to solve the problem you have, and only that problem, is the craft. The craft has become reliable enough to be an industry. It has not become so reliable that nature can be treated as a subroutine. A released organism still faces evolution, and evolution does not sign the design document.

Recombinant DNA was the first writing. In the 1970s, genes were cut and pasted into bacteria, and the bacteria made the protein. Human insulin followed. The pattern, a cell as a factory for a chosen protein, is now ordinary. Monoclonal antibodies extended it. An antibody is selected or designed, produced in cultured cells, and used as a drug. Dozens of such drugs treat cancer, autoimmune disease, and other conditions. They are expensive to manufacture and precise in target. They are what a large part of modern therapeutics looks like.

Sequencing turned outbreaks into genetic events. A pathogen can be identified and tracked by its sequence. Variants can be watched as they arise. The COVID-19 pandemic was the public demonstration: the virus was sequenced within weeks of recognition, and its subsequent evolution was followed in public databases. The same methods apply to foodborne outbreaks, to antibiotic resistance, and to the background surveillance that makes a new threat visible sooner. Surveillance is infrastructure. It works when it is funded between emergencies.

Gene drives and ecological interventions are the point where biotechnology leaves the lab and the patient and enters a wild population. A gene drive biases inheritance so that a trait spreads even if it confers no advantage. In mosquitoes, a drive that reduces fertility or that blocks a parasite could, in principle, reduce disease. The spread is the feature and the hazard. Once released, a drive can be hard to recall. Trials have been cautious, local, and reversible where possible. The caution is proportionate to the irreversibility.

Organoids and cell therapies sit at the edge of replacement. Organoids are small, self-organized tissues grown from stem cells. They model organs for research and, increasingly, for testing drugs. They are not transplantable organs. Growing full organs for transplant is a further goal, pursued through scaffolding, printing, and developmental biology. Cell therapies that replace or repair a patient’s cells are further along in blood and in some other tissues. The direction is the same. Cells are being asked to do therapeutic work that chemistry alone could not.

Containment is the standing discipline. Laboratory organisms are kept in by physical barriers, by dependence on nutrients they cannot find outside, and by the simple fact that a pampered strain often loses to wild competitors. None of these is absolute. The history of invasive species is a reminder that organisms sometimes thrive where they were not expected. Biotechnology adds designed organisms to the list of things that have to be kept where they are intended. The record so far is manageable. It stays manageable by continuing the discipline as the organisms become more capable.

The summary for a guide is that biotechnology has become an industry of reading and writing cells, with products in pharmacies, in fields, and in factories. It has not become a permission to redesign ecosystems casually. The tools are ahead of the wisdom in some areas and behind the need in others. Both statements can be true.

Cost is the filter. A therapy that works and costs more than a health system can pay does not change outcomes at scale. Monoclonal antibodies and cell therapies have faced this filter. Some have been brought within reach by production improvements and by policy. Some remain rare in practice. The science can succeed and the delivery can fail. A chapter on biotechnology that lists capabilities without prices describes a possible medicine. The actual medicine is the capabilities that survive the price.

Antibiotics are a warning inside the success. They are among the most effective biotechnologies ever deployed. Their effectiveness is eroded by evolution whenever they are used. Stewardship, new drugs, and diagnostics that distinguish viral from bacterial illness are the responses. The warning is general. A biological technology that creates a selective pressure will meet an evolutionary reply. The reply can be slowed. It cannot be forbidden by the original design. Biotechnology that forgets evolution will be surprised by it. The surprise is avoidable.

Dual use is the standing ethical fact. A technique that can make a vaccine can, in principle, be misused on a pathogen. The overlap is not a reason to stop the technique. It is a reason to screen, to train, and to maintain the norm that some experiments are not done without oversight. The norm has held imperfectly. Maintaining it is cheaper than the alternative. Biotechnology’s benefit is large enough to justify the field. The benefit does not erase the overlap. Living with the overlap, deliberately, is the adult version of the subject.

title: Space Exploration
paras: Spaceflight began as a political contest and became a scientific instrument. Both descriptions remain true.

Robots have done most of the exploring. Probes have visited every planet, landed on Mars, Titan, a comet, and an asteroid, and left the heliosphere. Orbiters map climate, gravity, and magnetic fields. Telescopes above the air see in wavelengths the air blocks. The scientific return on unmanned flight is the largest return in the history of exploration, measured in knowledge per voyage.

Human flight is harder to justify on science alone and has other justifications. People are versatile, slow to launch, and expensive to keep alive. The Moon is the near goal of present programs, with permanent or semi-permanent stations proposed and not yet built. Mars is the far goal, possible with chemical rockets, costly in radiation, time, and the consequences of failure. No one has gone. The engineering is a matter of commitment and trial, not of unknown physics.

The commercial change is real. Reusable rockets lowered the price of reaching orbit. Satellite constellations multiplied. Whether lower prices produce a self-sustaining space economy, or only a larger research and communications budget, depends on finding work in space that cannot be done more cheaply on Earth. Tourism and prestige are not that work. Manufacturing in weightlessness and power beamed from orbit remain demonstrations until they are businesses.

The scientific questions that spaceflight can actually touch are sharper than the rhetoric. Did Mars ever have life? What lies under the ice of Europa and Enceladus? How do stars and planets form, in detail the nearest examples can teach? Is there anything on the Moon worth using? These questions have instruments aimed at them. A guide should keep the questions in front of the destination. The universe described in the first part of this book is not reached by going there in person. Most of it is reached by collecting its light. Space exploration, at its best, is a way of collecting better light, and of touching the few worlds within reach.

Unmanned exploration has been the productive core. Orbiters and landers have rewritten the history of Mars, revealing ancient water and a cold desert that may still hide subsurface ice. Probes have sampled asteroids and returned the samples. A lander reached Titan. Voyagers left the heliosphere. Telescopes in space, free of the atmosphere, have seen in infrared, ultraviolet, and X-rays, and have measured the microwave background and the expansion. The scientific yield per dollar has been highest where people did not go.

Human spaceflight has different yields. It is harder, more expensive, and more inspiring to many. It has produced engineering knowledge, a continuous presence in low orbit, and a political demonstration that a state could do a difficult thing. It has not, so far, produced a scientific return comparable to the robotic program, because a person is a costly and fragile instrument. The argument for sending people is only partly scientific. It includes the possibility that people will eventually live off Earth, and the judgment that this is worth doing. The judgment is not a measurement. The costs and the risks are.

The Moon is the near object. It is three days away. It has water ice in shadowed craters, which could supply drinking water, oxygen, and propellant if the ice can be extracted economically. It is a place to practice living off-world before attempting Mars. Programs to return are underway. A sustained presence is a further step, not guaranteed by a few landings. Mars is months away, with radiation, dust, and a thin cold atmosphere. A round trip with chemical rockets is possible and long. The physiological and psychological costs of the duration are part of the engineering. No one has gone. The timeline is a function of money and persistence more than of unknown physics.

Reusable rockets changed the economics of reaching orbit. A stage that flies back and flies again costs less per launch than a stage that is thrown away. The change has increased the number of launches and enabled large satellite constellations. Whether it enables a space economy beyond communications, navigation, and observation depends on finding activities whose value exceeds the remaining cost. Tourism is a niche. Manufacturing in microgravity is a niche. Extraction of materials from the Moon or asteroids is a possibility that has not yet beaten the cost of extraction on Earth. The barrier is economic. It may move. It has not moved enough to make space a place of ordinary industry.

The scientific questions that justify the expense are concrete. Was there life on Mars, and is there any now? What is in the oceans of Europa and Enceladus? How do planetary systems form, in detail the samples and the close observations can answer? What is the inventory of near-Earth asteroids, and which of them are hazards? These questions have missions aimed at them. A guide should keep the questions ahead of the rhetoric. Space is not an escape from the problems of the previous chapter. It is an extension of the reach of measurement, and, perhaps, eventually, of settlement. The extension of measurement is already a success. The settlement is a project.

Debris and regulation are the mundane frontier. Low orbit is increasingly crowded. Collisions produce debris that can cause further collisions. Tracking, avoidance, and rules for deorbiting are now part of operating in space. The romance of exploration sits on top of a traffic problem. The traffic problem is solvable and not solved. It is a reminder that access to a new domain creates ordinary problems of crowding and external cost, and that those problems arrive before the domain is fully used.

Sample return is the method that joins remote sensing to the laboratory. Rocks from the Moon, from asteroids, and, in planned missions, from Mars can be analyzed with instruments that no spacecraft can carry. The analyses date surfaces, measure compositions, and look for traces that orbiters cannot confirm. Sample return is slow and expensive. It is how uncertain remote detections become certain laboratory facts. The certainty is worth the wait for the questions that matter enough.

International cooperation and competition both shape the program. Shared missions reduce cost and build redundancy. Competition accelerates schedules and duplicates effort. The mix has produced the present rate of flight. A reader can prefer one mode. The record contains both. Science missions have often been the cooperative ones. Human flight has often been the competitive one. The division is not a law. It is a history. Future missions to Mars or to the outer moons will test which mode can sustain a long, expensive effort. The test is ahead.

title: A History of Scientific Thought
paras: Science is a method that emerged slowly and then changed everything it touched.

The ancient world had observation, mathematics, and engineering. Babylonians tracked planets. Greeks argued that nature was lawful and, in some schools, that it was made of atoms. Archimedes did physics. The limitation was not intelligence. It was the absence of a settled habit of letting experiment overrule a beautiful system, and of institutions that would reward the overruling.

Medieval scholars in several civilizations preserved and extended the record. Algebra took form. Optics advanced. The recovery of Greek texts in Europe, joined to new instruments, set up the break of the seventeenth century. Galileo pointed a telescope at the sky and found it was not what authority had said. Kepler fitted orbits to data and accepted ellipses because the data demanded them. Newton wrote a law of gravity that worked in the sky and on the ground, the great simplification of an earlier chapter made mathematical.

The method that emerged can be stated without romance. Prefer explanations that make predictions. Compare the predictions to measurement. Keep the explanations that survive, and say how sure you are. Publish the measurement so someone else can try to break it. The last step is the social one. Science is individual curiosity organized so that individual error can be caught.

Later centuries extended the method into chemistry, geology, biology, and the study of societies, with uneven success. Geology discovered deep time. Biology discovered evolution. The twentieth century discovered the expansion of the universe, the structure of the atom, and the structure of the gene. It also discovered that institutions can be captured, that fraud occurs, and that a consensus can be wrong. The remedy on offer is the same method, applied again. There is no external guarantee.

The history is worth telling because it warns against two errors. One error is that science is a modern opinion, replaceable by an older story that feels better. The other is that science is a finished authority. It is a way of being wrong in public, with measurement attached, so that the next wrongness is smaller.

The method did not arrive on a single date. Aristotle collected observations and built systems. He also trusted the systems past the point where new observations should have corrected them. The Islamic golden age preserved Greek work, advanced algebra and optics, and insisted in its best practitioners on testing. Medieval European universities taught logic and natural philosophy and, at their best, disputed rather than only recited. The ingredients were old. The sustained habit of letting a measurement kill a beautiful idea was rarer.

The seventeenth century made the habit institutional. Scientific societies published results so that others could repeat them. Instruments, the telescope, the microscope, the air pump, the precise clock, extended the senses. Newton’s Principia showed that a mathematical law could cover heaven and Earth and could be used to predict. Prediction was the new prestige. An idea that predicted a return, a position, or a measurement earned a kind of trust that an idea which only explained the past did not.

Later centuries extended the habit into chemistry, geology, and biology. Chemistry became quantitative. Geology accepted deep time because the rocks required it. Biology accepted evolution because the pattern of life required it, and later found the mechanism. The nineteenth century also saw the beginning of statistical thinking, which allowed science to deal with variation rather than only with clean laws. The twentieth century saw the habit applied to the very small and the very large, and saw it fail, temporarily, where ideology overrode measurement. The failures are part of the history. They are why the social structure of criticism matters as much as the intelligence of the practitioners.

Fraud, error, and fashion exist. Results are withdrawn. Fields have pursued dead ends with confidence. The correction mechanism is slow and real: replication, peer criticism, and the eventual demand that a claim meet the world. The mechanism is imperfect. It is better than the alternatives that have been tried, which include authority, revelation, and the uncriticized intuition of clever people. A reader should trust the method more than any one result, and should trust a result more when independent lines of evidence agree.

The history also shows that science is done by people in societies. Funding, war, institutions, and accident shape what gets studied. They do not, in the long run, decide what is true. The expansion of the universe was not a political outcome. The structure of DNA was not a national one. Remembering the human setting prevents a false purity. Remembering the constraint of measurement prevents a false reduction of science to power. Both errors are available. The record supports neither.

Replication is the part of the method that readers hear about when it fails. In several fields, a fraction of published results do not replicate. The causes include small samples, flexible analysis, publication bias toward positive results, and occasional fraud. The response has been more preregistration, larger samples, open data, and a cultural shift toward treating replication as contribution. The existence of a replication problem in some fields does not infect every result in every science. Particle physics and molecular biology have different standards and different failure modes. The lesson is local vigilance, not global cynicism. The method includes the correction. Using the correction is the ongoing work.

Instruments are the forgotten half of the method. The telescope, the microscope, the balance, the spectroscope, the cloud chamber, the sequencer, and the gravitational-wave interferometer each opened a domain that argument alone could not reach. A history of science that follows only ideas understates the dependence on tools. Ideas suggested where to look. Tools decided what could be seen. The present frontiers are frontiers in part because the tools to cross them are new or do not yet exist. Building the tool is often the scientific act.

Openness is a design choice with a scientific effect. Results that are published in full, with data, can be checked. Results that are withheld cannot. The choice to publish was part of the method’s success. It allowed strangers to find errors. It also allowed the method to scale beyond a circle of acquaintances. Current arguments about open access, about preprints, and about data sharing are arguments about how to keep that property as the volume of science grows. The property is not automatic. It is maintained by norms and by infrastructure. Letting it erode would change the method, not only the business model of journals.

title: Mathematics, Humanity's Language
paras: Mathematics is not only a tool science uses. It is the language in which the most reliable descriptions of nature are written.

A falling apple and an orbiting Moon are the same equation. A vibrating string and a quantum wave function share a structure. The usefulness of mathematics in physics has been called unreasonable. It may be less mysterious than it sounds. We keep the mathematics that matches the world and discard the rest. The match is still striking. Imaginary numbers, invented for algebra, became the natural language of quantum mechanics. Geometries invented for their own interest became candidates for the shape of space.

Mathematics is also where certainty has a different meaning. A proof, once checked, does not expire. The infinitude of primes is not waiting on the next survey. This certainty is bought by talking about defined objects rather than about rocks. The application to rocks is a further step, and it can fail even when the proof stands.

Computation changed the subject without ending it. Proofs can be formalized and checked by machines. Conjectures can be tested to vast numbers, which is evidence and not proof. Mathematical biology, climate models, and cryptographic protocols are mathematics applied where the older guides had only physics in mind. Statistics is the mathematics of uncertainty, and much of what this book reports, from genomes to galaxies, arrives as a statistical claim. Knowing what a confidence interval is has become part of literacy.

None of this makes mathematics identical to the world. The map can be perfect and the terrain different. It does explain why a book about reality keeps becoming a book about equations, and why the equations, when they are right, outlast the words around them.

title: Information Theory
paras: In 1948 Claude Shannon gave information a unit. A bit is a distinction between two equally likely possibilities. Surprise can be measured. A message can be compressed down to its uncertainty, and sent through a noisy channel up to a calculable rate, with errors driven as low as desired. The theory was about telephones. It turned out to be about much else.

Biology noticed. DNA is a sequence, and sequences carry information in Shannon's sense as well as in the organism's. The genome is not only a chemical. It is a message, copied with error, compressed by evolution into a form that a cell can unfold. Neuroscience noticed. Perception can be studied as the reduction of uncertainty about the world. Physics noticed. Entropy, the disorder of thermodynamics, is information in disguise, a count of the arrangements a system might be in. Black holes, remarkably, have an entropy proportional to the area of their horizons, a clue that space and information are more intimate than they look.

The practical face of the theory is the digital world. Error-correcting codes make disks, phones, and spacecraft reliable. Compression makes transmission cheap. Cryptography, a cousin of the field, makes transmission private. The limits Shannon proved are still the limits. You cannot compress below the entropy and keep everything. You cannot signal faster than the channel allows and keep the errors down. Engineering lives inside those walls and has furnished the rooms lavishly.

Information theory also disciplines talk about knowledge. A scientific measurement is a reduction of uncertainty. A claim that cannot, even in principle, change what you expect to observe carries no information about the world. That standard will not settle every argument. It will retire some.

Shannon’s definition was operational. He asked how much a message can be compressed, and how fast it can be sent through a noisy channel with arbitrarily small error. The answers are the entropy and the channel capacity. Entropy measures uncertainty. A fair coin has one bit. A biased coin has less. A message can be compressed, on average, down to its entropy and not below, if everything is to be kept. A channel can carry information up to its capacity and not above, if the errors are to be driven down. These are theorems. Engineering lives inside them.

The theorems explain the shape of the digital world. Error-correcting codes make communication and storage reliable by adding structured redundancy. Compression removes unstructured redundancy. Together they are why a video can cross an ocean and arrive intact, and why a disk can hold what it holds. Cryptography, adjacent to the field, uses related mathematics to make a message unreadable without a key. The limits remain. You cannot get reliable communication above capacity. You cannot compress below entropy and keep the content.

Biology found the same currency. DNA is a sequence with redundancy and with meaning. Mutations are noise. The genetic code has a structure that reduces the effect of some errors. Evolution can be described as a process that accumulates information about the environment in the genome, in the limited sense that the genome becomes a record of what worked. The description is not a replacement for natural selection. It is a way of measuring one of its results. Cells also process information in real time: signaling pathways are networks that transform inputs into outputs. The analogy with circuits is useful and incomplete. Cells are noisy, slow, and evolved, not designed.

Physics found information at the base of thermodynamics. Entropy, in Boltzmann’s sense, counts the microscopic arrangements consistent with a macroscopic state. Shannon’s entropy and Boltzmann’s entropy are formally the same kind of quantity. The connection became sharper with black holes. A black hole has an entropy proportional to the area of its horizon, not to its volume. The proportionality is a clue that the information content of a region of space may be related to its surface. Arguments about whether information is lost when matter falls into a black hole have driven work in quantum gravity. The arguments are unresolved. They illustrate how far a theory of messages has reached.

The discipline information theory imposes on talk is valuable. A claim that cannot change any probability you assign to an observation carries no information about the world. It may carry other kinds of meaning. It does not carry empirical content. Science is the practice of preferring claims that do. The preference will not rank every sentence. It will retire the ones that are compatible with anything, and it will force the ones that remain to say what they expect.

The extension of information language to every subject is a fashion that the theory itself can discipline. Not every use of the word “information” refers to Shannon’s quantity. Sometimes it means knowledge, sometimes meaning, sometimes data. The quantity is precise. The metaphors are loose. Where the quantity can be defined and measured, the theory applies and the limits hold. Where it cannot, the word is a resemblance, not an application. A reader who asks whether the entropy has actually been defined will avoid most of the loose uses. The question is the theory’s gift to the rest of thought.

Compression and understanding are related and distinct. A theory compresses observations. A shorter description that still predicts is a better theory, in a sense Shannon made precise. The connection is real and has been used to compare models. It does not mean that the shortest program is automatically the true theory, or that human understanding is the same as compression. A compressed file is not an explanation. An explanation lets a person see why. Information theory supplies a limit and a measure. It does not supply the understanding by itself. Confusing the measure with the understanding is a modern error. The theory is clearer than the error.

Networks are information made structural. The internet, cellular signaling, and ecological food webs are networks that carry or process information in Shannon’s broad sense or in a related one. The structure affects what can be transmitted and what fails when a node is removed. Network science and information theory meet in the study of robustness and of bottlenecks. The meeting is practical. It informs the design of systems that should survive the loss of parts, and the analysis of systems, like power grids or ecosystems, that sometimes do not. Structure is not decoration. It is a constraint on flow.

title: Future Challenges
paras: The unfinished list is not a secret. It is the table of contents of the journals.

In physics, dark matter, dark energy, the quantum behavior of gravity, the matter-antimatter imbalance, and the masses of the neutrinos remain open. A confirmed quantum theory of gravity would be the largest unification since electromagnetism met optics. None is in hand. String theory and loop quantum gravity are research programs, not results to teach as facts.

In biology, the origin of life, the full circuit diagram of a cell, the basis of consciousness, and the control of aging remain open. Cancer is many diseases, some now treatable, none abolished. Pandemic risk is permanent, because evolution is permanent. Preparedness is a choice.

In Earth science, the rate of ice loss, the stability of circulation, and the response of clouds and ecosystems to further warming are the uncertainties that matter most. They will be smaller in twenty years. The emissions between now and then will have already occurred.

In technology, the alignment of powerful automated systems with human purposes, the safe use of gene editing, and the governance of surveillance are problems of design as much as of discovery. They will not be solved by a single paper.

A challenge is not a reason for gloom. The list of a century ago included the nature of the stars, the structure of the gene, and the cause of infection. Those items moved from mystery to mechanism. The present list is what remains after that success. It is a larger list only because the horizon moved.

The challenges in fundamental physics are specific. Dark matter has been weighed and not identified. Dark energy has been measured and not explained. Quantum gravity has candidates and no experimental confirmation. The matter-antimatter imbalance has a size and no established mechanism. Neutrino masses have a range and an unsettled origin. Each of these is a place where a measurement could change the framework. The framework has survived a great many measurements. It is not immune to the next one.

In biology the challenges are equally specific. The origin of life lacks a demonstrated pathway. The cell is not fully mapped: many genes have functions that are partial or unknown, and the interactions are incompletely known. Development, the process that builds a body from an egg, is understood in outline in model organisms and not in anything like complete circuit detail. Consciousness is unsolved in the sense already discussed. Aging is a set of processes with partial interventions. Cancer is many diseases, some now treatable. These are not vague frontiers. They are jobs with tools assigned to them.

Earth science faces a different kind of challenge: a system that can be measured and that is being changed while it is measured. The rate of ice-sheet loss, the stability of major circulations, the response of clouds, and the capacity of ecosystems to adapt or to fail are the uncertainties that dominate practical risk. They will be better known in twenty years. The emissions of those twenty years will already have been added. The challenge is scientific and temporal at once.

Technology’s challenges include the alignment and reliability of increasingly capable automated systems, the safe and equitable use of gene editing, the governance of surveillance that cheap computation makes possible, and the management of biological tools that are spreading as they cheapen. These are not purely technical. They have technical components. A system that cannot be understood by its operators, or a genetic change that cannot be confined, is a technical problem before it is a political one. The political one remains after the technical one is addressed.

The list is longer than a list from 1900 because the horizon moved. It is not longer because knowledge failed. The successes of the last century created new questions at a higher resolution. That is the ordinary progress of a science that works. A reader who finds the list daunting can equally find it a map of the interesting jobs. Both reactions fit the same facts.

Coordination is the meta-challenge. Several of the problems, climate, pandemic surveillance, the governance of powerful technologies, are shared. Shared problems require shared measurement and some degree of shared rule. The measurement is the scientific part. The rule is the political part. Science can supply the measurement and cannot supply the agreement. Pretending that the measurement settles the agreement leads to backlash. Pretending that disagreement about the agreement undermines the measurement leads to confusion. The two should be kept in their own columns. This book has tried to keep them so.

Some challenges are chosen and some are imposed. Dark matter is imposed: the measurements require an answer. A particular design of a technology is chosen: societies decide whether to build it. Treating chosen challenges as if they were laws of nature removes the responsibility for the choice. Treating imposed challenges as if they were optional delays the measurement. The list in this chapter mixes the two. Marking which is which is a useful habit. It keeps the sciences from being blamed for choices and keeps choices from being disguised as science.

Time scales differ, and the difference matters for action. A particle-physics experiment may take decades to build and run. A pandemic response has weeks. Climate policy has years to affect a trajectory that plays out over centuries. Treating every challenge as if it had the same urgency, or the same patience, misallocates effort. The sciences can say something about the time scales. They cannot rank the moral urgency. A reader who separates the time scale from the urgency will read both the science and the politics more clearly. The separation is a tool. It belongs with the other tools this book has offered.

title: Possible Futures
paras: Prediction is the weakest chapter in any science guide. It is included because readers will make one anyway, and a disciplined guess is better than a mood.

Some trends are sturdy. Computation will continue to cheapen for a while, then meet physical limits that shift the problem to architecture and energy. Biotechnology will continue to read and write genomes more cheaply. The climate will continue to warm until emissions fall to near zero and for some time after, because the ocean is slow. Population growth is slowing. Several large countries are already shrinking. The human future is not, by default, a graph of endless increase.

Some branches depend on choices. A world that builds nuclear plants, transmission lines, and renewable capacity looks different from a world that argues about them for another generation. A world that treats pandemic surveillance as infrastructure looks different from a world that rebuilds it after each outbreak. A world that develops machine intelligence inside serious constraints looks different from a world that does not.

The far branches should be labeled as speculation. Self-replicating industry on the Moon, a permanent Martian settlement, a life expectancy of a hundred and twenty healthy years, contact with another civilization: each is possible in the thin sense that no law forbids it. None is a baseline. Contact, in particular, remains a blank. The search has found no signal that survives scrutiny. Absence of evidence at our present reach is not evidence of absence across the galaxy. It is a limit on our listening.

The useful stance is the one the preface recommended. Reduce uncertainty where you can. Do not pretend that a scenario is a measurement. The future is a set of trajectories consistent with the laws in this book, narrowed by decisions. The laws will hold. The decisions are not the laws.

Some forecasts are constrained by demographics and by physics. Population growth is slowing. Several large countries have fertility below replacement and will shrink unless offset by migration. Aging populations change the economics of health and of work. Climate warming will continue until net emissions are near zero, and sea level will continue longer. These are not speculations in the free sense. They are consequences of present measurements and of inertia.

Energy and computation have trajectories that are sturdy and not infinite. The cost of solar and wind electricity has fallen for decades and will meet limits of materials, land, and grid before it meets a limit of sunlight. The cost of computation has fallen for decades and will meet limits of energy and of the physics of switches. Both can continue to improve in usefulness after the raw curves flatten, through better design. Neither will improve without bound on the old curve. Plans that assume the old curve forever are plans that will be revised.

Biotechnology’s trajectory is toward cheaper reading and writing of genomes and toward more precise cell therapies. The consequences depend on regulation and on what is done with the tools. A world that uses them for therapies and for more productive crops looks different from a world that uses them for unconstrained ecological release or for enhancement that only the wealthy can buy. The tools do not select the world. Decisions do.

Machine intelligence is the forecast with the widest error bar. Current systems are capable and unreliable. Future systems may be more capable and more reliable, or the present limits may prove stubborn. The social effects of even the present systems are still being absorbed. A forecast that treats a particular level of capability as inevitable by a particular year is not a scientific claim. A forecast that the cheapening of cognitive tasks will matter is already confirmed.

Settlement beyond Earth, contact with another civilization, and radical extension of human lifespan are possible in the sense that no known law forbids them. They are not baseline.
