Contact in particular is a blank. The search has produced no confirmed signal. The silence constrains the density and the loudness of technological civilizations within our listening range. It does not decide whether any exist. The correct statement is ignorance, bounded by the search so far.

The useful attitude toward the future is the attitude this book has taken toward the present. Prefer the measurement. Name the uncertainty. Update when the measurement changes. Scenarios are tools for thinking. They are not findings. The laws in the earlier chapters will hold. The choices will determine which of the lawful futures is the one people inhabit.

Histories of prediction are humbling. Forecasts of flight, of nuclear power, of computing, and of space have been early, late, and wrong in detail even when right in outline. The outline that survives is usually the one tied to a cost curve or to a demographic fact. The detail that fails is usually a date or a social assumption. A reader can take the constrained outlines in this chapter more seriously than the speculative branches, and can take both less seriously than the measurements in the earlier chapters. The order of trust is the order of contact with evidence.

Branching is the honest picture. At each point where a cost curve, a regulation, or a discovery can go more than one way, the future forks. Some forks rejoin, because physics constrains them. Some diverge. A single narrative future is a storytelling convenience. It is not what the evidence supports. The evidence supports a set of trajectories, weighted by what is already in motion, and open where decisions have not been made. Holding the set, rather than adopting a favorite member of it, is the discipline this chapter recommends.

Agency is unevenly distributed and real. Most people cannot choose the outcome of a research program. Collectively, through institutions, people choose funding, regulation, and infrastructure. Those choices select among the lawful futures. The selection is not fine-grained. It is enough to bend trajectories. A passive reading of the future, in which technology arrives and society adapts, understates the selection. An inflated reading, in which any future can be chosen, understates the constraints. The middle is the accurate place. Constraints bind. Choices select. The future chapters of a later guide will record which selections were made.

title: What Would Change in the Guides
paras: Isaac the earlier guides. They told an educated reader what the sciences had established, in prose that did not sneer and did not flatter, and they separated fact from guess. A guide with the same job today would keep most of his structure. Mechanics, chemistry, the cell, evolution, and the Solar System have not been repealed. It would replace chapters, and add chapters, where the world has changed under the book.

Entirely new chapters would be required for subjects that did not exist as settled fields. CRISPR and gene editing. mRNA medicine. The human microbiome. Gravitational waves as an observed phenomenon, not only a prediction. Exoplanets as a catalog rather than a hope. Dark energy. Quantum information. Artificial intelligence in the form of learned systems and large language models. The modern science of climate change, as measurement rather than as a paragraph of caution. Synthetic biology.

Other chapters would need to be rewritten rather than added. The origin of the universe, which the earlier guides. The gene, which he explained as a molecular discovery, is now a sequence that can be ordered, edited, and interpreted in the clinic. The brain, which he described anatomically, is now a system that can be recorded in large parts and perturbed in animals cell by cell. The periodic table is intact, and nanomaterials have been added to what the elements can be made to do.

He would also change the tone in a few places, if he followed his own rule of updating. He would be more cautious about simple forecasts of the year 2000, because several of his missed and several arrived early. He would treat computers as a scientific instrument, not as a curiosity of mathematics. He would give more room to what is not known, because the unknowns are now sharper. Dark matter is a better mystery than the old mystery of whether other galaxies existed. A sharp mystery is progress.

The aim of the present book is the aim of those guides. A single account, readable without a laboratory, of what an educated person should know about the world as science currently describes it. Not final truths. The present picture. Actually.
the earlier guides. A contemporary following that method would keep the architecture of his guides and replace the chapters the world has outgrown.

He would add chapters that had no stable subject in his time. CRISPR, because gene editing became cheap and specific. mRNA medicine, because a platform vaccine was designed from a sequence and deployed at global scale. The microbiome, because the microbial communities in and on the body moved from curiosity to organ. Gravitational waves, because they were detected and became a branch of astronomy. Exoplanets, because the census went from zero to thousands. Dark energy, because the acceleration was measured. Quantum information, because entanglement became a technology as well as a puzzle. Artificial intelligence, because learned systems became general tools. Climate science, because the warming and its cause became a detailed measurement. Synthetic biology, because genomes became files that can be ordered.

He would rewrite chapters he already had. The universe chapter would gain a standard model, a precise age, and named tensions. The atom chapter would gain quarks, the Higgs, and a completed inventory of the Standard Model, together with a clear statement of what the Model does not contain. The life chapters would gain a sequenced human genome, a far more detailed account of regulation, and a practical gene-editing technology. The brain chapter would gain large-scale recording, optogenetics in animals, and a clearer separation between the correlates of consciousness and the unsolved hard problem. The materials chapter would gain nanomaterials and a semiconductor industry that fabricates at the scale of atoms.

He would also change the tone in places, following his own rule. Forecasts in his earlier books were sometimes early and sometimes late. A later book would be more careful with dates and more willing to say that a capability exists without saying when a consequence will arrive. Computers would be treated as scientific instruments, not as curiosities. The unknown would be given more room, because the unknowns are sharper. Dark matter is a better mystery than the old mystery of other galaxies, because dark matter is required by measurements that are already in hand. A sharp mystery is a sign that the subject has moved.

The purpose of the present book is the purpose of those guides. One account, readable without a laboratory, of what an educated person should know about the world as the sciences currently describe it. Not a monument of certainty. A picture, dated, and open to correction. Actually.

One more change is worth naming. the earlier guides. The sciences have since grown further apart in their techniques. A single voice is harder and more necessary. Harder, because no one can be current at the frontier of every field. More necessary, because the educated reader still needs the picture in one place, with the joints between fields visible. This book is an attempt at that place. It will be wrong in particulars. It will have succeeded if a reader finishes it knowing what is established, what is open, and how the two are told apart.

Updating is part of the form. A guide that cannot be revised is a monument. A guide that is revised whenever a result changes is a tool. the earlier guides. A successor should be revised too. The present book is dated by its figures, by its account of tensions, and by the state of technologies that move quickly. The dates are a feature. They tell a later reader what was known when the book was written. They invite the correction. A book about science that feared correction would have misunderstood its subject.

The voice is a choice. the earlier guides. The present book has adopted that choice. Other voices are possible: more mathematical, more historical, more personal. The test of the choice is whether a reader who is not a specialist can finish a chapter knowing more than at the start, and knowing the difference between the solid and the open. If the book meets that test, the voice has done its job. If it does not, the voice is a surface. The surface is not the point. The point is the picture, and the honesty of its edges.

title: The Arrow of Time
paras: The fundamental dynamical laws are time-reversal invariant. The observed world is not. Entropy increases. We remember the past and not the future. The asymmetry is the arrow of time.

The thermodynamic arrow is the increase of entropy. It originates in the low-entropy initial condition of the universe. The early universe was smooth. Smoothness is a low-entropy state for the gravitational field. Subsequent clumping into stars, galaxies and black holes raises the entropy. The psychological arrow—the fact that memory and records point toward the past—aligns with the thermodynamic arrow because records form only when entropy increases.

The cosmological arrow is the expansion itself. Expansion does not by itself define a direction of increasing entropy. A contracting universe with the same low-entropy boundary condition would still possess a thermodynamic arrow pointing away from that boundary. Why the initial entropy was low remains unexplained. Proposals include special initial conditions, inflationary smoothing and selection effects. None is established. The existence of the arrow is nevertheless an observed fact about the solution we inhabit.

title: Black Holes
paras: A black hole is a region of spacetime in which gravity is strong enough that nothing, not even light, can escape to distant observers. The boundary is the event horizon. For a non-rotating black hole the horizon radius is the Schwarzschild radius, \( R_s = 2GM/c^2 \). For the Sun that radius is about three kilometers. For Earth it is about nine millimeters. Ordinary matter is not compressed to those densities. Stellar cores above a limiting mass can collapse past the point of no return.

Inside the horizon all future-directed paths lead deeper. At the center of the simplest solutions lies a singularity where curvature becomes infinite and the classical theory fails. Quantum gravity is expected to modify the singularity. No complete theory yet exists. Outside the horizon the spacetime is well described by general relativity. Orbits, lensing, and the motion of nearby stars match the predictions.

Black holes form from the collapse of massive stars and from the mergers of smaller black holes. They grow by accretion and by further mergers. Supermassive black holes, millions to billions of solar masses, occupy the centers of most large galaxies. The Event Horizon Telescope has imaged the shadow of the black hole in M87 and in the Milky Way. Gravitational-wave detectors have recorded the mergers of stellar-mass black holes. The objects are no longer hypothetical.

Hawking radiation is a quantum effect near the horizon. Virtual pairs are separated. One member falls in. The other escapes. The black hole loses mass. The temperature is inversely proportional to the mass. For stellar-mass black holes the radiation is negligible. For microscopic black holes it would be rapid. No such objects are known. The process raises the information question: whether the radiation returns the information that fell in. The question is unresolved.

title: Hawking Radiation
paras: In 1974 Hawking showed that a black hole emits thermal radiation. The calculation combines quantum field theory with the curved spacetime of a collapsing star. Near the horizon, vacuum fluctuations produce pairs of particles. One member of a pair falls inward. The other escapes to infinity. The escaping flux has a thermal spectrum. The temperature is \( T = \hbar c^3 / (8\pi G M k_B) \). It is inversely proportional to the mass.

For a solar-mass black hole the temperature is far below the cosmic microwave background. The hole absorbs more than it emits. A black hole of mountain mass or smaller would be hotter than its surroundings and would lose mass. As it loses mass its temperature rises. The final stages are rapid. The calculation assumes a classical background geometry. It ceases to be reliable when the hole approaches the Planck mass.

The radiation carries energy. The black hole’s mass therefore decreases. The process is slow for astrophysical holes and has not been observed. The theoretical result is accepted. It implies that black holes have a temperature and, by the first law, an entropy. The entropy is one quarter of the horizon area in Planck units. The derivation links gravity, quantum mechanics, and thermodynamics.

title: Dark Matter
paras: Galaxies rotate too fast. The orbital speeds of stars and gas remain high at large radii where the visible mass is insufficient. Clusters of galaxies are likewise too massive for the light they emit. Gravitational lensing maps a mass distribution that extends far beyond the luminous component. The missing mass is called dark matter.

The density of dark matter is approximately five times the density of ordinary baryonic matter. It does not emit, absorb, or scatter light at any observed wavelength. It interacts with ordinary matter primarily through gravity. Candidates include weakly interacting massive particles, axions, and primordial black holes. None has been detected in the laboratory.

On cosmological scales dark matter is required to explain the growth of structure. Baryons alone cannot cluster rapidly enough after recombination. The presence of a cold, non-relativistic dark-matter component allows the observed galaxies and clusters to form. The same component leaves a characteristic imprint on the cosmic microwave background that matches the measured anisotropies.
The nature of the particles remains unknown. Their gravitational effects are established.

title: Dark Energy
paras: The expansion of the universe is accelerating. Type Ia supernovae at high redshift are fainter than expected in a matter-dominated cosmos. The cosmic microwave background and the large-scale distribution of galaxies independently require a component with negative pressure. That component is called dark energy.

The simplest model is a cosmological constant. Its energy density is constant in time and equal to about 70 percent of the present critical density. The equation-of-state parameter is \( w = -1 \). More general models allow \( w \) to vary. Present data are consistent with a constant.

Dark energy dominates the expansion only at late times. In the early universe its density was negligible compared with matter and radiation. The transition to acceleration occurred when the universe was roughly half its present age. The future evolution depends on the nature of the component. A true cosmological constant produces eternal exponential expansion. Other models can lead to a different fate.

No laboratory detection of dark energy exists. Its only observed effects are cosmological. The measured value is many orders of magnitude smaller than the naïve quantum-field-theory estimate. The discrepancy is the cosmological-constant problem. It remains unsolved.
